*Sinners in Zion* returned to this theme with elaborate amplification. From start to finish, the goal of the sermon was fear. It is long, encompassing two preaching units, and was often repeated at later dates. The focus of the original text— and of Edwards' sermon— was less on pagans and infidels than on sinners among the people of God in Zion. These were the worst of sinners, for they ignored the light that was hidden from others;

<!-- p. 33 -->

their fate would be horrific. They would inhabit hell, a place so terrifying that to describe it strained the capacity of language. But not the capacity of Edwards, who exploited language as few before him had done. To approximate the world of hell, he used all the images and metaphors he could invent. Chief of these was the fiery furnace. “Now if a person should be brought to the mouth of such a furnace, and there should see how the fire seemed to glow so as presently to make everything that was cast into it all over white and bright with fire, and should know that he was now directly going to be cast into this furnace, would not fearfulness surprise him?” Indeed it would. But Edwards waited until the very end of the sermon to identify exactly who was poised on the edge of that furnace. With mounting fury he came to the concluding Application, looked out on his congregation, and declared, “*You* are the sinners in Zion!” That pit, he declared, was prepared for the people sitting before him. Hence the invitation: “Will you not now thoroughly awake out of sleep and bestir yourself for your salvation?” (p. 284).

In examining the composition of *Sinners in Zion*, one sees that Edwards was already at work perfecting the style for a Whitefield-like revival sermon. The form would have to promote and encourage extemporaneous delivery, and the content must shift from heaven to hell, from the joys of redemption to the horrors of the damned. In a further step toward freeing up his speech, Edwards began to include large white space breaks in his notes as a signal to extemporize. In place of fully written-out sentences, he began supplying simple but potent rhetorical cues: “You are warned by it”; “You are invited by it.”

#### A Second Sinners

About half a year after preaching *Sinners in Zion*, Edwards preached another sermon on sinners: *Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God*. It is not clear what effect this *Sinners* had on his own congregation. Probably not much. They, after all, had heard its substance only two weeks before. Awakening sermons often require unfamiliar audiences and spontaneous delivery. Certainly no reports exist of exceptional responses. But the next time he preached it, at Enfield, Massachusetts, on July 8, the effects were extraordinary.

Enfield had gained a reputation as a stubbornly unawakened town, seemingly proud in its ability to resist the Spirit. So when Edwards was called in, a number of ministers came to see whether he could melt the congregations' hard hearts. Eleazar Wheelock was one witness to the

<!-- p. 34 -->

showdown. He reported that before Edwards started his address, “the people hardly conducted themselves with common decency.” But that changed very quickly. “Before the sermon was ended,” Wheelock recalled, “the assembly appeared deeply impressed and bowed down, with an awful conviction of their sin and danger.”[^005-note63] The Reverend Stephen Williams of nearby Longmeadow also attended and recorded the event in his diary with striking immediacy:

went over to Enfd - where we met Dear Mr E - of N. H. - who preachd a most awakening Sermon from those words Deut - 32.35 - and before ye Sermon was done there was a great moaning - & crying out throught ye whole House - what shall I do to be Savd - oh I am going to Hell -. oh what shall I do for a christ &c &c - So yt ye minister - was obligd to desist - shreiks & crys - were piercing & Amazing - after Some time of waiting - the congregation were still So yt a prayr was made by Mr W - & after that we descendd from the pulpitt and discoursd - with the people - Some in one place & Some in another - and Amazing & Astonishing - ye powr - God was Seen - &c Severall Souls were hopfully - wrought upon yt - night & oh ye cheerfullness & pleasntness of thier countenances - yt receivd comfort - oh yt God - wd strengthen & confirm &c - we Sung an hymn & prayd &c despersd - ye Assembly.

Such was the power— and the fear— generated by this sermon that Edwards apparently never finished preaching it— possibly the only time such an interruption had happened to him except for the day several years earlier when the gallery of the old Northampton meetinghouse fell. Reflecting on the sermon, Williams wrote, “I Seemd affectd & movd-ready to dissolve in Tears &c-but cant well tell why.”[^005-note64]

*Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God* is arguably America's greatest sermon. It has been analyzed extensively both in this Edition and in other works.[^005-note65] But what is interesting for our purposes here is not the final text

<!-- p. 35 -->

as it appears in print, but the handwritten notes, reproduced in this volume for the first time. At the end of these handwritten notes is a brief, two-page outline of the sermon that Edwards prepared, probably for multiple deliveries with minimal notes or prompts.[^005-note66] When reading the fragment, as opposed to the fully written-out text, one can discern the almost “perfect idea” of an awakening sermon:

> 1. [Sinners] always exposed to fall. 2. Suddenly fall. 3. By their own weight. 4. Nothing but God that holds 'em up. (1) No want of power in G. (2) They deserve it. (3) They are condemned to it. 'Tis the place they belong to. (4) God is angry enough with them. (5) The devil if not restrained would immediately fly upon them and seize them as his own. (6) They have those hellish principles in them, that if God should take off his restraints. (7) 'Tis no security that there are no visible means of death at hand. (8) Their own care and prudence to preserve their own lives. (9) The schemes they lay out for escaping damnation. (10) There is no promise.

For all the attention paid to *Sinners*, virtually no one has noticed this highly condensed version. It confirms the novelty of the sermon, not only on the level of content and rhetoric in print, but of its extemporaneous abbreviation. Assuming that Edwards delivered this sermon on more than two occasions, we can see this two-page fragment text as the *real sermon*: the highly portable and powerful cue card that allowed multiple deliveries and unprecedented terror. Contained in these two pages was rhetorical dynamite.

Students familiar with *Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God* can read the outline and fill in the blanks as easily as Edwards. All balance is gone; speculative knowledge is peripheral; history is to be made, not understood. Awakening sermons aim to awaken, pure and simple. Only two emotions pertain, fear and rage: fear from the human perspective at the precariousness

<!-- p. 37 -->

of the human condition and the horrors of the devil and hell; rage from the divine vantage point. Edwards is perhaps most terrifying, indeed almost out of control, when speaking for God. God, in Edwards' angry hands, can hardly contain his loathing, anger, and hatred of sinners. “Yea, God is a great deal more angry with great numbers that are now on earth, yea, doubtless with many that are now in this congregation, that it may be are at ease and quiet, than he is with many of those who are now in the flames of hell.… The wrath of God burns against them, their damnation don't slumber, the pit is prepared, the fire is made ready, the furnace is now hot, ready to receive them, the flames do now rage and glow. The glittering sword is whet, and held over them, and the pit hath opened her mouth under them” (p. 406). In this selection and many others, it is grammatically unclear who prepares the pit of unimaginable horror. Is it the devil, as Edwards would have claimed in his more reasoned moments, or God himself? The very characteristics of God and Satan blend into one supernatural fury directed at unrepentant sinners seated— or groveling on the floor— before the preacher.

Pages 2 and 3 of Edwards' later four-page outline for *Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God*, 1741. Courtesy of the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University.

#### Edwards and the Millennium

To keep his congregation focused on the need to preserve the revival spirit, Edwards returned to the themes of history and the worlds of heaven and hell. In *Seasons of Ingathering*, Edwards effectively employed the image of Christ and the angels coming from heaven armed with sickles to separate the saved from the damned. The damned he represented as grapes about to be harvested. The angels would gather the damned and throw them into “the great winepress of God's wrath.” The use of the winepress, Edwards explained, “is to glorify [God's] wrath.… [Hell is] a place every way fitted for the purpose. Everything in it [is] contrived and fitted for that, as all the parts of a winepress are prepared for the making of wine from the grape. 'Tis the grand receptacle of all the vessels of wrath. God has prepared but one place of torment for all the whole universe that {remain impenitent}. There the devils [will torment them].” Lest his hearers not get the point, Edwards applied his text with a warning that hearkened back to earlier days: “God now seems to be withdrawing from many parts of the land. If God should withdraw from us, great calamity will surely come upon the souls of those that are left behind. I warned you before, in the last time of {awakening}, and my words are verified” (p. 488).

Reports of raw emotional excesses and lay exhorting in the revivals circulated rapidly after 1741, and, at first, Edwards sought to minimize them. In a sermon on December 21, *The Curse of Meroz*, he used the battle

<!-- p. 38 -->

of Deborah and Barak with the Canaanites as a type of the time “when that great battle between Christ and his enemies” would occur. With Armageddon in the balance, he pleaded with his congregation not to judge the revivals prematurely by their side effects. In words that anticipated his treatises on *Some Thoughts Concerning the Revival* and *Religious Affections*, he urged that the revivals not be judged by heightened bodily agitations. “'Tis no wonder at all that some are carried something beyond themselves.… There are undoubtedly imprudences and errors that attend the work of God, and always will be.… But must we therefore always harp upon them?” (p. 507).

If Edwards was captivated by history, it was not the history of America. Earlier accounts that seek to identify Edwards with an American (i.e. New England) exceptionalism miss the degree to which New England and America as discrete entities hardly figured in his earth narrative. For a brief moment in the height of the revivals, he turned his attention homeward to America as the possible seat of God's new heavens and new earth at the end of history. But this proved to be a passing speculation. Not only was America too small for his history, but earth itself had to take its place in a larger cosmos.

Related to exceptionalism is typology. Much has been made of Edwards' fascination with this exegetical discipline. Natural tropes as types elicited his most lyrical prose, for they fused the worlds of heaven and hell, creation and redemption. But the use of typology for nationalistic reasons, common with many Puritans before him, is not present. In none of his speculations did Edwards identify America or New England as *the New* Israel, the antitype for which ancient Israel was the type. And, except for the brief speculation in 1741, in no sense was New England the “vanguard of universal history.”[^005-note67] For Edwards, God's New Israel was the universal and invisible body of Christ— believers everywhere united in a “concert of prayer” for God's triumphant reign.

In the heat of Whitefield's tour, Edwards dared to hope (“posit” would be too strong a term) that “what is now seen in America, and especially in New England, may prove the dawn of that glorious day: and the very uncommon and wonderful circumstances and events of this work, seem to me strongly to argue that God intends it as the beginning or forerunner

<!-- p. 39 -->

of something vastly great.”[^005-note68] Except for this brief American-centered enthusiasm, Edwards always understood the millennium and the church in universal terms. However optimistic about “God's mighty power” at work, the vast majority of Edwards' pronouncements on the subject of the millennium preclude claims of an American exceptionalism. For instance, the April 1741 sermon *Importunate Prayer for Millennial Glory* was universal in its orientation. From revivals at home and abroad, Edwards proclaimed that “now God seems in his providence, in an especial manner, to be calling us to be ready for those [end] times.” But where were they to commence? The answer was, *everywhere*. From letters and magazines Edwards could document “so remarkable a pouring out of the Spirit of God in many places and the commotion the nations of the world seem to be in” (p. 372). Northampton believers should not be deluded into thinking they were the center of God's plans. They remained too ignorant of the “state of God's church in general.”

#### Occasional Sermons

Of course, revivals were not the only activities in this period. Part of every colonial preacher's life was the need to devise occasional sermons, and these continued month in and month out. Occasional sermons have only recently been understood for their unique place in the community, encompassing a variety of events from ordinations to funerals to fasts and thanksgivings. Fasts and thanksgivings represented especially important weekday occasions when ministers could address themselves to temporal and secular affairs. Of these, none were more pressing than war. In time, revival enthusiasm would wane and energies turn to war.

Edwards was a patriot as much as a revivalist, and in his military preaching one finds many themes common to all Puritan ministers, with one important distinction. To an uncommon extent he introduced angels into his occasional sermons no less than his regular preaching. In *God's Care for His Servants in Time of Public Commotions*, a fast-day sermon “for success in war, Feb. 26, 1741,” Edwards selected an apocalyptic text from Revelation 7:1-03 that featured four angels standing on the four corners of the earth. These angels, Edwards stated, serve under “command sent from heaven,” and God “makes use of the ministration of angels in regulating those events.” Again Edwards rehearsed profane history when, in the days after

<!-- p. 40 -->

Constantine, the angels “had commission to hurt the earth and the sea.” To supply hope, Edwards employs the prophecy in Revelation to assure his listeners that God will not allow great destruction until his “seal” is on the foreheads of all his saints. Mixing revival with war, Edwards was pleased to report: “We see that the angel that has the seal of the living God is very busy: his sealing work goes on in these American plantations; many are sealed daily in one place and another.… So we hear it has been in Pennsylvania, and in Carolina and Georgia, and in the Jerseys and New York, and in Boston.… God is taking care that the elect may not be hurt” (p. 359). Two months later Edwards delivered another fast-day sermon entitled *Importunate Prayer for Millennial Glory*. True to form, Edwards' focus here was not New England or America, but “the world.”

#### Second Thoughts

In June 1741, Edwards approved limited lay exhorting in a letter to Deborah Hatheway, an eighteen-year-old convert from Suffield who had no pastor to counsel her. In his advice, Edwards allowed lay exhortation on a private level and, in some circumstances, to larger circles: “I would advise you especially, to be much in exhorting children and young women your equals; and when you exhort others that are men, I would advise that you take opportunities for it, chiefly when you are alone with them, or when only young persons are present.” In a later letter to Deacon Moses Lyman, formerly of Northampton, Edwards conceded that while the revivals carried “some imprudences and irregularities,” yet “as to the work in general, they have all the clear and incontestable evidences of a true divine work.” As for the great “outcry against ministers riding about to preach the gospel,” such practices were neither novel nor wrong. In fact, most traveling clergy that he was aware of “scarcely ever are absent from their people on the sabbath.”[^005-note69]

Later that year Edwards appeared less sanguine about itinerants, whether lay or clerical. With spring thaw, a handful of ordained and lay itinerants had begun crisscrossing the region. The most famous was Gilbert Tennent. Settled ministers, even friends of the revivals like Edwards, were nervous about the direction revivals seemed to be taking. Increasingly, physical outworkings, accompanied by visions and trances, predominated. Many lay people began to identify these bodily effects as signs of regeneration.

<!-- p. 41 -->

The most sensational reports were of the young James Davenport, scion of a noble ministerial family and the youngest graduate in the history of Yale College. By 1741 his campaign for “saving” Connecticut moved into high gear. Claiming special powers of discernment, he routinely accosted settled clergy and labeled them “unconverted”— a term that was first widely applied to New England clergy by Whitefield. Davenport's campaign began in New London and moved from there up and down the Connecticut shoreline. In August his travels brought him to New Haven and to Yale, where he proceeded to harangue the minister Joseph Noyes as “an unconverted hypocrite and the devil incarnate.”[^005-note70]

The week following Davenport's denunciation of Noyes— and Yale— Edwards was scheduled to preach the commencement sermon to the faculty and students of Yale College. In circumstances as grave and portentous as his famous Boston lecture of 1731, *God Glorified in the Work of Redemption*, Edwards turned his attention entirely to the history-making present. He titled his sermon *The Distinguishing Marks of a Work of the Spirit of God*. The sermon echoed his earlier Northampton sermons *The Curse of Meroz* and *Keeping the Presence of God*, balancing warnings with an overall assessment of the revivals as a work of God. But this time, he spent considerably more time on the errors of the revival and the false signs that a seeming work of God was legitimate. Knowing the mood of Yale's faculty, he devoted long sections to “negative signs” of true revival, many of which had occurred in the immediate experience of his listeners. For the first time, he introduced the devil at some length, noting how Satan could mimic and induce many of the same signs of grace that true Christians sought as evidence of their justification. Bodily agitations, lively imaginations, and excessive fright— all were negative signs of a work of God.

Yet, when Edwards had laid the sum of the distinguishing marks in the balance, he backed away from his assault on the negative signs and pronounced the revivals in New England a work of God. How did he know? Because of the “positive signs” everywhere that could not be imitated by the devil. These included a heightened esteem for the risen Christ, a discernible change in way of life, a love of holy Scripture, a thirsting after doctrine and speculative knowledge of God's dealings with creation, and, most important, a new sense of love for God and humankind. Knowing his particular audience, as well as his own mind, Edwards laid particular emphasis on the need for “human learning” in the salvation process: “'Tis

<!-- p. 42 -->

too manifest to be denied, that God made great use of human learning in the apostle Paul, as he also did in Moses and Solomon.” With positive signs factored in, Edwards could only conclude “that that extraordinary influence that has lately appeared on the minds of the people abroad in this land… is undoubtedly, in the general, from the Spirit of God.”[^005-note71]

Yale's faculty were not persuaded. Having just been burned, first by Whitefield and then by their own Davenport, they could not share their former colleague's bright assessment of the state of religion in the land. The fervor remained too censorious and confrontational for it to be a work of God. Even their own students were a case in point of the religious climate's negative effects, and none more than the Yale College Class of 1741. Included in this group were Samuel Hopkins, destined to be Edwards' most prolific disciple; Samuel Buell, a soon-to-be evangelist par excellence in Northampton, of all places; and David Brainerd, who was expelled during his sophomore year after proclaiming that Chauncey Whittelsey, tutor in the college, had “no more grace than a chair.”

But beyond Yale, Edwards' commencement address proved to be a rhetorical triumph and was immediately forwarded to the press by the friends of the revivals in Boston and London. Partly because of their response to Whitefield, but even more in response to his native imitators, the clergy of New England had divided widely over whether the revivals were a work of God.[^005-note72] Many New Light friends of the revivals needed a moderate champion like Edwards, who was a strenuous advocate of revival but also firmly anchored in the Standing Order and ministerial elite. In the past, Edwards had sided with the elites against popular radicals. Throughout the 1730s, Mark Valeri observes, “Edwards focused his critique against popular discontent and sanctioned the social values of stability and deference, as a defense of, *inter alia*, his own social location. He himself was a member of the town's elite by blood, education, profession, and temperament.”[^005-note73] Edwards would do so again in the 1740s.

By January 1742, Edwards was worrying anew that Northampton was lagging. In a letter to his colleague Joseph Bellamy, he confessed that “religion in this and the neighboring towns has now of late been on the decaying hand.” Still, there was a bright spot: the youth continued to flourish. “There has been the year past the most wonderful work amongst

<!-- p. 43 -->

children here, by far, that ever was: God has seemed almost wholly to take a new generation, that are come on since the late great work seven years ago.”[^005-note74]

At the same time that apathy and contention were on the rise in Northampton, religious enthusiasm was reaching unprecedented heights in the aftermath of the activities of James Davenport and his associates. A concerned Edwards began to back off his encouragement of itinerancy— especially lay itinerancy. In part the choice was taken out of his hands when Connecticut passed legislation outlawing the practice. But beyond that, his own misgivings grew. In a second letter to Moses Lyman, in May 1742, he shared his reservations, especially over lay exhorting, no matter how sincerely grounded: “I hope you will consider the matter, and for the future avoid doing thus. You ought to do what you can by private, brotherly, humble admonitions and counsels; but 'tis too much for you to exhort public congregations, or solemnly to set yourself by set speech to counsel a room full of people, unless it be children.… Such things have done a vast mischief in the country.”[^005-note75]

In February 1742, a downhearted Edwards left for a two-week preaching tour around Leicester, Massachusetts. In his absence he appointed the recently graduated Samuel Buell to fill the Northampton pulpit. To Edwards' simultaneous joy and dismay, Buell proceeded to set the congregation on fire in a way Edwards had done in Enfield but not in his own Northampton. People cried out in meeting, and, as Edwards later described it, “the whole town seemed to be in a great and continual commotion, day and night.” He cautiously confirmed that the town's enthusiasm was “such in some respects as I never saw it in before.” Still, there were limitations: the greatest enthusiasm “was principally among professors; the appearances of a work of conversion were in no measure equal to what had been the summer before.” Buell stayed on for several weeks after Edwards' return, and their combined efforts were rewarded with “a very great revival of religion.”[^005-note76]

Meanwhile, extremes multiplied. Individuals were having visions and going into trances, lying motionless for twenty-four hours at a time. Among these was Edwards' wife, Sarah Pierpont Edwards, whose narrative of her ecstatic religious experience during this period so impressed her husband that he later used it— though in a sanitized form so as to divert criticism— in *Some Thoughts Concerning the Revival*. But other enthusiasts caused concern.

<!-- p. 44 -->

“When the people were raised to this height,” Edwards worried, “Satan took the advantage, and his interposition in many instances soon became very apparent: and a great deal of caution and pains were found necessary to keep the people, many of them, from running wild.”[^005-note77]

In mid-March Edwards sought a different avenue to build on the momentum, drafting a covenant renewal for the church. Covenant renewal had been used in New England churches since the late seventeenth century as a means of renewing loyalties to the religious and social ideals of the Puritan experiment. In essence, members of the church recovenanted, or rededicated, themselves through a document that affirmed their determination to follow the ways of God as a congregation. After the draft had been vetted by the church's “principal men,” the deacons, and the town's religious societies, the minister would lead “the people into a solemn public renewal of their covenant with God.”

To pursue covenant renewal at this time was a logical step for Edwards. Fifteen years of weekly preaching had taken its toll. His powerful rhetoric had spent its course, strains with the town elders were becoming increasingly personal. Even his wife was no longer exempt from criticism of her dress and style. If Edwards could not preach revival effectively, he could at least ritualize renewal. Covenant renewal rituals provided another means of reasserting the power of the church (and minister) over members' lives. But more pressing, these acts could renew and channel revival fervor. With its emphasis on lifelong Christian behavior as opposed to passing emotions, the covenant crystallized Edwards' prominent concerns of the previous two years.

On March 16, Edwards preached a preparatory sermon, *Renewing Our Covenant with God*. While conceding that many individuals had received a New Birth during the revivals, he declared the present as the time for a collective rededication. He hoped in this to avoid the downturn in enthusiasm of seven years earlier. If individuals would hold themselves and others accountable to the group, this would tie them together in the bonds of Christian love and watchfulness. Although ostensibly celebratory, the sermon is a surprisingly harsh jeremiad. Clearly Edwards was angry and frustrated with his congregation, especially the older members, and this strained relationship signaled the beginning of the end of his ministry.

The text of the covenant renewal, printed in a letter to Thomas Prince, was surprisingly long by colonial standards, and the tone of censure remained. Members were asked to lament “our past backslidings and ungrateful

<!-- p. 45 -->

departings from God.” Social commentary abounded as members were asked to pledge the civil good: “[W]e will not make our worldly gain, or honor, or interest in the affections of others, or getting the better of any of a contrary party, that are in any respect our competitors, or the bringing or keeping them down, our governing aim, to the prejudice of the interest of religion and the honor of Christ.”[^005-note78] Clearly, this was a covenant that would be impossible to fulfill.

Not surprisingly, then, in April 1742 a disappointed and denunciatory Edwards once again questioned the godliness of some of the enthusiasm. The Buell and Davenport revivals revived in him only misgivings. In *Keeping the Presence of God*, a fast-day sermon, he warned, in ways that anticipated *Religious Affections*, “'Tis a great mistake to think the devil can't come in. I have known it in abundance of instances: the devil has come in, even in the midst of the most excellent frames” (p. 530).

In these same months he expanded on his reservations, the need of the moment being “to distinguish hypocrites” and thereby purify the revivals. Edwards developed the ideas of *Distinguishing Marks* into a full-blown treatise entitled *Some Thoughts Concerning the Revival*. The massive treatise (378 pages) was Edwards' most ambitious to that date and confirms 1742 as a critical period of transition from attention to sermons and sermon series to a newly discovered interest in more formal treatises. In many ways, it marks a retreat to the speculative days of 1739 and the History of Redemption project. *Some Thoughts Concerning the Revival* was composed in late 1742 and published in Boston in March 1743.[^005-note79] Even then, Edwards hoped to see divisions among the clergy healed and sought to protect sincere converts from “diabolical opposers.” He well knew that where the world of heaven dawned brightest the forces of hell would be raised most mightily, and it was in this context that he hoped to enlist all New Englanders.

In other ways, *Some Thoughts Concerning the Revival* echoes and expands on *Distinguishing Marks*. In one important regard, however, Edwards introduced a new emphasis: the “affections”— itself a retreat from the ministry of fear he had earlier promoted in imitation of George Whitefield. Old Light opponents could never get beyond the old faculty psychology that separated the will from the affections and gave primacy of place to the will. In these terms, religious enthusiasm must be bad, for it gave the emotions primacy over the will. In a bold psychological innovation, Edwards

<!-- p. 46 -->

obliterated the sequential distinction between the affections and the will, arguing that “the affections of the soul are not properly distinguished from the will, as though they were two faculties in the soul. All acts of the affections of the soul are in some sense acts of the will, and all acts of the will are acts of the affections.”[^005-note80]

At that very moment in early 1742, he was apparently beginning sermons that would culminate in his *Treatise on Religious Affections*, published in 1746. With this momentous reconstruction, it became possible to provide a psychological grounding for the role of emotions in religion, if properly embedded in knowledge and a Spirit-given faith. Indeed, the role of the Holy Spirit was itself chiefly engaged with the affections, transforming the sense of the heart from love of self to love of God and, in the process, from the world of hell to the world of heaven. This, Edwards concluded, was the true grace of the revivals and the reason they had to be accounted a work of God: “[H]oliness has its seat chiefly in the heart, rather than the head: it therefore follows… that it consists chiefly in holy affections.… The informing of the understanding is all vain, any farther than it affects the heart; or, which is the same thing, has influence on the affections.”[^005-note81] Patricia Tracy recognizes that along with a reintegration of the psyche, “The real importance of *Some Thoughts*, when it is seen as a companion piece to the ‘Personal Narrative,’ is its self-confidence in defining true conversion.”[^005-note82] If he could no longer promote true conversion to a headstrong congregation, Edwards could at least define it for all posterity to read.

The period of the Great Awakening, so reflexively associated with Jonathan Edwards, was, in fact, not so great for him. In proportional terms, church membership in Northampton registered only modest increases. His parishioners, and even his own wife, responded more fervently to the preaching of other itinerants. Even his most famous sermon, *Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God*, was enthusiastically received only outside of Northampton. His older congregants blocked him at every stage, and even a covenant renewal failed to rekindle bonds of love and mutual affection.[^005-note83] Outside of Northampton, Edwards' attempts to reason his way to a rapprochement between Old Lights and New Lights fell on deaf ears.

<!-- p. 47 -->

Neither side was interested in accommodating the other. Far from being great, the years 1741–42 marked the beginning of the end for his Northampton ministry.

But all was not lost. Edwards still had the life of the mind, and to that he would return. The great treatises were on the near horizon and would clinch his international reputation. More important, the grand history of redemption remained. “Redemption,” he would later confess to the Trustees of the College of New Jersey, has “swallowed up my mind,” and has continually been “the chief entertainment and delight of my life.” From this project he knew that his destination was not in this world, but in heaven. In the end— perhaps not too far off— God's cause would triumph. Of that triumph, Edwards could be certain. He still had history to prove it.

## Christ the Spiritual Sun

<!-- p. 48 -->

In this sermon, preached in May 1739, Edwards works to make sinners aware of their sin. To do so, he first makes a distinction between sinner and saved. Here, and in parallel entries in “Notes on Scripture,” the “Blank Bible,” and “Images of Divine Things,” Edwards lays bare the nature of that distinction through the metaphor of the rising sun, provided by the prophet Malachi.[^006-note1] At this time, Edwards was seeking to rouse his congregation from the doldrums it experienced following the awakening of 1734–35. But sermons such as this also served to make his listeners receptive to the revival spirit in the coming months.

In exploring the differences between the unregenerate and regenerate, Edwards sets out to show that just as the sun is characterized by its life-giving light and heat on earth, so Christ is the spiritual Sun communicating saving light and heat to the soul. The effects of this light and heat on saint and sinner are polar opposites. For the sinner, the light is far too bright, not illuminating but blinding and oppressive. The heat is also too much to endure, scorching the sinner's conscience with its intensity. But for the saved, the light and heat of the sun provide nourishment and delight.

Throughout the corpus of Edwards' sermons, one encounters a handful of dominant metaphors. None, however, is more important to him than light, which he identifies in multiple settings with Christ, ‘the light of the world.’ This sermon has thematic and metaphorical treatments that are similar to those in earlier sermons, such as *Christ, the Light of the World* and *A Divine and Supernatural Light*, as well as a sermon on James 1:17 (66), preached in 1728, in which Edwards elaborates on the scriptural image of God as the ‘Father of Lights.’ As Edwards states in this earlier sermon, ‘God the Father is an infinite fountain of light, but Jesus Christ is the communication of this light.’ Employing both nature and Scripture,

<!-- p. 49 -->

in *Christ the Spiritual Sun* Edwards easily draws out the full implications of his metaphor. ‘The natural world,’ he states, ‘is full of images of things in the spiritual world, but the most bright and glorious image of Christ that we have in the whole natural world is the sun.’ As the sun fills the world with light, so Christ illuminates the spiritual world.

In developing the Christological significance of his text, Edwards simultaneously manifests his literary art. Edwards, a supernaturalist in matters of the soul, is equally a naturalist in matters of the imagination. Many preachers could enlist nature as an image of Christ, but none with Edwards' sensitivity to language and the aesthetics of delight.

* * *

The manuscript consists of one booklet of eighteen duodecimo leaves. Edwards dated the sermon ‘May 1739.’ At the top of the first page is an undated shorthand notation that reads, ‘Preached the second time from Isaiah 10:17.’ In revising for repreaching, Edwards discarded the original Application but added two leaves on which he wrote (in outlined form) a new one, which is printed in an appendix to this sermon. The two leaves are written on a piece of newspaper taken from a supplement to the *Boston Gazette* of Tuesday, May 13, 1746, and provides a *terminus a quo* for the repreaching date. The ink in which Edwards wrote these later pages is a darker shade of brown than the ink of the original composure, although the discoloration may have been affected by the difference in the paper.

Press, 1998], 302–4); “Blank Bible,” note on Malachi 4:1-02; and “Images,” nos. 83 and 85 (*Works*, *77*, 85), which all treat the ‘Sun of righteousness.’ Other sermons in this volume in which JE explores the distinction between the regenerate and unregenerate include *The Means and Ends of Excommunication*, *The Subjects of a First Work of Grace May Need a New Conversion*, *They Sing a New Song*, and *Seasons of Ingathering*.

## Christ the Spiritual Sun

> For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the Lord of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch. But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall.

Malachi 4:1–2.Malachi being the last of the prophets who wrote a little before the ceasing of the spirit of prophecy, we have in the text some of the words with which he shuts up the canon of the Old Testament. Wherein we may observe,

1. A time prophesied of, viz. the time of the gospel, here represented as the day that was approaching, and the time of the Sun's rising. There being no more prophets to come after Malachi to write prophecies to be added to the canon of the Old Testament, and so to increase the light of that dispensation, this Prophet, who writes the last book, concludes it with a prediction of the coming of the Great Prophet, and the return of the spirit of prophecy in him and the circumstances of his coming. The day spoken of in the text was the day of his coming, in the day and time of his kingdom that he should come to set up in the world; the same day that was spoken of in the first, second and third verses of the foregoing chapter: ‘Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the Lord of hosts. But who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner's fire, and like fullers' soap: and he shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver, that they may offer unto the Lord an offering in righteousness.’ 'Tis manifest that 'tis the same day that is here spoken of, for there, in the day of

<!-- p. 51 -->

his coming, it is said Christ should sit as a refiner's fire, and this fire is represented as the fire of a furnace that is for the purifying of silver; and here, the day is said to “burn as an oven.” This is the day of Christ's coming, the messenger of the covenant, or the day of the Sun of righteousness arising.

The times of the old testament were as time of night in comparison of the times of the new testament, because gospel light shall then be so much more clear and full: for though the old testament times were not left wholly without gospel light, yet what light they had was like the dim light of the stars in comparison of the light that was afterwards in the gospel day, when Christ the Sun arose.

And therefore Malachi prophesies of the beginning of this gospel day as the rising of the Sun. “The day cometh,” says he, and “the Sun of righteousness shall arise.” Hitherto, the church had been without the light of the Sun any otherwise than as reflected as it were from the moon and stars. It was a long night from the fall of man to the coming of Christ, and the prophets thereof joyfully foretold of the glorious day and the Sun's rising after such a long night of darkness.

The light of the prophets, that were as it were the stars of that night, went out sometime before the Sun arose. And Malachi, being the last of those stars that we have any account of the life of, the verily Prophet, when he was about to withdraw his shining, soon after which there were to shine no more such stars, he comforts the church under this cessation of their former, small, twinkling lights, with foretelling of the approach of day when the Sun of righteousness would arise; when, instead of the stars, they should have the light of the Sun itself, which should be immensely more glorious than of all the prophets or old testament stars. This day includes the whole time of Christ's kingdom after his coming, from its first setting up at his first coming till its consummation at his second coming.

2. We may observe the different consequences of this day's coming and the Sun's rising with respect to the righteous and the wicked. The coming of the day after such a long night will be no comfort to impenitent sinners. The Sun, when it comes to rise, whose light will be so joyful to others, will do them no good, but on the contrary will scorch and burn them. This day shall burn as an oven with respect to the wicked. Christ, that will then come, whose coming and rising will then usher in that day, will be as a refiner's fire, as 'tis said, Malachi 3:2. And his beams shall be like fire to the wicked. It will be a scorching sun to them. Yea, it shall set them a-fire as stubble, as dry and dead plants, and shall utterly burn them up and leave neither root nor branch. So firing and scorching to the wicked will be the

<!-- p. 52 -->

light of the sun, when it comes to rise, that when it comes to fill the world with its light, it will as it were turn the world into an oven to them.

But with respect to them that fear God's name, his beams shall not be scorching but healing, of a benign, pleasant, healthful nature. His light will be joyful to them; it will be a glorious morning to them when this Sun arises after such a long night, and their souls shall grow and flourish under the influences of that Sun, as living plants and animals grow and thrive under the warm beams of the sun, so that they shall “grow up as calves of the stall.”

When it is here said that the Sun of righteousness shall “arise with healing in his wings,” by “his wings” we are to understand his rays or beams. When we look on the sun in the heavens, his body appears to us as encompassed with bright beams going forth on every side, or as it were with pointed flames of bright light around about him.

These beams, according to the ancient eastern manner of expressing things, were called the sun's wings. The sun appears flying through the heavens, and those bright beams that come out of the body of the sun were what they were wont to call his— the sun's— wings.

So that the doctrine is this:

#### Doctrine.

#### That same spiritual Sun, whose beams are most comfortable and beneficial to believers, will burn and destroy unbelievers.

In speaking to this doctrine, I would:

I. Observe how that Christ is as it were the Sun of the spiritual [world].

II. Show what may be represented as the beams of this Sun.

III. Show how that the beams of this Sun will be most pleasant and profitable to believers.

IV. How these same beams, that are of such benign influence on believers, shall burn and destroy the wicked.

I. Christ is as it were the Sun [of] the spiritual world. The natural world is full of images of things in the spiritual world, but the most bright and glorious image of Christ that we have in the whole natural world is the sun. Christ is compared to the morning star, a fountain of water. What the sun is in the natural world, that is Christ in the world, and that on two accounts, viz. his glory and his influence.

*First*. Christ is as it were the Sun of the spiritual [world] on the account of the glory of his person. He is the brightness of God's glory.

<!-- p. 53 -->

*Second*. On the account of his influence. As the sun is a body of the greatest glory of any in {the natural world}, so it is a part of the material world that is of the greatest, most extensive influence. The extensiveness and universality of his influence is described, Psalms 19:6. “His going forth is from the end of the heaven, and his circuit unto the ends of it: and there is nothing hid from the heat thereof.”

The influence of the sun is either by its light or heat.

1. [By] light. [It] discovers {objects}, brings day, fills the world with its light. [It] fills [the viewer] with pleasure or pain according to the quality of the eye that beholds it. {The sun} makes other bodies lightsome that reflect his light.

So is Christ in the spiritual world. John 8:12, “I am the light of the world.” John 1:4, “The life was the light of men.”

2. The sun has great influence by his heat. What a vast alteration is made on the face of the earth {by the sun's heat}; how are the seasons governed; {how is the} face of the earth changed. All the living things depend on its influence by its heat.

With respect to both those emanations of the sun, viz. its light and heat, there appears to be an immense and as it were an inexhaustible fullness in the sun. [It is] not wasted in so many ages. [There is] enough for the supply of such a multitude. Not at all the less for anyone because so many others are supplied.

As the sun causes an universal resurrection of things as it were in two respects— first, every morning; second, every spring— so I come now,

II. To show what we may understand by the beams of this spiritual Sun, or its wings, as by an Hebraism it is expressed in the text. And here I would [not] at all strain the similitude or metaphor beyond what is naturally signified by it; and therefore to understand what is meant by the beams of the Sun of righteousness, we are to consider[^007-note1] that the rays or beams of the sun are those by which the sun is manifested and by which it has its influence.

The beams of the sun are those by which the sun is manifested. The sun appears to us, or is seen by us, no otherwise than by its rays or by the beams of light that its sends forth. All other things here on the face of the Earth are seen or discovered by the light or beams of the sun; but the sun is discovered only by his own light. The rays of the sun's light shining to our eyes, are those by which the sun's glory is manifested and made to appear to us.

<!-- p. 54 -->

And again, the beams of the sun are that by which it has its influence. All the influence the sun has on sublunary bodies to enlighten them, to comfort them, to cause them to grow and flourish, or, on the contrary, to cause them to wither and die: I say, all these ways of its influence is by its beams that it is continually sending forth.

And therefore by the beams of the Sun of righteousness we are to understand all that by which Christ makes himself known, or by which he communicates himself or diffuses his influence. And particularly, the following things must be understood as signified by his beams or wings, as 'tis expressed in the text.

*First*. His Word and ordinances. The glorious gospel of Jesus Christ is as it were the rays or beams of the light of the Sun of righteousness. 2 Corinthians 4:4, “Lest the light of the glorious gospel of Christ, who is the image of God, should shine unto them.” So the Word of God is called a light. Psalms 119:105, “Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light.” Verse Psalms 119:130, “The entrance of thy words giveth light.” Proverbs 6:23, “The commandment is a lamp.”

The gospel is the light by which the Sun of righteousness enlightened the world after the long night of darkness that there was before Christ came. The words that Christ spoke, and the particular passages of Scripture by which he is revealed, are as so many bright beams proceeding forth from the Sun of righteousness.

The gospel is the main instrument by which the influences of this Sun are derived on the hearts of men. So also the ordinances of the gospel are as beams by which Christ is made known and by which he influences men's hearts. The same things are exhibited in the sacraments of the gospel in another manner as are held forth in the Word. By these Christ gives us instruction, and by these he carries on his work, as well as by his Word. And therefore these also are as beams from this sun.

*Second*. The communications and influences of his Spirit on men's hearts. The Spirit of Christ is the messenger he sends forth, by which the Word and ordinances are made effectually to enlighten, enliven and quicken men's hearts. And therefore these communications and influences of the Spirit are as it were the beams put forth from that, by which he enlightens and warms and produces other effects in the hearts of men.

The sun's light and heat is his fullness of which the world receives. So the Holy Spirit, that Christ has not by measure, is his fullness of which the spiritual world receives and partakes.

*Third*. All the exercises of Christ's power whatsoever may be called his beams. That by which the sun has power and by which it produces all its

<!-- p. 55 -->

great and powerful effects are its beams, or rays; by these it warms, by these it cherishes, and by these it dries, scorches and burns.

So all the exercises and emanations of Christ's omnipotence are as it were the emissions of his beams, not only those effects of his power that are by the influences of his Spirit on men's hearts, but all other exertions of his power whatsoever.

*Fourth*. All manifestations of his attributes whatsoever, not only those that are made by his Word, but all appearances of his attributes in his works: his works in creation and providence, his works of providence towards godly men, and also towards the ungodly, in this and another world.

And also those appearances of his majesty and glory which will be made immediately hereafter, without any use of God's Word or ordinances. These displays— that which will be made of the majesty of Christ and awful glory of Christ to the bodily eyes of both good and bad at the day of judgment— these may properly [be] represented as the beams of the light or brightness of the Sun of righteousness. These are the shining forth of his glory, as the glory of the sun shines forth in his rays.[^007-note2]

I come now, in the

III. [Third] place, to show how the beams of this Sun are, and will be, most pleasant and beneficial to believers. There is no one thing so extensively pleasant and beneficial in the natural world as the influence or beams of the sun. Herein is an image of the great benefit of the beams of the spiritual Sun to all that believe on him. They are exceeding beneficial to them many ways:[^007-note3]

*First*. Hereby their souls are enlightened and divine things are discovered to them. The conversion of one that is brought to believe savingly on the Lord Jesus Christ is like the dawning of the day, {the} first shining of the light of the Sun in a soul that before was filled with the greatest darkness. Now divine things are discovered and made manifest that before were totally hid and covered as with a thick veil of darkness. Now things are seen as they be, in their proper forms and colors, in their true situations and relations. Now many glorious objects are discovered. When the Sun rises in the heart, then the Sun of righteousness, the most glorious object of all, is seen by its own light.

*Second*. The hearts of true believers are greatly comforted and refreshed with the beams of this. The day that this Sun brings on, when it arises, is

<!-- p. 56 -->

a pleasant day to them. As the light of the sun is sweet to the bodily eye, so, and much more, is the light of the spiritual Sun sweet to the spiritual eye of the believer. It is a pleasant thing for the eye to behold the sun, but much more pleasant to a believer to behold Jesus Christ that is fairer than the sons of men [Psalms 45:2]. It is refreshing to see the light of the sun down in the east to a man that has been lost and long wandering in the night, in a wilderness, groping in darkness, not knowing whither he went; but much more refreshing and sweet to behold the dawning light of the Sun of righteousness.

How comfortable and pleasant is the warmth of the sun when he returns after a cold winter. So, and much more comfortable to a believing soul, are the warm beams of the Sun of righteousness.

How does the face of the Earth seem to rejoice when the sun comes to shine pleasantly upon it in the spring. The pastures are clothed with green grass and many pleasant flowers that open their bosom to receive the sunbeams. How are the trees as it were clothed with garments of rejoicing, with green leaves and beautiful and fragrant blossoms, as though they sang and shouted for joy at the influences of the sun. Psalms 65:13, “The pastures are clothed with flocks; the valleys also.”

This is a lively image of that sweet spiritual comfort, joy and excellent refreshment that the souls of believers have under the beams of the Sun of righteousness.

*Third*. The beams of this spiritual Sun don't only refresh but restore the souls of believers. Thus it is said that the Sun of righteousness {shall arise} with healing {in his wings}. These beams heal the souls of believers. As we often see that when the trees or plants of the earth are wounded, the beams of the sun will heal the wound and by degrees restore the plant, so the sweet beams of the Sun of righteousness heal the wounds of believers' souls. When they have been wounded by sin and have labored under the pain of wounds of conscience, the rays of this Sun heal the wounds of conscience. When they have been wounded by temptation and made to fall to their hurt, those benign beams, when they come to shine on the wounded soul, restore and heal the hurt that has been received.

The sick soul by these beams is restored, as plants that have grown in shady and cold places appear sickly and languishing, if the shade be removed and the sunbeams come to shine down upon them, will revive and flourish; or as the clear shining of the sun after the rain.

The beams of this Sun heal of the mortal poison of the fiery serpent, as the children of Israel were healed by looking on the brazen serpent in the

<!-- p. 57 -->

wilderness. Yea, these beams don't only restore from wounds but from death; they don't only give light but life. The soul of a convert is raised from the dead by the shining of the beams of this Sun, as we see the rays of the sun in the spring revives the grass and herbs as it were from the dead and causes a resurrection of them from the dust, making 'em to spring out of the ground with new life. The beams of the Sun of righteousness, when it rises in the morning of the last day, will revive not only the souls but the bodies of the saints, will cause at once an universal resurrection of them; as we see in the morning when the sun returns, it causes all animals to rise out of a state of darkness and sleep, which is the image of darkness.

And as there is a kind of universal resurrection in the spring of trees and plants, after they seemed to be all dead.

*Fourth*. The beams of this sun causes the souls of believers to grow and flourish and bear fruit. They not only give life to them but strengthen life, and causes 'em to increase. As the sunbeams not only bring a plant out of the earth from the seed that seemed to lie dead and buried there, but causes 'em to flourish and increase and bring forth fruit, so do Christ's beams to the souls of believers. The soul flourishes under them, increases in grace, grows in strength and stature, buds and blossoms as the rose and brings forth fruit in its season, and its leaf fades not. As 'tis said in the text, “Ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall”; and also agreeable to that, Hosea 14:5-07, “I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon. His branches shall spread, and his beauty shall be as the olive tree, and his smell as Lebanon. They that dwell under his shadow shall return; they shall revive as the corn, and grow as the vine: the scent thereof shall be as the wine of Lebanon.”

*Fifth*. The souls of believers are adorned by these beams of this Sun. The church of Christ appears glorious as the stars by a reflection of the light of this Sun shining upon her, agreeable to Isaiah 60:1, “Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the Lord is risen upon thee,” as we see many objects appear bright by reflecting the light of the sun.

And as the sun adorns the fields and trees and plants of the earth, by his benign influences clothes 'em with a lovely green, adorns 'em with leaves and pleasant fragrant flowers, so is the soul adorned in being clothed with the righteousness of Christ, and so does Christ by his spiritual beams adorn the soul with holiness, whereby it has a sweet cast of divine glory on it and the most amiable appearance, agreeable to Balaam's description of the church in Numbers 24:5-06, “How goodly are thy tents, O

<!-- p. 58 -->

Jacob, and thy tabernacles, O Israel! As the valleys are they spread forth, as gardens by the river's side, as the trees of lign aloes which the Lord hath planted, as cedar trees beside the waters.”[^007-note4]

I come now, in the

IV. [Fourth] place, to show how those same beams of Christ which are so beneficial to believers will only burn and destroy unbelievers, or those that reject Christ, i.e. those that are finally unbelieving. And it is so the following ways:

*First*. As Christ's coming into the world to save sinners will be only an occasion of their greater misery. Christ's coming into the world to save sinners is by the prophet Malachi represented as the beginning of the day and rising of the sun. And that work which he wrought in the world in order to the redemption of sinners, whereby he so manifested his glory, and especially the glory of his mercy and love, may be compared to the shining of the [sun], or the sun's diffusing abroad his blessed beams, those beams which are so beneficial to believers.[^007-note5]

*Second*. Their enjoyments of the gospel and means of grace will turn to their greater and more terrible destruction. The gospel “is the power of God to salvation” to all them that believe (Romans 1:16). It is as the sweet, refreshing, healing, life-giving beams of the sun. But it will [be] an occasion of the greater torment and misery to the ungodly. The gospel, which is the vehicle of salvation to believers, is the vehicle of wrath and savor of death to unbelievers (2 Corinthians 2:15-16).[^007-note6] The gospel does but harden the hearts of those that continue in unbelief.

And it will be tormenting to 'em hereafter. Though now unbelievers are not tormented by it, but flatter themselves with it and make use of the glorious and joyful tidings it brings of God's infinite mercy and readiness to pardon as a pillow on which they may indulge their sloth and quiet their consciences in ways of sin; yet it shall be tormenting to them hereafter, when they shall [not] be able to flatter themselves and soothe their carnal inclinations and affections with it any longer, but the remembrances of those gospel offers and calls that they have had, and which they rejected, will be as fire in their souls, will fill them with inexpressible torment, and will make their souls like an oven. And it will be an inextinguishable fire, for they shall never be able to forget the glorious gospel

<!-- p. 59 -->

offers and opportunities that they once had and neglected; they shall never be able to expel the thoughts of them out of their minds, and the thoughts of them will forever be inexpressibly tormenting to them.

'Tis found in temporal things, that when a man is fallen into any great calamity, if he, looking back, sees that he had a very fair opportunity to have avoided, and that he has brought himself into this misery through his own folly when he might have escaped, this is what exceedingly adds to their trouble and is very much the sting of their calamity.

If they could look back and see that it was unavoidable, and that it came by no fault or neglect of theirs, it is comparatively easy to bear. We may judge therefore how stinging the reflection of unbelievers and gospel sinners will be in hell, when they have to conflict with everlasting burning, and think how clearly a way of salvation was made known to them; how often they were invited to accept of it; how long God waited upon them, for how small a matter; what trifles and vanities they were for the sake of which they neglected and made light of all these advantages, and so lost their souls and have ruined themselves to all eternity without remedy or hope.

*Third*. All the influences of the Spirit of Christ that those receive that finally reject him, will but turn [to] their great misery and sorrow. We observed that one thing that might naturally be understood by the beams of this spiritual Sun is his Spirit sent forth. These beams that prove so comfortable and profitable to believers, will also in the issue only prove scorching beams, that will torment and devour the finally unbelieving. Many such are the subjects of many influences and strivings of the Spirit of God while they live in this world. Christ comes to their door and knocks, not only in the calls of the gospel but by the strivings of his Spirit. Some such, while they live, have many awakenings and convictions and have many of the common fruits of the Spirit; but these in the issue never prove any benefit to them, but rather an occasion of far more dreadful wrath.

That is to be observed, that the greater any mercies are in themselves that persons have had and have neglected and abused, so much the more will they be an occasion of misery to those that have had them. But the common influences of the Spirit of God are the greatest mercies that God ever bestows on men, next to the saving influences of his [Spirit]. The external means of grace— as the gospel and its ordinances— are in themselves very great mercies, much greater than any worldly possessions; but the strivings of God's Spirit with ordinances are yet greater, and therefore the guilt contracted by the abuse of them is greater, and so the misery, that is the consequence, is more dreadful. And thus, all the strivings and influences

<!-- p. 60 -->

of the Spirit of God that ever final unbelievers are the subjects of, instead of proving benign life-giving beams as they are to believers, prove a scorching consuming fire to unbelievers.

*Fourth*. The future appearance of Christ in his glory at the day of judgment, that will be most pleasant and joyful to the saints, will be dreadful and amazing to those that have rejected Christ. At the day of judgment, the Sun of righteousness shall appear in its greatest glory; Christ shall then come in the glory of his Father, and all the holy angels with him. In the morning of that day, this Sun shall arise and shine forth with rays inconceivably bright.

He shall shine with a brightness far exceeding the brightness of the natural sun, even so much that the sun shall be turned into darkness before it. It shall appear dark in comparison of it.

This shall be the most joyful and pleasant sight to believers that ever their eyes beheld. It will be a thousand times more refreshing to them than ever was the sight of the rising sun to them that have wandered in a wilderness, through the longest and darkest night. The sight of [it] will fill their souls with unspeakable gladness and rejoicing. It will be a bright day to the saints. The beams of that glorious Sun that will then appear will make it bright. The earth will be lightened with his glory, and the light of his glory that the world will then be filled with will be a sweet light to them. That brightness that the disciples saw on the Mount when Christ was transfigured before them was some resemblance of it: that was most pleasant to the disciples, so that they said it was good to be there, and were for building tabernacles that they might dwell there; and Peter calls [it] an “excellent glory” that they saw there (2 Peter 1:17).

But this appearance, that will be so pleasant to believers, will fill the souls of unbelievers with amazement. The first sight of it will strike them with terror. They shall be for hiding “in the dens and in the rocks of the mountains” [Revelation 6:15]. Every ray of that glory that Christ shall then appear in will be like a stream of scorching fire, and will pierce their hearts with a keener torment than a stream of fierce lightning. They shall see Christ appearing in his majesty, and it will be dreadful majesty to them, that will fill 'em with horrors and set them a-trembling and gnashing their teeth, at the same time that it fills the hearts of the saints with rejoicing and their mouths with singing.

That day will burn as an oven indeed. That brightness that the light of Christ's glory shall fill the world with will be more terrible to them than if the world was filled with the fiercest flames. It will make the world like an oven to them, and as it were turn it into a furnace. Christ will then appear

<!-- p. 61 -->

an infinitely holy, just judge. The sight of this holiness and justice will be joyful to the saints; it will appear as a ravishing beauty in their eyes. But the ungodly will hate the sight of it. Christ's pure eyes will pierce their souls with torment, like piercing flames of fire that they cannot endure. Christ will then sit as a refiner and purifier of silver. He shall be as a refiner's fire that shall burn up the dross [Malachi 3:3].

So that day that will be the brightest and most pleasant to the godly that ever they saw, shall be the most dismal day to the others that ever they saw. The light of the same majesty and glory that shall fill the world with light to the one, shall fill it as it were with tormenting fire to the other. In his light shall be a paradise for the one and an oven or furnace for the other.

*Fifth*. And lastly, Christ's power, that shall be exercised in saving one, shall be exercised in tormenting and destroying the other. That Sun of God that is the Savior of believers, their best friend, their spiritual husband, will be the enemy of finally impenitent sinners. He will rule over believers with a golden scepter of grace and love, making them willing in the day of his power; but he will rule over unbelievers in wrath and with a rod of iron, dashing them in pieces as a potter's vessel [Psalms 2:9].

When he came at his first coming, he came to seek and save the elect. But soon after, he brought the amazing destruction of the unbelieving Jews, terribly destroying their city and country by the Romans.

So when he will come in a spiritual sense at the beginning of the expected glorious times of the church, he will come [not only] for the deliverance and healing and rejoicing of his church, but for the amazing destruction of Antichrist and other enemies of his church. These different effects of this spiritual coming of Christ towards the righteous and the wicked is eloquently represented in Isaiah 66:12-15. “For thus saith the Lord, Behold, I will extend peace to her like a river, and the glory of the Gentiles like a flowing stream: then shall ye suck, ye shall be borne upon her sides, and be dandled upon her knees. As one whom his mother comforteth, so will I comfort you; and ye shall be comforted in Jerusalem. And when ye see this, your heart shall rejoice, and your bones shall flourish like an herb: and the hand of the Lord shall be known toward his servants, and his indignation toward his enemies. For, behold, the Lord will come with fire, and with his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his anger with fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire.”

And so at the end of the world, when Christ shall come to the last judgment, he shall come to save his people and make 'em perfectly glorious and happy. But he will come to destroy all his enemies with the most fearful destruction, and to burn them in the fire of his wrath.

<!-- p. 62 -->

And there shall be a literal accomplishment of the words of the text: “Behold, the day of the Lord cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the Lord of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.” Then the world shall literally be on fire and shall be all like an oven, filled with the flames of the fiercest and most glowing heat. “The heavens being on fire shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat” [2 Peter 3:12]. And in this fire unbelievers shall be burnt and tormented, agreeable to 2 Peter 3:7. “But the heavens and the earth, which are now, by the same word are kept in store, reserved unto fire against the day of judgment and perdition of ungodly men.”

### [Application.]

Let this put persons upon examining themselves whether or no they are not unbelievers. Though you have a standing in God's vineyard, yet are you not barren? Then if so, consider what Christ did to the barren fig tree. Are you not rooted in stony ground? Are you not dry and dead plants?[^007-note7]

### Appendix to Mal 4:1-02

Have you [been] made sensible of your own blindness?

Have you seen the glory of this light that is shined into your heart?

Has it had a transforming influence upon you?

Has it given you new life?

Do you love this light?

[Do you] delight in the beams, {the} Word and Spirit?

Do you walk as a child of the light?

*Exh*. [1.] Take thorough and effectual care that you mayn't finally be found amongst the wicked but the righteous, that God may be a light to enlighten and not a fire to consume you. Earnestly seek to get into a converted state.

Make your calling and election sure.

Don't despise this light.

Give earnest heed to this light as it shines in the Word of God.

Don't knowingly sin against it.

[Don't knowingly sin] against the light of your own conscience.

<!-- p. 63 -->

Labor to see your own blindness.

Beg of God to shine into your hearts.

How glorious [is] the light.

[How] happy [are] those that behold it.

[The] sun is but a shade.

How blessed its influences.

Its beams.

How happy its influences in this world.

How happy its influences in heaven. Saints as flames. No night. Perfect light, no darkness.

You will shine.

[*Exh*.] 2. How terrible the fire. And God is a consuming fire.

The sun, that is so pleasant, is a dreadful fire.

If the omnipotent God be the fire in which sinners are to be tormented, well may the sinners in Zion be afraid and fearfulness surprise the hypocrites [Isaiah 33:14].[^007-note8] Well may they say […][^007-note9]

[^007-note1]: Following this word JE drew a cue to indicate an inserted passage, but no corresponding cue is in the sermon.

[^007-note2]: In revising for repreaching, JE made this point the beginning of a new preaching unit. He wrote out the text for the repreaching— Isaiah 10:17— and the revised doctrine, “That God who is a light to lighten the saints is a flame to consume the ungodly.”

[^007-note3]: In revising for repreaching, JE inserted: “1. They are acquainted with his glory.”

[^007-note4]: The first preaching unit ends here. JE's recapitulation of the text and doctrine are omitted.

[^007-note5]: MS: “believers will only.”

[^007-note6]: For a sermon on this text, see *Gospel Ministers a Savor of Life or Death*, printed below.
