<!-- p. 195 -->

The best have so little spiritual life and such remainders of death, are so dead and lifeless to what they are capable of being and to what they should be, that there is still room enough for them to pass under such a change as shall be like rising from the dead.

There is so much remaining darkness and blindness, that they still need to pass under a change that shall [be] like opening the eyes of the blind.

The godly still need to be more convinced of sin, and see more of its guilt and danger and dreadful nature; for those that have seen most of the danger of sin have never seen but little. They all need still to see a great deal more of their own hearts. They have a great deal of self-righteousness left. They need to be brought off from their own righteousness. They still need to come to repentance of their sins, and still need to come to Christ. They still need to have old things to pass away and all things in a sense to be become new in them.

*Second Answ*. They do especially stand in need of it who are weak in grace. Indeed, all are weak in comparison of that perfection which they shall arrive at in heaven. The saints are all children, infants in holiness in this world; but some are weak in comparison of others. The Apostle often speaks of weak brethren and “babes in Christ” [1 Corinthians 3:1].

Many, through their weakness in grace, have their grace scarce visible to themselves or others, unless it be at some special seasons of enlivening. Corruption in them, though it don't reign, yet prevails so far as greatly to disturb and disquiet and darken their mind, and causes 'em to behave themselves after such a manner as is much to the dishonor of God and religion.

They therefore do especially need to pass under a new work of God's Spirit upon their hearts, to lift 'em above their difficulties, to set 'em now at liberty, to cause them to live more as becomes saints. The Apostle tells the Corinthians that they were but babes, and through the weakness of their grace behaved like carnal unconverted men in many things. 1 Corinthians 3:1-04, “And I, brethren, could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal, even as unto babes in Christ. I have fed you with milk, and not with meat: for hitherto ye were not able to bear it, neither yet now are ye able. For ye are yet carnal: for whereas there is among you envying, and strife, and divisions, are ye not carnal, and walk as men? For while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?” And so he tells the Christian Hebrews that they were but babes, and therefore needed to lay the foundation of faith and repent anew. Hebrews 5:12-13, “For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and

<!-- p. 196 -->

are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat. For every one that useth milk is unskillful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe.” Because they were babes, they needed to be taught again the first principles, i.e. they need to be converted anew, to lay the foundation of faith and repentance anew; as the Apostle explains himself in the beginning of the next chapter: “Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God.”

*Third Answ*. Above all, they stand in need of a new conversion that have fallen in foul transgression, or are by degree got into very ill frames and ill ways. Such as are thus fallen, do especially need help.

'Tis with godly men in such circumstances as 'tis with wicked men: they are for a season in the way of wicked men, and in such circumstances, that continuance in them is inconsistent with a state of grace. Therefore such, above [all], seem to stand in need of being converted from the error of their way. The lambs of the flock that are feeble may much need the help of the shepherd, but the sheep that has fallen into a pit, or is in the jaws of the lion and bear, above all needs help. Peter, above all the disciples, needed the help of his Lord to convert him when he so shamefully fell that night wherein Christ was betrayed: for he began to sink, and if his Lord had not put forth his hand to help him, he would have been utterly overwhelmed, as when he was walking on the water and began to sink, of which we have an account in [Matthew 14:22-33].

I come now to the

III. [Third] thing proposed in the doctrinal handling of this subject, which is to show upon what accounts those that already have a principle of true grace in their hearts may stand in great need of such a change as has been spoken [of].

*First*. They may greatly need it in order to God's having of them the glory of his grace in making them saints. When God infuses grace into the hearts of any, and so makes 'em saints, it is a wonderful effect of his free grace. And God, when he makes a man a saint, does a thousand times as much for him as if he made him a prince. And certainly much honor is due to him from such as have been the subjects of such a wonderful favor.

But some that have a principle of grace through the weakness or decays of grace and prevailing of corruption, behave themselves so for a season as greatly to dishonor this grace; as David gave great occasion to the dishonor {of God's grace in the matter of Uriah}. Men, from what they see in them, are ready to question whether there be any such work of God as conversion, yea, even to question the truth of all religion.

<!-- p. 197 -->

And if they don't, they conceive ill thoughts of religion and of the grace of God that has no better effects, as though it were only an encouragement to sin.

Therefore some godly persons do greatly need to be the subjects of a new conversion, that this reproach may be wiped off, that others, seeing their good work, may glorify {the honor of God's grace}. By their becoming the subjects of a new work, grace, that was much obscured, may come to shine and appear amiable in its holy fruits; and when it is thus, this is greatly to the glory of God's grace in conversion.

That which is needed in the saints in order to God's having the glory of his grace in making them saints, is very needful indeed: for to that end were they elected and converted and justified, that they might be to the praise of the glory of God's grace. Ephesians 1:5-06, “Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved.”

*Second*. 'Tis sometimes needful in order to their having the comfort of their conversion. Some that are converted, through the weakness of grace and the prevailing of corruption, can't take the comfort of it. They meet with abundance of difficulties, temptations, doubts and darkness.

And so it is with those that have fallen into great sins, or very bad frames and ways. They are like a poor lost sheep that has no comfort of the shepherd's fold. And there is no likelihood that ever they will be delivered without a new work of the Spirit causing as it were a new conversion. While they are as they are now, it is vain to endeavor to remove their doubts and difficulties. Let what signs of grace soever be laid down for them to try themselves, they won't satisfy them. Let 'em advise with whom they will, let them be persons never so skillful, they can't remove their troubles. But a new work of God's Spirit as it were raising their dead souls and causing light to shine out of darkness, would soon remove their difficulties, so that they might rejoice in hope of the glory of God.

*Third*. The case may be so with those that have a real principle of grace in their hearts, that a new conversion may be necessary to their salvation. Christ's words, in the text and context, seem to intimate that it was necessary to Peter's salvation that he should be converted after his fall. Christ says to him, “Simon, Simon, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat: but I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren”; which implies that, if he had not been converted, his faith would have failed and Satan would have had him. If Peter had not been converted after his fall, he would not

<!-- p. 198 -->

have persevered in the faith and profession of Christ. He would have fallen under that threat, Luke 12:9, “He that denies me before men [shall be denied before the angels of God].” 'Tis necessary to our salvation that we should with our mouth make confession of Christ (Romans 10:10). They don't believe to the saving of the soul, but draw back. Hebrews 10:38-39, “Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him. But we are not of them.”[^023-note6]

Though God has promised that the righteous, when they are cast down, shall rise again and not fall into mischief, yet that don't hinder but that their rising again should be necessary to their salvation as the established invariable way to it. Repentance, after such falls, seems by God's constitution to be necessary in order to forgiveness, and their forgiveness to their salvation.

And so a new conversion may not only be necessary to salvation, as a recovery from a way of sin may be necessary prerequisite to salvation by divine constitution, but also as the way of growth in grace is the established way to salvation. God has been pleased to appoint that the saints shall come to Zion in a way of going from strength to strength [Psalms 84:7].

And therefore the work of God's grace that is sometimes wrought in the hearts of those that before were very weak in knowledge and grace, or in whom grace was under peculiar disadvantages, is in order to their salvation. So the work that was wrought in the heart of Cornelius by Peter's preaching was in order to his salvation, though he was a good man before, as appears by Acts 11:12, Acts 11:14; and he showed us how he had seen an angel in his house, which stood and said unto him, “Send even to Joppa, and call for Simon, whose surname is Peter, who shall tell thee words by which thou and all thy house shall be saved” [Acts 10:1-07].

### Application.

[*Use*] I. Of *Instr*.

*First*. Hence we may learn how far godly persons should be from looking upon it that their work is done. They must be in a very great error, and must act very absurdly, who think it is proper for them to strive earnestly in religion, to watch their hearts, and be very strict in their walk, and laborious in reading and hearing and praying, till they hope they have obtained something of a saving nature; but then look upon it, that they have no more need of such striving in religion, as though all their purpose is

<!-- p. 199 -->

attained, and that they have nothing further to strive after. If they have obtained a saving change, yet they are at a very great distance from what they should be; the kingdom of heaven within them is but as a grain of mustardseed. They still need to pass under a very great change, and 'tis what they should therefore still be seeking after with no less diligence than they sought the first saving change.

And indeed, for persons, as soon as they have obtained an hope that they are converted, presently to grow more slack in religion, less engaged in their minds about it and more remiss in their endeavors, is the way for 'em soon to come to those circumstances wherein persons, above all others, stand in need of a renewed conversion. For 'tis the way for 'em by degrees to sink into a very dead, carnal, unchristian frame of spirit and have their corruptions prevail more and more, till they carry them away as a flood.

There is sometimes a great deal of talk of conversion amongst us— meaning the conversion of natural men— but 'tis pity there is no more said of godly persons' conversion. There is doubtless a great deal of need of it, by the general appearance of the state of religion in this town. There are a great many that have some grace in their hearts, that do stand in very great and special need of being converted; and 'tis pity that such a conversion is not more thought of, and talked of, and sought after.

*Second*. Hence we may learn how that godly persons may apply to themselves, and improve for their own good, what they hear preached especially to natural men. There is but little that is said in sermons to natural men but what godly men may very properly hear for themselves. There are but few exhortations that are given to natural men from the pulpit but what godly men may apply to themselves as in many respects suiting their case. If the minister endeavors to show natural men the dreadful guilt that sin brings, and the dreadfulness of the wrath of God, to awaken them, godly persons need to be awakened as well as they. They also need to be convinced more of the great evil of sin and the dreadfulness of God's wrath.

If that be delivered in a sermon that is to convince natural men of the utter insufficiency of their own righteousness, this the godly may take to themselves. For they also need to be convinced of the insufficiency {of their own righteousness}.

[The godly also need to be convinced of their] utter helplessness.

If they are exhorted earnestly to seek conversion, [the godly also need to be exhorted to seek conversion].

If they are exhorted to strive, in order to it, to be violent for the kingdom

<!-- p. 200 -->

of heaven, to follow on to know the Lord, {the godly also need to be exhorted to strive}.

There are but few of those directions that are given from the pulpit to natural men, in order to their conversion, but what are proper for the godly to attend and follow in seeking a renewed conversion.

Christ and his apostles commonly were not wont to make any distinction between saints and sinners in those exhortations and directions that they gave to seek God's grace and the salvation of their souls. In the eighteenth [chapter] of Matthew, Christ says to his disciples, “Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of God.” He did not direct himself only to Judas. So when he says, in the fifth [chapter] of Matthew, twentieth verse, “Except your righteousness shall exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees, ye shall in no case enter into the kingdom of heaven,” he speaks to his disciples; as you may see by the beginning of the chapter. So he says to 'em again in the twenty-sixth [verse], “Verily I say unto thee, Thou shalt by no means come out thence, till thou hast paid the uttermost farthing”; which is a direction in order to escape hell. So again, twenty-ninth [and] thirtieth verses: “And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell. And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell.”

So Christ in the same sermon, wherein he is still speaking to the disciples, in the seventh chapter, thirteenth [and] fourteenth verses: “Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.”

And so the apostles, from time to time in their epistles, give directions what those that they write to should do for their salvations; and yet write to those that they have charity for as saints, and faithful in Christ Jesus.

*Third*. Here we may learn that there are but few petitions that are proper to be put up to God by natural men but what are also proper for the godly. Some persons that have had hope that they were converted, but are full of doubts and fears, complain that they are at a loss how to form their petitions: whether they should pray to God as those that are unconverted, or as those that are converted. But the difficulty is not so great as some imagine; for whether they are converted or unconverted, most of

<!-- p. 201 -->

those requests that are proper to be put up by an unconverted man are proper for them. Let 'em pray that God would give them his Spirit to awaken them; this is proper for them, whether they have any true grace or not. And so let ['em] pray that God would enable to strive for salvation, and that he would help 'em to enter in at the strait gate. Let 'em pray earnestly that God would show 'em their own hearts; {that God would} bring ['em] off from own righteousness; {that} God would convert 'em; {that God would} give a true sight of Christ, and enable 'em sincerely to close with him and trust in him alone for salvation. Let 'em pray that God would open their blind eye; {that God would} cause light to shine out of darkness; and that he [would] raise their dead souls to life.

Such petitions are proper to be put up to God by a minister, as one that speaks as the mouth of a congregation; and they are proper petitions to be joined in by the whole congregation, both saints and sinners.

*Fourth*. Hence we may learn what is the proper course for them to take in order to satisfaction that are much exercised with doubts about their good estate through their having been long in dead and carnal frames, viz. earnestly to seek that they may be converted. When those that are truly godly have fallen into such frames and have long continued in them, the almost certain and infallible consequence of it [is] great doubts about their good estate. When grace is so buried with corruption, it won't be easily seen, and there will be many doubts whether there be any.

Now the proper course to be taken in such a case, in order to satisfaction about their good estate, is to strive to enter in at the strait gate and to be violent for the kingdom of heaven; to strive and cry to God for his converting grace; to cry after wisdom and lift up their voice for understanding.

Very commonly, the course that is taken in such cases, in order to a resolution of the doubts that arise, is to try themselves by signs. And indeed, that ought not to be left undone. But when that course alone is taken, it almost universally proves in vain. Unless there be a new work of God's Spirit to lift the soul out of its dead carnal frame, all the best signs and the most searching trying discourses are found in vain; the doubts will remain.

The properest and best course for all such persons to take to be delivered from their doubts, is immediately, without delay, to apply themselves, to seek the grace of God opening their blind eyes and quickening their dead souls, as earnestly as if they knew they never yet had received anything of it. And if this course was more earnestly taken instead of spending a great deal [of] time in examining and looking over the first work

<!-- p. 202 -->

and past experiences, there would be fewer complaints of difficulties, doubts and fears among professors than now there is.

*Use* II may be of *Exhortation* to such as have had hope that they have been the subjects of a saving change yet, notwithstanding, earnestly to seek that they may be converted. I would direct this exhortation to all such— for as has been shown, 'tis proper for all— but especially exhort such to it in whom grace, if they have any, is very low, and such as have been long in dead and carnal frames of spirit, and have not behaved themselves as becomes Christians. Consider what has been said of the great need you stand in of a new change. And further to stir you up to seek it, consider two things:

*First*. When the godly are thus, through God's grace, the subjects of a new change, it commonly brings 'em into much more happy circumstances than their first change. When God works a second work, it shall not be for nothing; he commonly thereby carries the soul to a much greater height in holiness than ever it was brought to before: to much greater degrees of the knowledge of God, to a firmer faith, to be more rooted and grounded in love; to have more [of] the mastery of the corruptions of the heart, and to have greater strength against temptation and to serve God in a more steady even manner; and to enjoy a more settled peace of conscience, to live more constantly [and] comfortably in the enjoyment of much more of the light of God's countenance.

What a blessed alteration was there in Peter after that conversion that is spoken of in the text. He that was then so cowardly, so afraid to own his Master: how courageous does he appear after his recovery, how bold in the cause of Christ, and how full of the Spirit of God does he appear to be, by what we read of him in the second and following chapters of the Acts.

*Second*. Godly persons, after such a renewed work of God's Spirit upon them, are commonly not only in a much happier state themselves, but much more able to help others. Hereby their knowledge and experience and strength is greatly increased, and, having been tempted and delivered, they are the more fit to help others under temptation. And by the great access which they have received of light and strength themselves, they are abundantly the more fit to instruct and strengthen others. Hence the direction that Christ gives to Peter in the text: “When thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren.” So that if you obtain such a change by a new work of the Spirit of God upon your heart, you are not only likely to be a much happier man yourself, but to be a much greater blessing to all that are about you; and others are like to be the happier for it, as well as you.

[^023-note1]: JE deletes: “This seems to have been the Case also with Zaccheus who yet came down at Xs Effectual Call & X told him says to him this day is salvation come unto this House.”

[^023-note2]: MS: “it at.”

[^023-note3]: JE left a blank space in the MS.

[^023-note4]: JE wrote “so G. is wont also,” but did not complete the thought, so the phrase is treated as an intended deletion.

[^023-note5]: The first preaching unit ends here; JE's recapitulation of the text, doctrine, and first proposition are omitted.

## Gospel Ministers a Savor of Life or of Death

<!-- p. 203 -->

George Whitefield has just left town, having preached four sermons in the Northampton meetinghouse and one in the Edwards home. Whitefield preached on every occasion to packed houses; the audience hung on his every word, wept, cried out. Now that he is gone, the town is still in an emotional state. It is up to the settled pastor to keep the pitch high. But he must also bring some order and perspective to bear, make some sense of what has happened.

Edwards chooses a text that conveys the power of the word preached, and of the persons who are privileged enough to deliver it. Those who proclaim the gospel are a savor of life to the saved and of death to the damned.[^024-note1] He then draws forth three propositions. The first is ambiguous: “Those ministers that faithfully preach the gospel of Christ are accepted of God, and are as a sweet savor to him, whether they are successful or not.” This could refer to Whitefield, whose effect may not have been universally the same. It could also refer to Edwards himself, the settled pastor who has been unsuccessful in inspiring his people to a revival spirit for some time. We can only speculate on whether Edwards is anticipating the long-term response to Whitefield or perhaps applying a salve to his frustrated hopes. Successful or not, Edwards avers that “faithfulness” in carrying out one's obligations, particularly as God's ambassador, is what God looks at and will reward.

The remaining propositions unquestionably pertain to Whitefield. When God sends a messenger to preach the gospel, the effect will be great— either to “great good or great hurt.” If the people of Northampton will not heed the word, then a messenger like Whitefield is justified in doing as the apostle Paul did to unbelievers: shaking the dust of their town from his feet and leaving them to their fate. Third, the case is especially striking when God sends “a messenger that is eminent, and whose labors God has been wont to accompany with an extraordinary blessing.”

In the Application, Edwards attempts to distinguish Whitefield's medium

<!-- p. 204 -->

from his message. In doing so he makes clear that, however much he respects Whitefield's talents and the blessings that attend them, he has reservations about his methods and teachings.[^024-note2] He asks his listeners to differentiate the impression that Whitefield left upon them through the *way* he preached from what good, if any, his *message* had for their souls. Was the gospel of Christ, as he preached it, a sweet savor to them, or were they more pleased with Whitefield's “aptness of expression” and “clearness of illustration”? Is all they can talk about the “eloquence of the preacher,” his “fervency” and “beautiful gestures,” his “becoming, beautiful manner of address”? Instead of dwelling on these things, they should be examining themselves about the abiding effects: bringing forth good fruit, making good improvement of the preaching. God expects much from the people of Northampton because he has given them much, Edwards states. If they simply talk about reformation and the great things of religion but do not carry it over into action, “We shall be condemned out of our own mouths.” Let all, Edwards urges, do their part to promote the work of God.

* * *

The manuscript comprises nine duodecimo leaves. Edwards inscribed at the top of page one, “Private meeting, Octob. 1740.” The History of Redemption symbol appears at the upper left-hand corner. As is often the case with Edwards' sermons composed for private meetings, the text is sketchy throughout.

## Gospel Ministers a Savor of Life or of Death

> For we are unto God a sweet savor of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish: to the one we are the savor of death unto death; and to the other the savor of life unto life.

II Corinthians 2:15–16.The Apostle was the most eminent minister of the gospel. He preached in many places.

Above all others, [he was] the most remarkable for his success. But yet his success was not alike in all places, amongst all sorts of people, nor with different persons in the same places and among the same sort of people.

[His] success least where had been great advantage long enjoyed.

The Apostle, in the verses immediately preceding the text […]

The meaning of the words is this: “We are unto God a sweet savor of Christ, in them that are saved, and in them that perish”; i.e. “The work that we do in preaching the gospel, whether it be effectual or no, is acceptable to God. If we are faithful, our labor is an acceptable offering to God, and he smells a sweet savor in our offering.” We are a sweet savor of Christ. Christ is the rose, the gospel is the savor of the rose. God is well-pleased in Jesus Christ. When he was offered up, it was a sweet savor to God. And the name of Christ is a sweet savor to God, as ointment poured forth. And therefore the apostles, that published his name abroad in the world, and so honored and glorified that name, they diffused that sweet odor. And that knowledge of the name of Christ that the apostles spread abroad, and that was both in elect and reprobates, should be to the glory of Christ, and therefore was acceptable to God. This seems to be the meaning of the first verse of the text.

The second verse is thus: “to the one we are the savor of death unto death; and to the other the savor of life unto life”; i.e. “Though our preaching Christ is always acceptable to God, and a pleasant savor to him,

<!-- p. 206 -->

whether we preach to elect or reprobate, yet 'tis not always a sweet savor to those that we preach to: for to the elect, or those that are saved, 'tis a sweet savor, as well as to God; 'tis a savor of life. We are to them a savor of a living Redeemer.” They believe him to be a risen and glorified Savior. They receive him as one risen from the dead, and now reigning in life, and exalted to give life to others. So the church, in Canticles 1:3, speaks of Christ's name as “ointment poured forth.”

“A savor of life unto life”; i.e. it is not only a sweet savor to them, but a refreshing and life-giving savor.

To the other he is “a savor of death.” Christ[^025-note1] crucified is not a sweet savor to them, but a stinking savor, a savor of death, as a savor of a dead carcass. Christ crucified is to them a stumblingblock. They look upon him as crucified, as dead still.

“Unto death.” And the savor, as ['tis] stinking to them, as of a dead carcass,[^025-note2] so it brings them to death.

#### [Propositions.]

From the words of the text, I would observe several propositions:

[*Prop*.] I. Those ministers that faithfully preach the gospel of Christ are accepted of God, and are as a sweet savor to him, whether they are successful or no.

Sweet savor to God.

God delights in his Son Jesus Christ.

[God] delights in what is to his glory. For this end, God hath done great things.

The preaching of the gospel is the principal means of glorifying Christ.

'Tis greatly to Christ's glory, though unsuccessful.

Christ will be glorified in the damned.

And then God accepts the faithfulness of his ministers. 'Tis a great work. And faithfulness in it will have a proportionably great reward.

*Prop*. II. When God sends a messenger that faithfully preaches the gospel among a people, it will be effectual either for the great good or great hurt of every one that hears it.

God compares his word to the rain (Isaiah 55:10-11).

The word of God will take hold of all that hear it, one way or another. Zechariah 1:6, “But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not take hold of your fathers?” The word of

<!-- p. 207 -->

God is precious in his sight and shall not be [sown in vain],[^025-note3] though men trample it under foot. [It is a] precious ointment, a sweet savor. In this sense heaven and earth shall pass away before one jot or tittle [shall pass away from the law]. Every part of the message that God sends shall be effectual.

And the effect shall be great, answerably to the preciousness of the word. The greatness of him whose word it is.

But the effect will be exceeding different with different persons: to the elect, their eternal salvation, [to] reprobates, everlasting condemnation.

All the elect do get good by the word of God at some time or other, saving good; but there may be some particular messengers and messages from God they may not get good by, and then, though it will not issue in their damnation, yet it [does] greatly wound {their souls and is} a savor of death to them in a sense, hardens them exceedingly, brings 'em under very sorrowful and melancholy circumstances.

And as this is true of persons, so it is of a people.

So it was of old with Christ, what he did. And Capernaum [and] Bethsaida, {in rejecting the mighty works which had been done in them, what a great wound did they} bring on themselves [Matthew 11:21-23].

How dreadful was the destruction that came on Jerusalem.

So with the apostle Paul. Against some “he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean: from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles” [Acts 18:6].

Christ commanded his disciples to wipe off the dust of their feet, to signify that their very ground was accursed [Matthew 10:14].

*Prop*. III. It is especially thus when God sends a messenger that is eminent, and whose labors God has been wont to accompany with an extraordinary blessing.

The text speaks especially of the apostle Paul, who, as was observed before, was a very eminent messenger of God: eminent in knowledge: more abundant revelations; in grace in faith and love, in labors, in sufferings.

Eminent in success.… Extensiveness throughout great part of the world.

And therefore it was his word, or the word of God as dispensed by him, that was especially a sweet savor of Christ, and so was to some a savor of life unto life and {to other a savor of death unto death}.

So much the more precious the means are, so much the greater will

<!-- p. 208 -->

their effect be. There is so much the more of God in the means, and where God is, he will not be in vain. Where he comes, there he will work, either in a way of mercy or in a way of wrath.

#### Application.

*Use* I may be of *Self-Exam*. Let us hence be led to examine ourselves whether the gospel of Christ has been a savor of life unto life {or a savor of death unto death}. It is of great importance that we should know. Three things by which I would desire you to try yourselves:

*First*. Whether the gospel of Christ that is preached is become a sweet savor to us.

Do our souls relish it much after the manner as the body relishes a sweet perfume? Is it like ointment poured forth to our {souls}, an excellent fragrance?

Persons may be very variously affected with the preaching of the word, and yet not have it thus as a sweet savor.

May desire it from regard to their salvation.

May be greatly pleased with the aptness of expression. Clearness of illustration.

Eloquence of the preacher.

Fervency. Beautiful gestures.

Becoming, beautiful manner of address.

May be in a kind of rapture by it. Even with joy receive it.

So elevated, ready to follow the preacher to the ends of the earth. So [were] some of Christ's hearers.

Filled with admiration. And glorify God, praise God. So the Jews (Matthew 9:8). And yet not that sweet relish, as sweet nourishing food to the soul.

Do you receive it as a savor of life, with a firm faith in Christ as a living Savior?

*Second*. Does the effect abide? This distinction we find of the profitable hearers from all others. [Does it] take deep root?

*Third*. Does it bring forth fruit? This we find to be the main distinction between [profitable hearers and others] in the parable of the sower and the seed [Matthew 13].[^025-note4]

<!-- p. 209 -->

That {we may know whether the gospel of Christ has been a savor of life unto life},

*Use* II may [be] of *Exh*. Let us be hence exhorted to be in good earnest in making a good improvement of the late labors of that servant of God, whom God has sent to us from afar, that it may be effectual for our great good and not for our great hurt.

Let us consider how we have backslidden. How rare [are] conversions, [how] rare convictions.

This seems to have been what he chiefly aimed at— to stir us. Quicked. Rouse [us up]. Wise virgins and foolish.

And how earnestly and fervently and affectionately did he exhort us and entreat us.

How God has added this extraordinary means to all other means that have been used.

Last of all, God sends the best means. Last of all, he sent his Son. And if they are ineffectual, then a casting off is commonly nigh.

Not one of us but what shall receive either great good or hurt by it.

God has sent him hither for some end or other.

Let us consider how remarkably he has been blessed and succeeded in other places.

If we are [not stirred up], it will look badly on [us], as though God would set us forth and distinguish us from the world as especially unworthy of his presence and deserving his frowns.

Shall bring the curse of the unlooking lord upon us [2 Kings 7:2].

God expects a better reception and improvement of his means from us than from others, for we have received much more than others.

God and men expect more.

His servant may well expect more.

God's people abroad may well expect more.

Shall it be said of us as of the Pharisees of old, “The publicans and harlots enter into [the kingdom of God before you]?” [Matthew 21:31].

If we don't improve the means as to awake out of sleep and forsake our worldliness and our {sins}, we shall [be] condemned out of our own mouths. Our mouths are full of commendation of the preacher.

We shall show ourselves very hypocritical. We have made a show of a good reception and entertainment. Like the people that cried, “Hosanna!” many tears have been shed. These tears are hypocritical tears that are followed with no lasting alteration in the frame of the heart.

If his labors should be ineffectual, our case would [be] in many respects

<!-- p. 210 -->

very parallel with that of Jerusalem in Christ's and the apostles' times [Matthew 23].

The Jewish church then was like Gideon's fleece [Jdg 6].

Let us therefore not content ourselves with talking much of the man and setting forth the excellency of his manner of delivery, his fervency, affections and the like. But let us be his epistle of commendation, written not with ink and pen {but “with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever”} [Job 19:24].

And let us seriously consider what things have been snares to us. I know the circumstances of the town are very difficult.[^025-note5]

'Tis in vain for us to expect as long as the Achan [is still within our camp {Jos 7}]. If an angel from heaven was sent […].

Let us not content ourselves only with keeping days of prayers. It will be all in vain. It was in vain for Joshua to lie upon his face [Jos 7]. Saul had the kingdom taken from him for sparing Agag [1 Samuel 15]. And what reason have we to fear that, if we {don't forsake our sins}, the kingdom of heaven will be taken from us.

Don't let us only now and then, in a cold and indifferent manner, talk about a reformation, and one and another say what a good thing it would be {to forsake our sins}; but let every one of us set ourselves in earnest to do our part in our places, every one for himself, forsaking his own heart, reflecting on past decays, confessing them to God. Each one mourning for our own {sins}, crying to God to return to [us]. Let every one reform himself in his thoughts, in his closet, in the house of God, in his family, in his dealings and conversation with his neighbor.

And let us, every one, set to it, to alter what is amiss in the state of the town, going to it with good will and resolution.

And let not these endeavors be only now, for a little while, but let 'em be continued henceforward. Let the remembrance of our past backslidings, and the dreadful consequences of them, and shame for them, make us forever to dread a returning to them anymore, and cause us most carefully to watch and guard against the first beginnings of, and all temptations to, such an apostasy.

[^025-note2]: MS: “as to arise stinking to them is a as of a dead Carcass.”

[^025-note3]: JE's omission. The insertion is based on imagery from the Parable of the Sower (Matthew 13), which JE chose as the text for a sermons series delivered immediately after Whitefield's departure from Northampton (and which he refers to below; see following note).

[^025-note4]: See JE's sermon series on Matthew 13:3-07, the Parable of the Sower, which, among other things, is an extended treatment of Whitefield. For a summary and analysis of the series, see Ava Chamberlain, “Brides of Christ and Signs of Grace: Edwards's Sermon Series on the Parable of the Wise and Foolish Virgins,” in *Jonathan Edwards's Writings: Text, Context, Interpretation*, ed. Stephen J. Stein (Bloomington, Indiana Univ. Press, 1996), 3–18.

Trumbull, *History of Northampton* [2 vols. Northampton, Gazette Printing, 1902], *2*, 93).

## Praying for the Spirit

<!-- p. 211 -->

In this fast-day sermon from November 1740, which is short on Doctrine and long on Application, Edwards berates his congregation for not being sincere in their prayers for the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Here, as elsewhere, Edwards asserts that God is a prayer-hearing God who is willing to bestow blessings on those who ask for them in a sincere manner.[^026-note1] Some blessings, however, are more “excellent” than others, and God likewise stands ready to bestow these more excellent things— things which fallen humankind desperately needs— in answer to prayer.

The Application is a call to realize sins, repent of them, and cry to God. If God is willing to give excellent blessings to his people, then they should not merely pray for temporal, outward things, which are “mean and worthless.”[^026-note2] They should instead concentrate on praying for spiritual benefits— sanctified natures, enjoying the love, presence, and communion of God, divine peace and joy, and eternal life— “which are more excellent things than the other.” And yet, though Northampton has been in “pinching want of spiritual supplies year after year,” its people have not sought to God to relieve them. Edwards upbraids the congregation, pointing out that a “great part of you pretended to have been converted a few years ago.” What has happened? Everyone now is consumed with temporal concerns; all act as if money and land are their “chief good.” In an apparent reference to the ongoing dispute over public access to the town's

<!-- p. 212 -->

common lands,[^026-note3] Edwards sardonically asks whether God converted them to “bite and devour one another and fill his house with broils and contentions.” To Edwards' mind, the divisions within the town, and the misguided priorities they engendered among its inhabitants, threatened to cause the Spirit to pass over Northampton.

Edwards then launches into an impassioned plea for united prayer to secure the greater, more excellent blessings of the Spirit's presence. His conviction of the importance of united prayer as a means of furthering revival, evident here for the first time, grew stronger as he became involved with Scottish ministers in promoting transatlantic days of prayer and in publishing the *Humble Attempt* in 1747. For now, however, Edwards' earnest message is for his congregation alone: Christ is at hand, offering himself, but another chance may not come. “Now is the time,” Edwards proclaims, “Now God is near.” Do not pray in a “cold, indifferent” manner but earnestly. Do not ask merely in words while at the same time “resisting the bestowment in practice.” Put aside old differences and come together before God, the giver of spiritual blessings. Edwards concludes by turning consecutively to the elderly, heads of families, and young people, beseeching each to do what they can, within their spheres, to cry to God earnestly for the pouring out of the Spirit on the town.

* * *

The manuscript consists of fourteen duodecimo leaves, the last of which is blank. At the top of the first page Edwards wrote, “Fast for pouring out of the Spirit, Nov. 1740.” A shorthand notation appears at the end of the second proposition, which reads, “From hence to [double bracket] preached the second time,” followed by a date of January 1750. The double bracket appears at the end of the Doctrine. There are numerous changes made to the text, some when the sermon was originally preached and some for repreaching. The later ink is easy to distinguish as it is much darker and finer. Edwards also drew pick-up lines to section off paragraphs he omitted when repreaching. An earlier reader of the manuscript wrote and underlined the numeral “40” across the verse at the top of the first page.

<!-- p. 213 -->

[^026-note1]: See, for example, “The Most High a Prayer-Hearing God” (preached Jan. 8, 1736), in Sereno Dwight, ed., *The Works of President Edwards* (10 vols. New York, 1829–30), *6*, 314–27 (hereafter referred to as Dwight ed.).

[^026-note2]: The people of Northampton and environs had reason to be concerned about temporal affairs, which may have accounted for their inattention to matters of the Spirit. Hatmaker Ebenezer Hunt wrote that the year 1740 brought, in the spring, a measles epidemic, and then later in the year, an “Abundance of cold, rainy weather. About Nov. 20 the great river froze over, & some days after there was a great rain which occasioned the greatest flood the first week in December that has been known for 35 years. After the flood ceased, there were four weeks of excessively cold weather; the eaves of the houses scarcely dropped all the time. Then we had a great thaw followed by cold weather until late in the spring.” Hunt, Diary (extracts), in Judd MS, v. 1, Mass. Series, pp. 24–25, Forbes Library, Northampton, Mass.

[^026-note3]: “The question turned upon the right of the general public to cut wood and timber upon pasture and unimproved commons.” Trumbull, *History of Northampton*, *2*, 93; see also Tracy, *Jonathan Edwards, Pastor*, 148.

## Praying for the Spirit

> How much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?

Luke 11:13.This discourse of our blessed Savior, [of] which the text is a part, is occasioned by one of his disciples asking him to teach 'em to pray. The disciples were as it were Christ's family, and he used to pray with them. Christ had just now been to prayer with this his family and, when he had done, one of his disciples said to him, “Lord, teach us to pray as John taught his disciples” [Luke 11:1]. Accordingly Christ grants their request and gives 'em for a pattern that prayer commonly called the Lord's Prayer.

But then he teaches them that merely to say the words of a prayer is not sufficient, but that they must be earnest and importunate. He represents this by the comparison of one of them going to a friend at midnight, {and saying unto him, Friend, lend me three loaves; for a friend of mine in his journey is come to me, and I have nothing to set before him. And he from within shall answer and say, Trouble me not: the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give thee. And Jesus says unto them, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth} [Luke 11:5-08]. Then Christ, to encourage 'em thus to pray for the blessings they need, assures 'em of success if they do so. Verses Luke 11:9-10, “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you. For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth; and to him that knocketh it shall be opened.” And to confirm what he had said, he compares their asking what they need of God to a child's asking food of its parents: “If a son shall ask bread of any of you that is a father, will he give him a stone? or if he ask a fish, will he for a fish give him a serpent? Or if he shall ask an egg, will he offer him a scorpion?” [vv. Luke 11:11-12]; and concludes with this verse, wherein is the text: “if ye then, being evil, know how to give good gifts unto your children: how much

<!-- p. 214 -->

more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?” [v. Luke 11:13].

Three things we may take notice of in the words of the text:

1. The blessing asked for, viz. the Holy Spirit, which is the greatest blessing that can be asked. 'Tis that by which we are sanctified and quicked, by which we have spiritual life, by which we are conformed to God and have his image, and have the redemption of Christ applied to us and so are possessed of all the blessings of his purchase. In short, 'tis that by which we are actually possessed of true holiness and happiness.

2. We may observe who this blessing is asked of, viz. a heavenly Father.

3. His readiness to bestow it when it is asked: God is[^027-note1] much more ready than earthly parents {to give good gifts unto his children}.

And there is a twofold reason implied in the manner of expression why God is more ready to bestow this blessing than earthly parents are to bestow bread on their children when they ask it. The reason is intimated by signifying:

(1) What manner of father he is of whom this gift is asked. 'Tis a heavenly Father. Not an earthly father such as children come to and ask bread of, but an heavenly Father who, as he exceeds earthly fathers in glory and excellency, so he does in goodness and love, as much as the heaven is high above the earth. “If you then, being evil,” Christ says, “know how [to give good gifts unto your children: how much more shall your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to them that ask him?]” As an heavenly Father is infinitely high above an earthly father, so heavenly love and kindness is infinitely above all earthly love. Isaiah 55:8-09, for my ways are not your ways, “saith the Lord. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.”

(2) What manner of blessing is it that is asked, viz. the Holy Spirit. The manner of expression seems plainly to carry this in it: that God will be peculiarly ready to bestow the Holy Spirit on them that ask him. If you, being evil, know how to bestow earthly good things, earthly food, on your children, how much more shall your heavenly Father be ready to bestow the Holy Spirit, that blessing which is so much better than what is earthly, that his children stand so much more in need of than they do of earthly food, and that will do 'em so much more good?

We see that earthly parents, the more need their children stand in of anything and the more beneficial and profitable it would be to 'em, the more ready they are to bestow. Surely therefore our heavenly Father will

<!-- p. 215 -->

be very ready to bestow the Holy Spirit on his children, a blessing that will be so infinitely beneficial and profitable to 'em. The blessing is as much above those earthly blessings, that earthly food which children ask for of their parents, as the heavenly Father that bestows it is above those earthly fathers. 'Tis an heavenly blessing that is bestowed as well as an heavenly Father that bestows it, and this is one reason why God will be more ready to bestow it.

If we, when we stand in need, ask earthly bread of God, he will be much more ready to bestow this upon us than earthly parents are, but much more when we ask [for] the Holy Spirit.

#### Doctrine.

#### Of the more excellent nature any blessing is that we stand in need of, the more ready God is to bestow it in answer to prayer.

With men it is otherwise. They are much more ready to bestow things of small nature.

*Prop*. I. God is a prayer-hearing God. There is scarce anything that is more frequently asserted of God in Scripture than this, that he stands ready to hear prayer. Psalms 65:2, “O thou that hearest prayer, to thee shall all flesh come.” 'Tis often said, if we seek him he will be found of us. 'Tis asserted, Psalms 34:10, that “they that seek the Lord shall not want any good thing.” [In] Psalms 50:15, we are directed to call upon God in a day of trouble and, 'tis added, he will {deliver thee, and thou shalt glorify him}. [In] Psalms 86:4-05, God is said to be plenteous in mercy to all that call upon him; and [in] Psalms 145:18-19 the Lord is said to be nigh to all that call: “The Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him, to all that call upon him in truth. He will fulfill the desire of them that fear him: he also will hear their cry, and will save them.”[^027-note2]

[*Prop*.] II. Some blessings that we need and should pray for are of a more excellent nature than others.

[*Prop*.] III. God is most ready to bestow the most excellent blessings we need in answer to prayer.

*First*. 'Tis more agreeable to the[^027-note3] infinite goodness of God's nature.

*Second*. 'Tis more agreeable to the design of God the Father in the great contrivance and work of God in redemption, more to the glory of his grace. Romans 9:23, “that he might make known the riches of his glory on

<!-- p. 216 -->

the vessels of mercy.” Ephesians 1:5-07, “Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, to the praise of the glory of his grace, wherein he hath made us accepted in the beloved. In whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace.” And ch. Ephesians 2:4-07, “But God, who is rich in mercy, for his great love wherewith he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, hath quickened us together with Christ (by grace ye are saved); and hath raised us up together, and made us sit together in heavenly places in Christ Jesus: that in the ages to come he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in his kindness toward us through Christ Jesus.” To glorify his Son, [God is ready to bestow the most excellent blessings].

What God has done in the means of procuring good for us shows [the riches of his grace]. The bestowment of the greatest mercies is more agreeable to what God has done.

*Third*. The more Christ has success, [the more God is ready to bestow the most excellent blessings]. Christ died principally to purchase blessings of the most excellent kind, and therefore he doubtless is most worthy to bestow [them]. God the Father is most forward to do that which will most gratify and answer his Son's intercession.

*Fourth*. Those desires that are expressed in prayers for the most excellent blessings are the most excellent desires, and therefore God will be most ready to gratify 'em.

*Fifth*. 'Tis especially agreeable to his covenant. There are absolute promises of these blessings here, but not of any particular temporal blessings, but only under certain conditions, provided they are best for us. These are always best. These therefore are most absolutely promised.[^027-note4]

### Application.

*Use* I. Of *Instr*.

*First*. If God be so liberal to us, we should not be straight-handed.

*Second*. Hence how much are those to blame that seek those things that are mean and worthless more than those blessings that are spiritual and divine. If God be most ready to bestow those blessings that are most excellent, then surely we should be most ready to seek 'em.

The blessings that we need are of two sorts: temporal and spiritual. Our heavenly Father knows that we have need of these things. We need food

<!-- p. 217 -->

and raiment and habitations to shelter us from the weather, and we need the help and society of friends. And some have these things in much greater plenty than others; there are different degrees of temporal enjoyments. Some han't only food and raiment, but are fed with the richest dainties, and are clothed in robes and adorned with gold and pearls, and dwell in stately palaces and possess vast treasures and reign over kingdoms.

But there is another sort of blessing that the children of men are capable of and that they stand in need of, which are through the influences of the Holy Spirit: such as the sanctification of our natures, our being made partakers of the divine nature, having the love of God shed abroad in our hearts, being united to the Son of God, being the children of God, having the presence of God, the light of his countenance and communion and fellowship with him, having divine peace and joy and living a divine life, and being hereafter possessed of eternal life and glory— which are more excellent things than the other, as high above all the temporal enjoyments of princes as heaven is high above the earth. They are infinitely the most necessary, the most profitable, the most honorable, the most pleasant and delightful and satisfying, and the most durable blessing.

And yet men, even nominal Christians, do commonly seek that other kind of enjoyments, those mere worthless things, with much the greatest earnestness. When they are in want of these outward things, they are much more concerned about their want than about their want of those divine blessings, and are far more assiduous in seeking of them. They don't need any preaching to stir them up to take thorough care to obtain those outward things. Whenever they begin to be a little in want of those things, they begin to [be] pinched for want of bread to eat, and they are hungry; and if they ben't come to that but only foresee the danger of it, how will they bestir themselves. And if they begin to suffer for want of those things, how much do they make of their sufferings. They think themselves sorrowfully out, if at any time they ben't well provided for with food and clothing, or wood to burn, or fodder for their cattle.

But when their souls pine and languish for want of spiritual blessings, when they go without spiritual food day after day and it be a time of great scarcity and even famine on that account, how little are they affected with this. They seem to be quiet with it. How little do we hear of any cry of their necessitous, distressing circumstances.

And if there be anything said about it, how it is only a few faint, ineffectual speeches. And at the same time, [they] show by their practice that they ben't very uneasy with it; they ben't awakened with their necessitous

<!-- p. 218 -->

circumstance, as when they begin to pinch for want of outward things. They can suffer month after month, if not year after year, without making any great stir about it.

And what is said about [it], as if it were a lamentable thing, is only words of course. And when God is prayed to to bestow those blessings, 'tis more as a matter of form than anything else. If rain be withheld and there be a drought, everybody is concerned. It is spoken of and lamented how the grass withers, and how the corn dies, and what a poor crop there is like to be; and there is, it may be, a great deal of praying for rain. But there may be a spiritual drought year after year, and not only in their crop, but no harvest at all in spiritual respects. Souls may be generally withering and drying up. And God is not very earnestly sought to, not because God is not as ready to bestow these blessings as the other— for he is, as has been shown, more ready to bestow them. If God were much more backward to bestow them than he is temporal blessings, yet if there were any possibility of obtaining them it would concern [us] to seek them with vastly greater earnestness and diligence than we do temporal things, they being infinitely more necessary for us and will be so much more profitable to us. But when that is not the case, but God is as ready, and more ready, {to bestow spiritual blessings}[^027-note5] as well— the things[^027-note6] more worthy to be sought on their own account— it shows the absurdity of such a negligence with respect to seeking of them, when we are so engaged in seeking the world.

If there had been such a withholding of temporal blessings in this town as there has been of spiritual blessings for some years past, yea, if it had not been one half so long, we should not have borne it so patiently as we have borne a withholding of spiritual blessings. The town would long ago [have] been alarmed, all souls, high and low, young and old, children crying to their parents and parents crying over their children, all would have been terrified. And there would doubtless have been many meetings to contest what we should do for supplies; and if supplies could not have been had without, persons would have gone far for them. Yea, if necessary provision had not been to have been had[^027-note7] nearer, we should have sent beyond the seas for provision.

But here we have lain in groaning circumstances in our souls, in pinching want of spiritual supplies year after year, and but little appearance of

<!-- p. 219 -->

a general concern about it. [We] ben't much engaged about to get supplies, though they have been ready at hand. And God has been ready to bestow if we had had an heart to seek it of him. Romans 10:6-08, “Say not in thine heart, Who shall ascend into heaven (that is, to bring Christ down from above)? Or, Who shall descend into the deep (that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead)? But what saith it? The word is nigh thee, even in thy mouth, and in thy heart: that is, the word of faith, which we preach.” We have been bestirring ourselves about other things and making a great bustle and noise. We have bestirred ourselves about a market for our cattle, and we have bestirred ourselves about the inner commons, and have very notably bestirred ourselves in some other matters;[^027-note8] but we have not stirred up ourselves to lay hold on God, or to turn from our sins and earnestly to seek the returns of God's Holy Spirit.

Let us seriously consider this day how much God has been neglected among us of late by young and old. What have we been spending our time about this four years past? Have we acted as a people that have been sensible of the wants of their precious souls? Have we behaved ourselves as a people that are sensible that they are strangers and sojourners on earth, and have no continuing city here, and that look for a city that has foundations, {whose builder and maker is God} [Hebrews 11:10]; that han't their treasure or hearts in this world but in heaven? Have we behaved ourselves as becomes the children of an heavenly Father that knows they must live upon bread of his providing?

Great part of you pretend to have been converted a few years ago, and if it was so, what was you converted for? What did [God] call you to? Had he no work for you to do? Did he call you to be idle? Did he convert you and make you his children for nothing but to pursue the dust of the earth, or did he call you into his family to bite and devour one another and fill his house with broils and contentions? And had God nothing better to bestow upon you, when he had made you his children, than a little money or land, that you seem so much to behave yourselves as if you thought this was your chief good?

'Tis time for you seriously to bethink yourselves. You have been wandering long enough. You have sojourned long enough in Meshech [Psalms 120:5]. 'Tis time now to return to your God and to come with weeping and lamentation, laying your hands on your mouths and laying in the dust before God, and to abhor yourself in dust and ashes, and to cry to God

<!-- p. 220 -->

that he would turn you from your backslidings and wash you from all those pollutions with which you have been polluting yourselves.

*Use* II may be to exhort God's people in this town earnestly to cry to God for the renewed pouring out of his Holy Spirit upon us. You see by what been said under this doctrine what great encouragement there is for us to seek this mercy of God, for this is the most excellent of all blessings that a people stand in need of; and therefore, as you have heard, God is more ready to bestow it in answer to prayer than any other blessing. And therefore there is no reason in the least to scruple but that we may obtain this blessing if we set our hearts and souls to seek it. Doubtless we may have it if we will. Christ says of it in the context, v. Luke 11:9, ask and receive.

We have seen in some instances how ready God is to hear prayer for such a blessing as rain. There have been often remarkable answers of prayer given for that blessing in time of drought. But God is much more ready to bestow spiritual showers; he is more ready to shower down of his Holy Spirit than he is rain.

And God don't only give us peculiar encouragement in his Word to ask it of him but he, at this time, is in his providence making an offer of it to us. Christ evidently, at this very time, is come, stands at the door with this blessing in his hand ready to bestow it upon us, waiting to see whether we will have it or no. Now is the time for us to cry to God for this mercy; now God is near; now is the time for us to call upon him.

Here Christ stands with this great and precious blessing in his hands. You may hear his voice. Evidently he stands at the door and knocks. Will ye have this blessing of him or no? Will you lay aside your sins, your parties, your contentions; will you leave all other things and set yourselves, with all your hearts and souls, to seek this mercy? Christ now offers that, if you will open your mouths wide, he will fill them. Don't refuse to do it, though[^027-note9] your mouth is full already with the food of your lusts that you will not spit out but hide as sweet morsels under your tongues and keep still within your mouth.

Don't now begin one and another to make excuse about your having bought oxen that you want to feed and to sell. Don't say we have bought land there, we must needs go and see it, or we needs come to a division of it; we have worldly affairs that we must needs settle. Don't refuse that glorious feast that Christ now is calling you to for the sake of your farms or your cattle or any other concerns whatsoever.

I am bold to say that God is now offering the blessing of his Holy Spirit

<!-- p. 221 -->

to this town, and I am bold to say we may have it only for asking. Indeed, if we ask in such a manner that, at the same time that we ask, we show that we have no sense of the value of the blessing we ask, and that we don't much desire it— if we ask in such a manner as implicitly to ask and deny[^027-note10] at the same time— then we have no reason to think we shall be heard.

At the same time that we pretend to ask this mercy we may, in effect, ask a denial, by two things:

*First*. By a cold, indifferent asking without any engagedness of spirit, only asking in a formal manner. Such an asking is an asking of the mouth but not of the heart. 'Tis no prayer in the sight of God. It don't at all argue want of readiness in God to bestow this blessing, that he insists on such an asking as is in some measure answerable to the value of the mercy asked for. Needful to prepare us {for this blessing is an understanding of its value. It is} best for us {to pray with engagedness of spirit}. There is more mercy shown in such a way of bestowing {this blessing than if God did not insist on an asking that is answerable to the value of the mercy asked}.

When Christ speaks in the text of God's readiness to bestow the Holy Spirit on them that ask it, and when he says in the context, ask and receive, {seek and ye shall find, knock and it shall be opened unto you}, he don't mean that God will bestow it without importunate prayer, as appears by his preceding words: “I say unto you, Though he will not rise and give him, because he is his friend, yet because of his importunity he will rise and give him as many as he needeth” (v. Luke 11:8). This explains what Christ means when he says ask, {and it shall be given you}.

*Second*. Asking in words but, at the same time, resisting the bestowment in practice. This is another way of begging a denial at the same time that we ask— asking for God's Spirit to deliver us from our sins and, at the same time, manifesting by our practice that we are not willing to be delivered, but are resolved to hold on; asking for the Spirit[^027-note11] to awaken us and make us deeply concerned about {the things of religion} and, at the same time, going into vain company and taking a course to shout out or drown all concerns; asking for a spirit of love and peace and, at the same time, showing in practice a design to continue in contention, or take a cause that directly tends to foment division. Prayers won't be heard unless they are without wrath (1 Timothy 2:8). If any this day hold old scores, let 'em not imagine [that God will hear their prayer].

This is not the way that you must seek this blessing that Christ now is offering

<!-- p. 222 -->

us. For this is indeed not to seek it [at] all, but to resist it, to seek the contrary, to ask that we may go without it. But if one really seeks this blessing, we may have it. The reason why we han't had it bestowed already is [that we have not really sought it].

I am bold to say, that if you will seek this blessing and take no more pain for it than most of you take every year for a little worldly profit, you shall have it. God will bestow it upon [you]. It is a great deal more certain that you will have success in this.

And how much more worth is it than all those temporal things you labor for from year to year? We have had experience of the worth of such a blessing, and we shall be above all inexcusable if we don't earnestly seek it.

Therefore let all souls now stir up themselves. Aged people, let them cry earnestly for such a mercy, that they may have the advantage of one more such blessed season to prepare for death in before they go out of the world, and that they may say with good old Simeon, “now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word. For mine eyes have seen thy salvation” [Luke 2:29-30].[^027-note12]

Let heads of families earnestly cry to God for this blessing. Let concern for yourselves and compassion for your poor children, that you have been the instruments of bringing into the world, stir you up. If God should not any more remarkably pour out his Spirit upon us, in all likelihood most of your poor children, the bigger part of the rising generation, will burn in hell to all eternity. Consider [that] you have been the instruments of bringing children into the world in a miserable state and condition, under wrath, and will you not earnestly seek a blessing by which they may be saved?

Let young people now earnestly cry to God. Let sinners cry to God. Let saints cry to God. Let all cry for the pouring out of the Spirit on their own souls and on others. Let all that are admitted near to God, to communion with God, improve that opportunity.

Let us put away all our abominations, cast away our idols. Let young people put away all vanity, all those diversions that have a tendency [quench the Spirit].

And let elder people have done with whatever tends to hinder, let what will become of one affair and another. Let this be your resolution: that you will not do anything that shall tend to quench the Spirit of God; that you will rather cast yourself on providence and wait upon God with respect to the issue of difficult affairs.

<!-- p. 223 -->

And seeing there is some hopeful beginning of a work of God {in this town}, let us be tender of it, deal gently with it as a newborn child, take heed that we don't quench the fire that is newly kindled by any means whatsoever. We may soon extinguish it to our shame and sorrow.

And if there be anyone here that won't do his part in seeking this blessing but, on the contrary, will, for his own worldly interest, or out of spite against any of his neighbors, or for the sake of any less does permit that which tends to quench the beginnings of a work of God, and so will not enter into the kingdom of God himself, nor suffer those that are entering to go in: how justly might it be with him as it was with the unlooking lord in Samaria, who would not hearken to what Elisha, his minister, said to him about the plenty in Samaria, who had this curse denounced upon him, that he should see it with his eyes but should not eat thereof [2 Kings 7:2]. How justly might such an one go forever without any benefit of a pouring out of the Spirit and without any of his saving influences on his heart. Let none, therefore, by any means do anything to hinder such a blessing, lest it should be thus with him.
