## They Sing a New Song

<!-- p. 224 -->

The Great Awakening was preeminently about the “New Birth,” a dramatic spiritual moment when the individual, despairing of personal ability to effect forgiveness of sins and salvation, completely surrendered his or her soul to Christ. While Edwards' preaching often dwelt on the horrors and sufferings of eternal damnation, this was not what made the revivals “new” to him. What was new was the New Birth, and Edwards' reflections on this brought forth some of his most powerful and evocative sermons.

This thanksgiving-day sermon from November 1740 belongs to the category of joyful sermons that Edwards often repeated during the awakening period. It is also distinctive for how it explicates its text, Revelation 14:3. In most of his sermons, Edwards begins by expounding the verse or verses, then moves on to the Doctrine and concludes with the Application. But this sermon can best be described as an extended Explication of the verse itself: “They sing a new song.” There is not even a customary announcement of a doctrine; rather, Edwards takes each of the words of the text and expounds on its referent in a series of propositions. Who are *they*? What does it mean to *sing*? What is *new*? What is the *song*?

Edwards begins by playing with numerology, though he remains well within his Reformed heritage in doing so. The multitude of 144,000 mentioned later in the text, he states, is of purely symbolic significance, a multiple of twelve— a holy number. The number twelve is prevalent throughout the Bible, from the twelve tribes to the twelve apostles through the multiples of twelve found in all the specifications of the Holy City in Revelation. Edwards states, “The true church is always reckoned by twelve.”

From this mystical starting point, Edwards moves on to consider who it is that sings a new song. He applies the differences between the faithful virgins (the elect, referred to in Revelation 14:4) and the “great whore” (the damned) from the vision of John to the sinners and the elect of the present day. Not only does this vision represent a reckoning with Antichrist (for Edwards and others in the Puritan tradition, the Roman Catholic church) to come, but it also illustrates the current differences among individual sinners and saved.

<!-- p. 225 -->

After discussing the implications of who sings this new song, the elect, he then develops the significance of the word “new.” Unlike the “old” songs, this new song cannot be learned, only received. And once received by the saints, it gives forth a beauty and harmony that renders all other earthly songs “wholly out of tune.” The new singing differs from the songs of love and joy before the fall, and it is distinct from the praise that believers are capable of in their fallen state— after the fall and before regeneration. The time and quality are new, following the two former states, and new in terms of excellency, superseding all praise of the Lord performed in the past. What, then, is new? The hearts of the elect, the object of praise, the matter of praise, the mercies received, and the melody of the heart.

The song itself is also distinctive. Although believers cannot know the song here on earth, they can ascertain some of the song's qualities. Besides being new, it is the most excellent song ever sung, a heavenly song greater than any that precedes it. The song is sung to celebrate “the glorious salvation of Christ and God's infinite grace and love in that work.” Always the logician, Edwards reasons that because the song honors the most glorious subject, it is only fitting that it be the most glorious song ever sung.

After discussing the singers and the song, Edwards moves on to details of how one learns the song and who is able to learn it. In fact, these aspects of the sermon hark back to earlier sermons such as *A Spiritual Understanding of Divine Things Denied to the Unregenerate*, preached in 1723, and, most famously, *A Divine and Supernatural Light*.[^028-note1] In the former sermon, Edwards made an epistemological distinction between sinner and saved, arguing that there are certain types of knowledge that are denied the sinner. This knowledge is unveiled during regeneration, and the song referred to in *They Sing a New Song* is the response to this revealed wisdom. This song is unique, therefore, not merely as a part of this spiritual knowledge but as an expression that results from it. In describing the latter, Edwards is moved to rhapsodic prose. So, too, in this sermon one senses Edwards straining to bring the full force of language to bear on the beauties of regeneration. His efforts culminate in some of the most lyrical, evocative prose ever encountered in a sermon.

* * *

<!-- p. 226 -->

The manuscript is twenty-four duodecimo leaves. At the top of the sermon Edwards wrote, “Thanksgiving, Nov. 13, 1740.” It is divided into two preaching units, which Edwards preached in the forenoon and afternoon of the same day. The symbol for the History of Redemption project is found in the upper-left-hand corner of the first page. There are markings indicating that this sermon was repreached at least two times. We have a record of one of these on the sermon, where, in what is now a very faded ink, Edwards wrote “Novem. 1752.”[^028-note2]

<!-- p. 227 -->

[^028-note1]: See *Works*, *14*, 67–96, and *Works*, *17*, 405–26.

[^028-note2]: Elsewhere we may have record of a second of these repreachings. On Dec. 30, 1741, the Rev. Daniel Wadsworth heard “Mr. Edwards” deliver a sermon on Revelation 14:3 in Hartford, Connecticut, and recorded the event in his diary, but he does not specify if “Mr. Edwards” is JE or his father. We do know that Wadsworth heard JE deliver at least one sermon during the awakening, on Matthew 11:12 (b) (595). This sermon was originally preached in Northampton in Feb. 1741, and Wadsworth heard it repreached on Apr. 15, 1741 (*Diary of Rev. Daniel Wadsworth* [Hartford, 1894]).

## They Sing a New Song

> And they sung as it were a new song before the throne, and before the four beasts, and the elders: and no man could learn that song but the hundred and forty and four thousand, which were redeemed from the earth.

Revelation 14:3.In the five first verses of this chapter we have an account of a vision that the apostle John had of the true church, that steadfastly adhered to Christ in the time of the great Antichristian apostasy wherein the world wandered after the beast and was corrupted with the delusions and idolatries of the Romish church. The Antichristian church, or the church of Rome, is in this book called the great whore, but the true church is represented as the faithful spouse of Christ. And so the souls of those men that polluted themselves with the idolatries and abominations of the church of Rome, are represented as whorish women that are false to their covenant with him to whom they had been betrothed and prostitute themselves to others. But the souls of true believers are represented as chaste virgins that kept themselves pure for Christ alone, to whom they were betrothed, that they might at last on their marriage day be presented as chaste virgins to Christ, and so were not defiled with women; i.e. when the rest of women were defiled, these kept themselves pure.

Verse Revelation 14:4, “These are they which were not defiled with women; for they are virgins. These are they which follow the Lamb whithersoever he goeth. These were redeemed from among men, being the first fruits unto God and to the Lamb.” They were redeemed from amongst men. When the greater part of men were left of God to Antichristian delusions, these were by the sovereign grace of God distinguished and saved from the infection. They followed the Lamb whithersoever he goeth. While the rest of the world wandered after the beast with seven heads and ten horns, these followed the Lamb as their shepherd wherever he went.

<!-- p. 228 -->

Though in order to follow him they must go through great sufferings, must suffer cruel persecution from the Antichristian church, yet they would not forsake him.

And their reward is that, when they had gone through these sufferings, they appear with the Lamb on Mt. Zion with his Father's name written in their foreheads. And here is represented their joy that they have as the reward of their sorrows and suffering, by the joyful songs of praise they sang in the second and third verses.

Concerning that joyful singing of praises to God that John heard in his vision, we may observe:

1. Who they are that sing, viz. the 144,000, i.e. Christ's church or company of true saints whose souls were virgins that followed {the Lamb whithersoever he went}. The number 144,000 don't signify any certain number, but a very great number, though a small number in comparison of those that had apostatized. It is a mystical number. There is some mystery in this number of 144,000. We find throughout this book that the true church is always reckoned by twelves, as there were twelve patriarchs, twelve sons of Jacob, “twelve tribes of the children of Israel” (ch. Revelation 21:12), and “twelve apostles of the Lamb” (ch. Revelation 21:14). So the New Jerusalem had twelve gates and at the gates twelve angels. And the wall of the city had twelve foundations; and the measure of the city is twelve thousand furlongs; and the measure of the wall of the city was 144 cubits, which is twelve times twelve [Revelation 21:16-17]. And so it is said the tree of life in the midst of the street of the city “bare twelve manner of fruits, and yielded her fruit” each month throughout the twelve months of the year (ch. Revelation 22:2). And so in the seventh chapter 'tis said that the number of those that were sealed in their forehead with God's seal, were twelve thousand out of each of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel— of the tribe of Judah twelve thousand, and the tribe of Reuben twelve thousand, etc.— in all, 144,000, that is, twelve times twelve thousand.

And this is the number that the true mystical church of Christ is represented by in the text: 144,000 that “were redeemed from the earth.” These are they that are represented as singing praises in the text.

2. We may observe what is said of the song that they sing. And there are two things I would observe:

(1) That 'tis said to be new song. “And they sung as it were a new song before the throne.”

(2) That it was a song peculiar to them, that none but they sung and none but they could sing and none but they could learn.

<!-- p. 229 -->

#### [Doctrine.]

And these two things that are said of the song that is sung by Christ's church of true saints are what I would make my subject of discourse this day:

I. I would show how that those that [are] Christ's redeemed ones, in the holy praises they offer up to God, do sing a new song; and,

II. How that no man can learn that song but they.

And then I would make some application.

I. I would show how that those that are true saints and redeemed from the earth, do sing a new song in the sincere praises they offer to God. And here,

*First*. I would observe, in the general, that “new” is a relative term and has respect to something else that, in comparison, is called “old.” So the song of praise that is sung by Christ's truly redeemed ones is called new with relation particularly to two things:

1. With relation to what was in man's first state under the first covenant. Man in his first state before the fall had a disposition to praise his Creator, for he was then perfectly holy. And therefore the love of God reigned in his heart, which will necessarily dispose to the praises of God. His heart was not only full of love but full of joy. Man was then in an happy state, without anything to trouble him, and everything smiling upon [him]; his heart was full of bliss so that then he could joyfully praise God in a paradise of delights.

And he had great occasion to praise God then, for God was exceeding bountiful to him, did great things for him, made him a little lower than the angels, crowned him with glory and honor and set him over the work of his hands, planted a paradise for him and set him in very honorable and happy circumstances. These things gave great occasion for songs of praise. But now the saints sing a new song. The song of praise that the redeemed of Jesus Christ sing to God is a new song compared with the joy and love and praise of man's first state.

2. The song of the redeemed saints is new when compared with what was in their fallen and natural state, as they were worldly, when they were in a miserable condition, exposed to everlasting ruin, and their hearts full of enmity against God. They might have their hearts full of outward mirth and might rejoice in their youth, and their hearts might cheer them in the days of their youth and might rejoice in their outward possessions, and

<!-- p. 230 -->

in their sinful pleasures and their temporal advancement. Natural men may fare sumptuously, and may entertain themselves with music and dancing and sing songs for their pleasure and diversion. And not only so, but men in a natural state may seem to praise God by singing psalms and spiritual songs to him.

But the song that those that are the redeemed of Christ do sing, is a new song as compared with all that ever is in their natural state.

And the song that the redeemed saints sing to God is new with relation to these things: first, as later in order of time; second, as 'tis more excellent.

(1) 'Tis called new with respect to them, as 'tis later than they and succeeds them. Anything in common speech is said to be new, with respect to something that is called old, when it is later in order of time and when it begins or [is] introduced upon the failing or ceasing of the other. Thus if a man is said to be clad in new apparel, 'tis with respect to old that he has put off. So if he has a new habitation or has a new name, it supposes some former habitation or name that ceases and is succeeded by what now is. To this purpose is the Apostle's observation on the gospel covenant being called a “new covenant.” Hebrews 8:13, “In that he saith, A new covenant, he hath made the first old. Now that which decayeth and waxeth old is ready to vanish away.”

The song that is sung by the saints is called a new song in this respect, as it is founded in that great renewing work of God's power and grace, the work of redemption, or the restoration and renovation of things by Jesus Christ.

The first Adam failed in the work that he was to do, and God has appointed us a new surety. There is a new covenant, and a new and living way of entering into the Holy of Holies.

The world was as it were destroyed by the fall. And Christ came into the world as it were to create a new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17). The songs that are sung in this new creation are not such as were sung in the old. Everything there is new. God, when about to create the new heavens and new earth, says, Revelation 21:5, “Behold, I make all things new.”

Particularly that song is founded in the great works of God, whereby he brings to pass a new state of things.

*1*. That great work that was wrought, by which redemption was wrought out for fallen [man], consisting in the incarnation, life, death and resurrection of our blessed Redeemer. These things were new things, such as the eyes of angels nor men ever beheld before. That the Son of God should be incarnate, that God should become man, was a new thing. That the Lord of glory should become a man of sorrows, that he that was God

<!-- p. 231 -->

over all, blessed forevermore, should die such an accursed death, were new and strange and wonderful things.

The works of God that were consequent on this were new things, such as the pouring out of [the] Spirit that was in the days of the Apostle, the calling of the Gentiles from heathenism, the conversion of the heathen world.

And there yet remain new things of that nature to be accomplished, in the bringing the whole world to the Christian faith and settling the world in that state of light, peace and holiness that shall be in the latter days, when the wolf shall dwell with the lamb. These things are spoken of as new things. Isaiah 42:9, “Behold, the former things are come to pass, and new things do I declare: before they spring forth I tell you of them.” And then it follows in the next verse, “Sing unto the Lord a new song, and his praise from the end of the earth.” And so Isaiah 43:18-20, “Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing; now it shall spring forth; shall ye not know it? I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert. The beast of the field shall honor me, the dragons and the owls: because I give waters in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert, to give drink to my people, my chosen.” The city of God founded by this work of redemption is called the New Jerusalem. These redeemed ones, that sing the new song spoken of in the text, are the inhabitants of the city.

This glorious work of God in redemption lays a foundation for this new song, as it supplies new matter for a song of praise, things to be the subject and theme of praise that are new and such as neither men nor angels never sung of, never saw nor heard of before.

Man in innocency had many glorious works of God to sing of, works of creation and {God's goodness}. But the redeemed of Christ have a new song to sing.

Man in innocency had great instances of God's goodness to make the subject of songs of praise. But {the redeemed of Christ have a new song to sing}.

The angels had great things to sing of, and we read that they “sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy” (Job 38:7).

Moses and the children of Israel, when they were redeemed out of Egypt by {God}, had great things to sing of. They sang the song of Moses.

But they that are redeemed by the wonderful works which Christ has wrought from captivity to the devil, from eternal destruction, have a new song to sing. They have not only the song of Moses but also the song of the Lamb (Revelation 15:3).

<!-- p. 232 -->

God gave Adam an earthly paradise and he gave the children of Israel an earthly Canaan, and they had great cause to sing praises to God. But they to whom God gives the heavenly Canaan and an heavenly paradise, have a new song to sing of works of God's love and goodness, far beyond those.

The old Jerusalem, which Israel were possessed of by the warlike acts of David redeeming it out of the hands of the Jebusites, was a glorious city. There was the temple built, a most magnificent structure, and the people of that city had great cause of praise. But they that are by Christ entitled to the New Jerusalem, have a new song to sing of the privileges and blessings of a city very diverse from that; and as hereby[^029-note1] the glorious gospel of Christ is published, the world is supplied with that new word of life out of which this new song is learned; and also as hereby is purchased a new ability and disposition to sing praise to God.

*2*. This new song of the saints is founded in the great work of God in renewing their nature, and the benefits that attend. Both this and the other are parts of the work of redemption in its largest extent— only that that was spoken of before was the perpetration, and this is the application, of redemption. Both belong to the work of the new creation.

By this work of God in renewing the heart, the man that is the subject of it becomes a new creature or is a new man, as it is often said in Scripture. And therefore no wonder that his song is new: for we are told that “old things are passed away” and “all things become new with him” [2 Corinthians 5:17]. [The] hearts of the redeemed are new. He has a new spirit put within him (Ezekiel 11:19). Their natures are new. In some sense their bodies are new. They have new eyes. They are renewed in the whole man. They are said to be “a new lump,” having put away “the old leaven” (1 Corinthians 5:7). They are newborn babes (1 Peter 2:2). They have new garments, for their filthy garments are taken away and they are clothed with change of raiment. And they have a new name. Revelation 2:17, “He that overcometh I will give him a white stone, and in the stone a new name written, which no man knoweth saving he that receiveth it.” And ch. Revelation 3:12, “I will write upon him my new name.”

And as other things concerning 'em are new, so they sing a new song. The song they then sing is new in several respects:

a. They have a new object of praise. They now praise him that sits upon the throne and the Lamb who, though they are from everlasting, are new to them. They are newly known by them.

<!-- p. 233 -->

When they were unknown, they were never truly praised by them. But now God and Christ are revealed to them in that infinite glory and goodness whereby they are worthy to be praised.

b. They have new matter of praise. And they now have an understanding of those glorious works of God's power and wisdom and infinite mercy and love that the angels desire to look into and do praise God for, which they never understood before.

The wisdom of God in the glorious work of redemption, and the sovereign grace of God, and dying love of Christ to sinners, are new things to them. They now can make 'em the matter of their songs, but never could before.

And then they have received new mercies themselves. God has done great things for them that are new things. God has delivered [them] “out of the pit wherein is no water” [Zechariah 9:11]. He has taken their feet out of the miry clay and set 'em upon a rock. Psalms 40:2-03, “He brought me up also out of an horrible pit, out of the miry clay, and set my feet upon a rock, and established my goings. And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the Lord.” He has delivered out of spiritual captivity, has by his mighty power overcome the strong man armed. He has gloriously rode forth in the chariots of salvation in their behalf. He has broken the heads of Leviathan in pieces, has subdued Satan under their feet, and caused them to tread on the lion and adder and to trample under foot the young lion and dragon [Psalms 91:13]. He has called 'em out of darkness into marvelous light. They who were far off are made nigh by the blood of Christ. God has forgiven all their sins and blotted 'em out as a thick cloud. And they have received the adoption of children. God is become their father, and they are become God's sons and daughters.

Here is new matter of praise for [them], matter enough to fill up a new song and to keep them singing to all eternity.[^029-note2]

c. The melody of the heart with which they sing is new. Before they knew but how to sing praise to God: they were unlearned; they could make no melody in God's ear; they had no skill in divine music; they had not learned the tune, nor could they sound one harmonious note. Their hearts were like an instrument that is unstrung and broken, wholly out of tune. The notes were most jarring and discordant. If they pretended to sing praise to God, it was howling and not singing in God's ears.

<!-- p. 234 -->

But now God has put their hearts in tune. Now there is some inward harmony. Now there is divine harmony that is melodious unto God.

Thus the song that the saints sing is new with respect to what went before, as 'tis later, and as it succeeds and is introduced on the decay and removal of it.

(2) 'Tis called a new song, as 'tis more excellent than what preceded. Old things are removed, and new ones introduced, for the sake of their preferableness and superior excellency. Men are not wont to pull down an old house, to build a new one in its place, but that they may have a better habitation. So they don't put off their old garments, to put on new, but that they may be better clothed. And especially is it so in all God's dispensations, whereby he removes that which is old to make way for something new. The old covenant is abolished and a new covenant established that has a better surety and better promises. The old way into the Holy of Holies is abolished and a better way prepared, a new and living way. The old priesthood of Aaron ceases, and the new priesthood of Christ introduced that is after the order of Melchizedek (Psalms 110:4, Hebrews 5:6), established by the word of the oath forevermore. The old creation vanishes away, and God creates a “new heavens and new earth” so much more excellent than the former, that 'tis said the former shall not be mentioned “nor come into mind” [Isaiah 65:17]. The New Jerusalem is more excellent than the old.

And so the new song that is sung by the redeemed from the earth is more excellent than anything that preceded. It is the most excellent song that ever is sung by any of the children of men.

We often read in Scripture of a new song. And whenever it is mentioned, there is evidently respect to its excellency in its being so called. So Psalms 33:1-03, “Rejoice in the Lord, O ye righteous: for praise is comely for the upright. Praise the Lord with harp: sing unto him with the psaltery and an instrument of ten strings. Sing unto him a new song; play skillfully with a loud noise.” So Psalms 96:4, at [the] beginning, “For the Lord is great, and greatly to be praised.” So the beginning of Psalms 98, “O sing unto the Lord a new song; for he hath done marvelous things.” So Psalms 144:9 and Psalms 149:1, and Isaiah 42:10.

This song is more excellent than anything that was before the fall. The matter of the song is more glorious. The subject matter of the new song is principally the glorious salvation of Christ and God's infinite grace and love in that work, as appears by Revelation 5:9. “And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation.”

<!-- p. 235 -->

This work of God is more wonderful and more glorious by far than anything that Adam in innocency had to praise God. Yea, this is the most glorious subject that the angels in heaven themselves have for their songs. They once sang praises to God for the work of creation, when God laid the foundations {of the earth} and the morning stars sang together. But now, since they have seen the work of redemption, these morning stars sing a new song, and the work of redemption is principally the subject of their praises; as now that is their tune, “Worthy is the Lamb that was slain,” is in Revelation 5:11-12, “And I beheld, and I heard the voice of many angels round about the throne and the beasts and the elders: and the number of them was ten thousand times ten thousand, and thousands of thousands; saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb that was slain to receive power, and riches, and wisdom, and strength, and honor, and glory, and blessing.” The benefits that the saints receive by Christ are far beyond anything that our first parents enjoyed in innocency. They had happiness indeed, but they had no confirmation of it. They had no promise that they should never lose it, but {rather a threat they should lose it}.

And besides, their privileges are greater in other respects. {They have a} more excellent union {with God, a} greater manifestation of the love of God, {and} a better inheritance.

So their song is far more excellent than anything that was before their conversion, as much more excellent than all their external formal praises that they offered to God before conversion as light is more excellent than darkness, or as gold is more precious than the dirt. One word or note of this new song, as sung by a sincere heart, is worth more in God's account than all the praises of all the formal professors of religion from the beginning of the world to the end of it.[^029-note3]

I come, in the

[II.] Second place, to show how no man can learn that song but Christ's redeemed ones.

This will be manifest by considering two things:

*First*. By considering what things are requisite in order to learning this song.

*Second*. How these requisites are obtained.

*First*. By considering what things are requisite in order to men's learning this song. And there are two things: first, that they should be able to know the song; and second, that they should have ability to sing it. Learning a song implies a learning the song that is to be sung so as to have that

<!-- p. 236 -->

in our minds. But that is not all that is necessary: but we must also learn to sing. Men may have learned the words of a song by heart, and yet not have learned the tune.

1. Therefore, in order to men's being able to sing this new song, 'tis requisite that they should be able to know the song. They must know what is to be sung. They must have the knowledge of those things that are the subject matter of the song. The song is spiritual, and the things that are the subject matter of it are spiritual and divine: the glorious perfections and excellencies of God, especially in that new and most excellent manifestation of them that is made in the works of the new creation by Jesus Christ; the glory of God as it shines in the face of Christ; the glory of God's power and wisdom and holiness, justice and faithfulness, as manifested by him; and especially the infinite and glorious riches of divine grace and love in a Redeemer, appearing in the incarnation, life, {death and resurrection} of Christ, and in the appointed way of salvation by Christ, by faith in him; and also as appearing in the application of redemption, the glory of God and Christ as appearing in the conversion of the soul and in carrying on the work of grace unto glory.

Such things as these are the matter of this song, and therefore, in order to the song's being learned, these things must be learned. He that is ignorant of these things is ignorant of the new song.

2. There must be an ability to sing. Not only the matter of the song must be learnt, but also the music of the song. But the music of this tune consists in the melody of the heart. Ephesians 5:19, “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord.” As in order to learn the music of other songs, the voice must be tuned, so in order to learn the music of this song, the heart must be tuned. The music of this new song consists in holy admiration, in exalting thoughts of the glory of God and the Lamb and the great things of the gospel; and in divine love, in loving God for his excellency appearing in the face of Christ, in holy rejoicing in God and in delight and complacence of the soul in Jesus, whereby we, having not seen him, do love him and “rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory” [1 Peter 1:8]. They that are unacquainted with this spiritual melody, they can't learn to sing that new song.

These are the things that are requisite to the learning this song.

*Second*. We may consider how [these] requisites are obtained.

1. They are the fruit of the redemption or purchase of Jesus Christ. Christ has purchased for a certain number that knowledge of the glorious excellency of God and Christ, and of the infinite riches of his grace

<!-- p. 237 -->

appearing in the way of salvation. That excellent heavenly light that shines into the soul, and gives it a view and understanding of those excellent things, is a blessing purchased at the price of Christ's precious blood. And so that ability, that harmony of the soul and melody of the heart, consisting in holy love and joy and delight in God and Christ, is a precious benefit that is the fruit of the same purchase. This heavenly melody is dear; it costs Christ's precious blood.

And if these things cannot be obtained any other way than by the redemption [of Christ], then we may see the reason why none can obtain them but those that are redeemed by Christ. As 'tis said in the text, “no man could learn but the {hundred and forty and four thousand} that were redeemed from the earth.”

2. These things are imparted in the saving work of God's Spirit on the soul. In this work it is that God gives the soul that divine light and knowledge of the glorious and joyful things that the gospel reveals, which are the subject of this song.

And in this work it is that the heart is put in tune, and it is put into a capacity and disposition truly and sincerely to praise God and to make that heavenly melody, which is made in singing this new song, by exercising these divine principles of divine love and divine joy. “The love of God is shed abroad” in the heart by the Holy Ghost (Romans 5:5). And spiritual rejoicing is called “joy in the Holy Ghost” [Romans 14:17]. This saving work of God in the heart is redemption by power, as the other is redemption by purchase. And seeing it is thus— that this knowledge of the things to be sung, and the ability to make the melody of the song, is imparted no other way than by the saving work of the Spirit, whereby the soul is redeemed by power— hence we may see another reason why no man can learn that song but they that are redeemed. Other men are dumb and dead as to any such heavenly exercise as this. They can exalt their idols, but they can't exalt God. They can rejoice in the objects of their lusts, in their worldliness and in their carnal pleasures, but they can't rejoice in Christ Jesus. They can howl, but they can't sing the new song.

This song, whenever it is learnt, must be learned out of the gospel. But none can truly understand the gospel of Jesus Christ but his redeemed ones.[^029-note4]

But I now proceed to make application of what you have heard this day concerning this new song.

<!-- p. 238 -->

#### Application.

*Use* I may be of *Warning*, to warn young people against learning and singing lewd songs. How very disagreeable will that be for those that hope either that they are or shall be of that blessed holy company spoken of in the text, whose souls are pure chaste virgins that follow the Lamb, and that shall be with the Lamb on Mt. Zion in white robes, and shall forever sing the new song of holy praises to God and the Lamb.

Thus it is with you: you hope to be of this company, and hope that singing this divine song shall be your eternal exercise. If you knew that it would not be so, how would you be terrified and amazed. If it should now be told you from heaven, that you never should learn this song and never be admitted into that glorious company that sing it, how would it astonish you. With what frighted amazed hearts would you go out of the meeting house, if your despair would suffer you to go out and your astonishment would not disenable you from going anywhere.

But you depend upon being sometime or other of that society and learning this song. To what purpose else is it that you come to meeting and attend any of the means of grace?

And if this be the case, why will you sing songs of so disagreeable and contrary a nature— vile, impure songs that you should abhor to take into your mouth, that tend to stir up lusts and to pollute the soul, and make it like unclean devils? Such songs are little better than songs of praise to the devil. You serve your lusts and serve Satan by them.

Some of you hope that you already belong to that holy company on Mt. Zion, and that you have already learned that song. If it be so, nothing can be more shocking than the thought of such an one employing his voice in singing vain lewd songs. Think with yourself how the mind of the apostle John would have been shocked and put into a strange surprise, when he saw the vision that we have an account of in the text and context, and saw the Lamb on Mt. Zion with that holy company with him of 144,000 that were redeemed from the earth, and heard that sweet and excellent melody of the new song they sung, if then, of a sudden, he had perceived some of the company leave off their new and holy song and break out in lewd laughter and jollity, singing some filthy, bawdy song. How amazing do you think this would have been to him? You that think yourselves of the redeemed from amongst men should abhor such a thing as bad as you would abhor hell itself. And if you are indeed of that company, as you think yourself to be, you will abhor it. 'Tis impossible it should be otherwise. You will not practice it. You will abhor to do so more than to take the

<!-- p. 239 -->

corruption of the most filthy Achan into your mouth [Jos 7]. If you have a sanctified nature, such songs will stink in your nostrils and grate upon your ears more than the most hideous howlings.

[*Use*] II is of *Exhortation* to all earnestly to seek that they may learn this new song. You that never have been converted and are not of that company that are with the Lamb, but are poor perishing sinners, aliens and strangers, are far off, are the children of the night and of darkness, and are the children of that wicked one, wretched slaves of sin and Satan: let what you have heard stir up in you an earnest desire to be converted, that you may also sing that new song. Hitherto you knew not what it means; 'tis in a language you don't understand.

And you that hope you are converted, to you also is this word of exhortation. Earnestly seek that you may learn to sing this new song. If you have been taught of God, and do already know something of it, yet how very imperfectly have you learned it. You make but a poor head at least at singing this song. You are now beginners in it, and how miserably do you blunder in it. You are like children that do but lisp and stammer.

This song is a song of perfect harmony, of sweet and heavenly melody; but so imperfectly have you learned it that when you do your best at singing of it, there are a great many jarring discordant notes. There are many other sounds mixed that don't belong to the song and that do greatly mar the music. O what need have you to seek earnestly that you may better learn this excellent song, that you may sing it more regularly and make more of that excellent melody that belongs to it!

Therefore let all that are here present look upon this exhortation as belonging to them, and seek to learn this new song. And here, let the following things be considered:

*First*. The melody of this song is most acceptable to God. The great God is delighted with it. 'Tis acceptable to Jesus Christ. He accepts of such praise, and never rejects it. If we sing this new song in our hearts when we are alone and retired from the world, to spend some time in secret between God and our own souls, Christ will come to us and will as it were listen to the melodious notes, and will reward us with some token of his favor. If we sing this new song in our public assemblies, it will be to worship God in the beauty of holiness, and will be the way to have God delighting to be in the midst of us. In singing this new song to God and the Lamb, our thanksgiving days will be acceptable to God. This song is more pleasing to God than the offering up of thousands of rams and ten thousands of rivers of oil.

*Second*. This song is not only acceptable to God, but most sweet and delightful

<!-- p. 240 -->

to the soul of him that sings it. It is the pleasantest song in the world. The singing of songs is used as a token of mirth and rejoicing. Singing and rejoicing are wont to go together. When carnal persons meet together to sing songs, it is in token of carnal mirth. But there is no joy like that which is expressed in singing this new song. This is that pleasure that the Psalmist speaks of in Psalms 135:3, “sing praises unto his name; for it is pleasant.” And so Psalms 147:1, “Praise ye the Lord: for it is good to sing praises unto our God; for it is pleasant; and praise is comely.” The melody is pleasant to the angels, and pleasant to the Lamb of God, and pleasant to him that sits upon the throne, and most pleasant to the soul that makes the melody. The act of praise is an abundant reward to itself. He that sings it has communion with God in it, for in the same time that there flows a stream of love out of the heart towards God, there flows a more full stream of love from God into the soul. At the same time that he praises God with a sweet voice, Christ with a sweeter voice speaks peace to the soul and manifests his love to it.

As 'tis said in the text, that no man could learn that song but the redeemed from the earth, so no man knows the sweetness or intermeddles with the joy of this song but they.

The sweetness and delight is too excellent for any but they. God will not suffer any but those that are his peculiar favorites to taste it.

How great does the rejoicing of this company that John saw in his vision seem to be in singing this sweet song. So engaged were they in it, and so loud and sweet was the melody of their united voices, that John seems not know how to express it, and therefore uses various similitudes. Says he, it was “as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of a great thunder,” and as “the voice of harpers harping with their harps” [Revelation 14:2]. The joy and praise and melody were inexpressible.

*Third*. This song is fit to be sung in the mournful and sorrowful times. We have always reason to sing it, whatever afflictions we may be under, and there is support and joy to be had in the melody of it in the darkest times. This is the song that God gives in the night (Job 35:10), i.e. in the night of affliction.

'Tis very proper to sing this new song on a death bed. And many of the saints have sung it then, and thereby have triumphed over death; yea, many have sung this new song in the flames of martyrdom and have exulted in the midst of torments. The joy and sweetness of it is enough to carry the soul above pain and above the cruelty of men and devils.

*Fourth*. This is the song that is sung by the glorious company in heaven. Singing this song is the principal employment of that assembly, in which

<!-- p. 241 -->

they employ themselves continually and of which they are never weary. With the melody of this song does heaven ring, as with the voice of many waters and the voice of a great thunder, as in the verse before the text: “And I heard a voice from heaven as the voice of many waters, and as the voice of a great thunder: and I heard the voice of harpers harping with their harps.”[^029-note5]

So far therefore as we sing this song on earth, so much shall we have the prelibations of heaven. In this way we shall have something of heaven in our closets and in our families.[^029-note6] And this will make our public assemblies some image of heaven, and will make our sabbath days and thanksgiving days some resemblance of that eternal sabbath and thanksgiving that is solemnized by that innumerable company of angels and spirits of just men made perfect.

*Fifth*. This song is that which is sung by Jesus Christ himself in heaven, and therefore 'tis called the song of the Lamb. As 'tis promised to believers that they shall be partakers with Christ in the honor of his new name (Revelation 3:12), so they shall also partake with him in the joy of his new song. When Christ rose from the dead and ascended into heaven, then he received a new name, i.e. he was as God-man advanced to new honor. So at the same time he began then to sing a new song, which he sings still and will sing to all eternity.

Christ is the head of the church, the leader of all the 144,000 that are on Mt. Zion with him, and when they sing that new song, they do but follow him. 'Tis he that leads them the way in it, as the elder brother and priest of the family, so far as the song is to praise God the Father. Christ, when he was upon earth in his state of humiliation, went mourning; and when he was in the garden in his agony, he groaned and cried with strong crying and tears, and when he was on the cross he cried out, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” [Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34]. But when he ascended into heaven, then his sorrow was turned into joy, and his mourning and crying into singing. And this joy believers shall partake with him in. John 17:13, “That my joy may be fulfilled in yourselves.”

*Sixth*. If you learn this song and begin to sing it here, you will sing it to all eternity. They that once learn this song never forget it. The life that Christ gives his saints is everlasting life. The new name he gives them is an everlasting name, that shall not be cut off. And so the new song that he teaches them is an everlasting song.

<!-- p. 242 -->

They that now learn this new song, the time will soon come when they shall do nothing but sing. They shall cry and mourn no more. Isaiah 35:10, “And the ransomed of the Lord shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and mourning shall flee away.”

In a little time, and they shall sing the new song with saints and angels in heaven, and shall sing it there with Jesus Christ. And at the day of judgment, when Christ shall have gathered together all his elect and they shall be all together in complete glory, then shall they ascend up to heaven with Christ and enter into that glorious city with the voice of singing, singing praises to God the Father. Then will Christ's heart rejoice, and he will sing to God, and they shall rejoice and sing with him.

*Seventh*. In vain will all our singing be if we han't learned to sing this song. We may sing psalms sabbath after sabbath, we may keep thanksgiving days; but no song is acceptable to God but this. Without this, all our learning the rule of singing and endeavors to perfect ourselves in that art will be in vain. We shall make no melody to God.

*Eighth*. Consider how soon an end will be put to all other songs and all other singing but singing this song. As to those lewd songs that are sung by vain youth, how quickly are their mouths stopped. How soon does death come and turn their tone. And as to the formal singing of hypocrites, an end will soon be put to it, and they shall never sing anymore but, instead of that, shall curse and blaspheme with devils in hell.[^029-note7] And the time will come when this world will come to an end and then, after that, there never shall be any other song or any other singing remaining but this that we have heard of.

*Ninth*. If you don't learn to sing this new song, the time will soon come, that when God's servants “sing for joy of heart, you shall mourn for sorrow of heart and howl for vexation of spirit” (Isaiah 65:14). You shall see your neighbors hereafter full of joy and shall hear them singing, and you shall see “many come from the east and from the west, and shall sit down with Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, in the kingdom of heaven” [Matthew 8:11], falling down in the kingdom of God, singing the new song, when you shall wail and gnash your teeth, and shall howl with devils with most doleful and dolorous lamentations and cries. Thus it shall be at the day of judgment, when you shall see a shining glorious company at the right hand of Christ singing the new song, and you shall be at the left among devils and shall shriek with dismal outcries at the hearing of that dreadful sentence,

<!-- p. 243 -->

“Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels” [Matthew 25:41]. And consider that there never, never will be an end to that mourning and that howling.

So many and great motives are there, together with many more that might be mentioned, to induce earnestly to seek that we may learn this song.

I will conclude with three things that may be of direction to [those] that are desirous of learning this new song:

1. 'Tis Christ that must teach this song. You can learn it of no other way. 'Tis he that is the author of the song, and the skill of those that can sing it is too excellent for any other to impart but Christ. As there is none that can learn [it] but those that are “redeemed from the earth,” so there is no creature in heaven or earth that can teach it.[^029-note8]

Therefore you must go to God. You must cry to him to grant you instruction, to impart the knowledge of the subject matter of this song, and to put your heart in tune, [to] give you that blessed skill.

2. The way for you to learn this new song, is first to mourn with a broken heart for sin. Christ says in Matthew 5:4, “Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted”; and in the sixth [chapter] of Luke, v. Luke 6:21, “Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh.” And 'tis said in the one hundred and twenty-sixth psalm, v. Psalms 126:6, that “He that goes forth weeping, bearing precious seed, shall doubtless come again with rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.”

So the greater your sense is of sin and of your own utter unworthiness upon that account, and the deeper your mourning is for it, the more perfectly are you like to learn the new song and to sing it with greater joy and exultation of spirit.

They that deeply mourn for sin shall have that fulfilled to 'em, in Isaiah 61:3, “To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness; that they might be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that he might be glorified.”

3. In order to learn the new song, you must hear the melody of the voice of Christ in the gospel. You have heard that the glorious gospel is that out of which this song is to be learned, and that 'tis Christ that must teach it. And this is the way that he teaches it: by causing the soul to hear the melody of his own voice in the gospel.

<!-- p. 244 -->

'Tis Christ that speaks to us in the gospel. Many hear his words, but they perceive no sweetness in them. They perceive no pleasantness in his voice, in the doctrines and invitations and promises of the gospel. 'Tis all an insipid thing and dead letter to them. But to the godly, Christ's mouth is found to be most sweet. You must perceive the sweetness of the voice. You must see the glory of those doctrines, and the sweetness of those invitations, and the exceeding preciousness of those promises.

This must teach you those things that must be the subject of your song. And this must draw your heart, and put it into tune, and fill it with love and joy, which is the excellent harmony and heavenly melody of the soul.

[^029-note2]: In revising for repreaching, JE changed this sentence to read as follows: “Here is new matter of praise for [them], matter enough to fill up an endless song of praise that will keep them singing to all eternity.”

[^029-note3]: The first preaching unit ends here. JE's brief recapitulation of the text and propositions has been omitted.

[^029-note4]: JE deletes: “This song is too excellent for men to attain to the knowledge of themselves, and 'tis too excellent for men or angels to teach.”

[^029-note5]: In revising for repreaching, JE crossed out the quotation of this verse.

[^029-note6]: I.e. in personal and family devotions.

[^029-note7]: In revising for repreaching, JE crossed out the words “in hell.”

[^029-note8]: Before repreaching this sermon, JE changed this sentence to read as follows: “As there is none that can learn [it] but those that are ‘redeemed from the earth,’ so there is none other can teach it but the Redeemer.”

## Bringing the Ark to Zion a Second Time

<!-- p. 245 -->

In this sermon from December 1740, Edwards uses typology to issue both a pointed warning and an exhortation to his flock. Like the Israelites of old under David, the inhabitants of Northampton had enjoyed in the past “special tokens and privileges of God's presence,” but they have incurred God's anger and caused his departure because of their errors. Using the biblical account of the return of the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem in 1 Chronicles 15, Edwards warns his people not to abuse the new outpouring of God's Spirit.[^030-note1] His instructions on the proper way to do this arise from what he sees as the particular problems from which his people suffer.

Edwards begins by rehearsing some of the history of the ark of the covenant, the special and powerful token of God's presence among the ancient Israelites. Because of Israel's sins, God allowed the ark to be taken for a time by the Philistines. On its return, the ark was kept at Kirjath-jearim, “a place in the outskirts of the land.” When David became king, the Israelites attempted to bring the ark to Jerusalem. But they did so without due consideration and reverence. When the cart on which the ark was conveyed was about to topple, an attendant named Uzzah touched the ark to prevent it from falling, for which he was struck dead. Therefore the ark was kept at the house of Obed-edom, a “stranger.” Only on the second attempt were the Israelites successful in bringing the ark home to Jerusalem, because this time they properly heeded God's directions.

Edwards quickly dispenses with the doctrinal handling of the story. Tokens of God's presence should be treated in a due manner; people have suffered for ill treatment of such privileges, and, if they continue in error, can expect to suffer more than previously. The preacher is intent on pressing home the lesson to “this church and congregation” and so is long on Application here. For Edwards, the special token of God's presence in Northampton has been its revival seasons, particularly the most recent

<!-- p. 246 -->

one of 1734–35. Then was the greatest blessing of all, but it was abused and God departed. God demonstrated his anger by visiting certain “breaches” upon the town: Edwards cites Joseph Hawley's suicide in 1735 and the falling of the church gallery two years later.

With the naming of these ominous events, so engrained in the town's collective memory, Edwards embarks upon a meticulous indictment of the congregation's sins during the last awakening to help them avoid repeating them this time around. All the while, he sustains the typological identity that New Englanders felt they shared with Israel of old, though here that identity works to condemn them. When the people of Israel tried to bring the ark to Zion the first time, they were proud, irreverent, and disobedient. So were the people of Northampton triply culpable during 1734 and 1735.

What is striking about the rest of the sermon is Edwards' focus upon curtailing freedom of religious speech— not the right itself, but rather the abuse of it. Privately at this time, as in “Images,” nos. 104 and 120, Edwards is meditating on the importance of “bridling” certain members of the body, especially the tongue.[^030-note2] For the specific purpose of this sermon, he points out the most heinous sin of Israel in this case was that they “placed religion rather in profession and show than in obedience.”

Here Edwards provided himself with the opening he needed to enumerate Northampton's shortcomings, in particular its hypocritical profession. In “Miscellanies,” no. 951, written shortly after this sermon, Edwards derided “talk of experiences”: “The profession that persons make of the divine gifts they have received from God, and their declaring their experiences abroad, is like the wind that accompanies a cloud.”[^030-note3] This private observation was based directly on what Edwards saw in his congregants. So too was his derision of talk in this sermon. During the previous revival, the people of Northampton, like the Israelites, were lifted up with pride; they bragged widely of the great work in the town and of their personal experiences. Civic pride combined with individual conceit to drive away the Spirit. For example, people made a “righteousness of spiritual experience.” Converts asserted that they were “wholly brought off” from their own self-righteousness. This, Edwards asserts— and here is the key pastoral problem in this sermon— is “a great mistake”; self-righteous principles are not eliminated by conversion but remain in the regenerate as well as the unregenerate. Unfortunately, this mistaken assumption only

<!-- p. 247 -->

encouraged individuals “to set out your own experience as much as you could do,” or to relate their experience in a boastful manner and in other inappropriate ways.

Having warned his people to guard their speech, Edwards presents his formula for not quenching the Spirit. In everything, he warns, we should not forget our unworthiness. Be more circumspect; keep watch on your hearts and behavior; heed God's commands; be more humble in talking about your experiences, and do not treat religious things in a “light manner.” How confident Edwards was that his people would follow his exhortations is debatable. But it is clear from this sermon, as well as others in this period, that he was determined to establish proper limits this time around, even if it perhaps meant a lower degree of religious excitement.

* * *

The sermon consists of one booklet of sixteen duodecimo leaves. At the top of the first page Edwards inscribed the date, “Decem. 1740.” At a later date he drew five “decibel” marks on the front page, apparently an indication that the sermon was a personal favorite of his or of his audiences or both. While there are no repreaching notations, there are some later additions and changes made by Edwards in the sermon. Also, on the last page, written in pencil by a nineteenth-century owner of the manuscript who apparently repreached it himself, is a list that reads: “Baptism. Catechising. Journey. Proclamation. Service at 1:30 to be signified by the ringing of the bell.”

Leaves 9 and 10 are made from a piece of a discarded letter by Edwards. What remains of the text reads, “Rev. and dear sir, Brother Pierpont of New Haven sometime since sent to me and my wife, to desire that we would come down the […].” In all probability, James Pierpont had invited his sister and brother-in-law down to New Haven for the Yale College commencement in September. Edwards' note, written to Pierpont in that month, states that the couple would indeed come, weather permitting.[^030-note4] The note also mentions that Edwards has “sent word of it already to Mr. Russell,” i.e. the Rev. William Russell of Wethersfield, to whom this discarded letter may have been directed.

<!-- p. 248 -->

[^030-note1]: In early 1739, JE had written a lengthy and intricate entry on Psalms 68, written on occasion of the ark's arrival on Mt. Zion, in “Notes on Scripture,” no. 319, in which he states that the psalm “was the most remarkable type of the ascension of Christ that we have in the Old Testament” (*Works*, *15*, 297–302).

[^030-note2]: *Works*, *11*, 90–91, 95.

[^030-note3]: *Works of Jonathan Edwards*, *20*, *“Miscellanies,” 833–1152*, ed. Amy Plantinga Pauw (New Haven, Yale Univ. Press, 2002), 210.

[^030-note4]: JE to James Pierpont, [Sept. 1740], in *Works*, *16*, 86.

## Bringing the Ark to Zion a Second Time

> And said unto them, Ye are the chief of the fathers of the Levites: sanctify yourselves, both ye and your brethren, that you may bring up the ark of Lord God of Israel unto the place that I have prepared for it. For because ye did it not at the first, the Lord our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order.

I Chronicles 15:12–13.Here I would observe,

1. What that affair is about which David here gives charge, viz. the affair of bringing up the ark into Zion, to the place that David had prepared for it. The ark was a type of Christ, and it was the symbol of the divine presence with that people. The people Israel had no image in their temple to represent God, as the heathens had images in their temples to represent their gods; but they had an ark, or a chest overlaid with gold, wherein were the law, tables of the covenant. And this was the symbol of the divine presence, first in the tabernacle, and then in the temple.

Over the ark, or upon the ark, there was the mercy seat, which was the throne of God where he sat, and where he dwelt between the cherubims in the tabernacle and temple. God's giving the children of Israel the ark to be among them, was a token that God was among them and dwelt with that people as his people. And therefore the presence of the ark in that land was esteemed the greatest privilege that that nation enjoyed above other nations. They accounted it their glory— and so indeed it was, when we consider that that presence of God went with the ark. And therefore when the Philistines took the ark and carried it away out of the land, and the wife of Phinehas heard that the ark of God was taken, cried out, “The glory is departed from Israel: because the ark of God is taken; the glory is departed from Israel: for the ark of God is taken” [1 Samuel 4:21-22].

After the Philistines had returned the ark, it was left a great while at Kirjath-jearim, a place in the outskirts of the land. Therefore it is said that

<!-- p. 249 -->

while the ark abode in Kirjath-jearim, that “all the house of Israel lamented after the Lord,” because the time was long, even twenty years (1 Samuel 7:2). They looked upon it a sorrowful time, when Israel had not God dwelling in the midst of them but upon their utmost borders, as though he was not willing to come amongst such a sinful people anymore, and was ready to depart again, and leave 'em and go into another land, as he had lately done.

But after David was made king, it was a joyful time among them, for then David had leave and direction from God to bring up the ark of God from Kirjath-jearim into Zion. And therefore they went about this work very joyfully, as we have an account in the thirteenth chapter of this book. They were glad to see the ark coming again after such long absence, but their joy lasted but a little while: for God made a breach among them and turned aside to the house of Obed-edom the Gittite, a stranger, and sojourned there. But after a while, David seems to have had a leave and direction from God a second time to fetch up the ark of God into Zion; and it is upon this occasion that David gives this charge that we have in the text. So that his charge here given is with relation to that which [was] a special token of the presence of God in Israel, and was about their treatment of that which was Israel's special privilege and glory; it was concerning the joyful occasion of God's coming to dwell amongst them again after long absence.

2. We may observe what the charge is that he gives, which in substance is to sanctify themselves and treat the ark in a due manner.

3. We may observe the special reason why he thus[^031-note1] insists on such a charge, viz. what they had suffered by an undue treatment of the ark before: “For because you did it not at the first, the Lord our God made a breach upon us, for that we sought him not after the due order.” They did not behave themselves as they ought to have done in bringing up the ark before, when the Levites ought to have carried [it]. They put it upon a cart to be drawn by oxen. God had in the Law given direction how the ark should be carried {by the Levites (Numbers 3)}, but it seems they had forgotten the Law or had not been duly observant of it. And then, when the oxen shook it, Uzzah, one that drave the cart, put forth his hand to secure it, and God break forth upon him and smote him that he died.

He had no leave to touch the ark, but only in such a manner and at such times as God directed. There was no direction in the Law about their taking hold of it on any such occasion, nor would there have been any such

<!-- p. 250 -->

occasion, if the Law had been attended and the Levites had carried the ark with its staves instead of the oxen's drawing it. By this means their joy was at an end, and God refused for the present to go up and take up his settled abode in Zion amongst his people there.

But now David has leave to go again and bring up the ark, and this is the reason he insists in this charge that now they should treat the ark in due order and in a manner agreeable to God's Word, that they no more suffer in like manner for their error.

#### Doctrine.

#### When a people have once suffered by any errors they have committed in their treatment of special privileges and tokens of God's presence, they should beware that they ben't guilty of those errors the second time.

The following reasons may be given of the doctrine:

I. There should at all times be the utmost care to treat the tokens of God's presence in a due manner, and that both upon account of the greatness of the being that is present, and the preciousness of the privilege that a people have by the tokens of his presence. The greatness and honorableness of the Being whose presence is manifested should excite to the most diligent heed how to behave ourselves. If some great prince should come among us, would not [it] awaken care in us to behave ourselves properly towards him? Should not we be watchful lest we should behave ourselves some way indecently and offensively on such an occasion? How much more when the King of kings manifests himself present among a people. How careful was Moses of his behavior on Mt. Sinai, when he understood that God was there and see the tokens of his presence in the burning bush.

And how was Jacob's attention awakened at Bethel, when he waked out of sleep and understood that God was there (Genesis 28:16-17). Says he, “Surely God is in this place; and I knew it not. He was afraid and said, How dreadful is this place! for this is none other than the house of God, this is the gate of heaven.” And so when God came down on Mt. Sinai in the presence of the people, what care was required of them in their behavior, how more certain bounds and limits set, which every one must take heed to himself that he did not transgress, lest the Lord should break forth upon him. So it is said, Ecclesiastes 5:1-02, “Keep thy foot when thou goest to the house of God, and be more ready to hear, than to give the sacrifice of fools: for they consider not that they do evil. Be not rash with thy mouth, and let not thine heart be hasty to utter any thing before God: for God is in

<!-- p. 251 -->

heaven, and thou upon earth: therefore let thy words be few.” Which implies as much as that we ought to have the utmost care of every step we take and all our behavior in a place where God is present, to be very attentive and heedful, and not foolish and rash with our foot or our mouth, when he is present that is so much above us.

And then, if we consider how precious the privilege is that a people have in the special tokens of God's presence, it should engage them to treat such a privilege in a due manner. Men are wont to be very careful of that which they esteem very precious; it shall be safely laid up in the choicest place and shall be kept and handled with the utmost care.

II. What a people have suffered for their error in their treatment of such a privilege in times past, ought to be taken as a warning from God to take heed to themselves for the time to come. We should learn righteousness by God's judgments. There is a voice in the providence of God as well as in the Word of God. God speaks once, yea, twice, and man perceives it not; but he opens men's ears to discipline by his rod [Job 36:10].

The breach that God [visited] upon Uzzah was on purpose to teach the children of Israel that error, and it was so taken and improved.

III. If they continue in their error, they can expect no other than still to suffer for it. As God has showed his displeasure once, so he will doubtless still be displeased in the commission of the same error. Yea,

IV. If their error be repeated, they may well expect to suffer more than they did before, and that because their sin will now be added to. To the same error they were guilty of before, will be added obstinacy and regardlessness of the warning God has given 'em; and so God will be more displeased, and therefore greater tokens of his displeasure may be expected. And as God's design in his judgments for sin in his people is to teach them and convince them of their sin, if they don't hear when he calls and warns, they may expect louder warnings of the same kinds, that they may be made to hear and understand.

### Application.

I proceed now to make application of this to our case, in this church and congregation, with respect to our treatment of our special privileges and tokens of God's presence, that God has heretofore granted and now grants amongst us.

In these days of the gospel, the professing people of God have no such external token and symbol of the presence of God as the ark, that may go from 'em and come to 'em again, as the ark went from Israel into the land

<!-- p. 252 -->

of the Philistines, and sojourned in Kirjath-jearim, and then was brought up into Jerusalem. But the tokens of God's presence in his church now are spiritual. The way that God manifests himself to be amongst a professing people now is by the influences and operations of his Holy Spirit upon them. At a time of the pouring out of God's Holy Spirit upon a people, God appears amongst them in a more glorious manner than of old he appeared amongst the children of Israel, above the mercy seat over the ark.

We in this place have had such tokens of God's presence amongst us in times past, especially in that remarkable season that began about seven years ago. And God is now again in great mercy granting us a measure of that same token of his presence, whereby we possess a much greater privilege than the children of Israel did in having the ark among them; and doubly[^031-note2] have as much cause to take heed to ourselves, with respect to our treatment of such a privilege, as they had to take care how they handled the ark.

There is great reason to consider and inquire whether God did not see some things displeasing to him in our treatment of such a privilege when we last enjoyed it. You know the awful breach that God made upon us in the time of it, towards the close of it, over one of the principal men in the town.[^031-note3] And the awful breach God not long after made in the house of public worship, in the time of our solemn assembly, putting us into a terrible surprise, breaking us off from the public exercise— an accident by which many lives were greatly exposed, and many were sorely wounded.[^031-note4]

And, which is more than all, God departed from us and left us. The joy of bringing up the ark lasted but a little while; the ark turned aside from us and did not come to take up its settled abode in our Zion. We were soon left, and sunk into a very dull, cold, dead state. Which was very unexpected to ourselves and others after so great and wonderful an appearance of God amongst us.

It was a joyful time in Israel when they were bringing up the ark from Kirjath-jearim, after it had been there so long and they had lamented after the Lord. But how soon was their joy at an end, how unexpectedly did God turn aside from them. So who would have thought, that saw what a blessed joyful season it was, in that remarkable wonderful season, that times would be so soon and so greatly altered.

<!-- p. 253 -->

Certainly these things may be sufficient to put us upon strict inquiring whether we sought the Lord after the due order: whether there was not some considerable and notable errors that we were guilty of in our treatment of so great a privilege, while we enjoyed it. It greatly concerns us to find out our former errors, and to beware of 'em, now God is graciously returning to us again and we are going about the joyful work of bringing up the ark the second time.

That we may so do,

I shall, first, show wherein the error consisted that was committed in Israel in their bringing up the ark the first time; and second, shall lead you to inquire whether we have not been guilty of the same errors in the last time of the remarkable tokens of the presence of God among us, and shall warn against them for the future.

I. I would show wherein the errors consisted that was committed in Israel in bringing up the ark the first time. It seems to have consisted in these three things, viz. pride, irreverence and disobedience.

*First*. In pride. When the children went about this great work, they were very joyful. It is said, 1 Chronicles 13:8, that “David and all Israel played before God with all their might, and with singing, and with harps, and with psalteries, and with timbrels, and with cymbals, and with trumpets.” But they seem to have gone about the work in too self-sufficient a manner, not with a due sense of their exceeding sinfulness and utter unworthiness of such a privilege as that God should dwell among them and that the ark of his strength should be brought to them. They did not sanctify themselves beforehand. When they went about bringing up the ark the first time, we read nothing of their offering up any sacrifices for their sins, as they did the second time. The second time, after God had smitten 'em and humbled 'em, then they were sensible of their need of sacrifices for their sins, and therefore went about it with sacrifices offered to God. As we read, 1 Chronicles 15:26, “They offered seven bullocks and seven rams.” The first time, they had forgot themselves and offered no sacrifice, as not considering how unworthy they were of such a privilege as they hoped now to enjoy. One would think they had reason enough to consider their need of sacrifices the first time, considering how God had testified his displeasure against them in departing from them, forsaking the tabernacle of Shiloh, and delivering the ark into captivity to the Philistines as he had done, and after that remaining so long in Kirjath-jearim; but they did not reflect upon it, nor consider their own unworthiness. And so it seems to have been from their pride and self-sufficiency that, when they were about

<!-- p. 254 -->

such a great work, they never consulted God's law to see in what manner the ark ought to be carried. They were not sensible of their own blindness and ignorance; they thought their own word sufficient to direct 'em in this matter, and so substituted their own inventions in the room of God's institutions. They put the ark into a new cart to be drawn by oxen— and that a very unsuitable way of carrying it— in a proud conceit of the sufficiency of their own wisdom to direct them.

So it seems to have been from pride in Uzzah that he presumed to lay hold on the ark, when he had no warrant from God's law so to do. He looked upon it, that he had a great privilege; God had put great honor upon his father Abinadab's family, in that the ark had remained there for twenty years. And who should be appointed to drive the cart in which the ark was carried but he and Ahio, and he was lifted up with those things. And it was this that made him so forward and presumptuous, so boldly to handle the ark of God.

*Second*. Another part of their error was irreverence, which was very much a fruit of the other. They treated the ark, upon which the name of the Lord of hosts was called, in an irreverent manner. They were full of joy, and their hearts were lifted up on the joyful occasion; and in the midst of their rejoicing, they forgot themselves and handled the ark in a bold irreverent manner. If the people's hearts had been so full, as it ought to have been, of reverence towards the ark, they would not have set oxen to draw it; and if Uzzah's heart had been possessed with due reverence, he would not have presumed to touch it, excepting only as directed and commanded by God's law.

*Third*. The third part of their error was that they placed religion rather in profession and show than in obedience. There was a great deal of profession and show of respect to God among them. They gathered all Israel together, from all quarters of the land, a mighty company of them, to attend the ark. This had a great show of respect.

And then, as the ark went along, they praised God. It is said, they played “with all their might, with singing, with harps, and with psalteries, and with timbrels, and with cymbals, and with trumpets” [1 Chronicles 13:8]. In this, again, they made a great profession and show of respect.

And then, when the oxen stumbled and shook the ark, and it seemed to be in danger of falling, and Uzzah put forth his hand to hold it, that again had a show of respect. But at the same [time], they were very negligent of obedience to God's commands. When they so abounded in testimonies of respect, in profession and show, they were greatly wanting in obedience, not considering that to obey is better than sacrifice, and to

<!-- p. 255 -->

hearken than the fat of lambs: for at that very time, they were in direct disobedience to some of God's commands, as they were in carrying the ark in a cart drawn by oxen, when God had commanded that it should be carried on the shoulders of the Levites. And so Uzzah brake God's law in laying hold on the ark, for the ark was never to be touched but in such and such a manner, and on such and such occasions, as the law of God particularly prescribed.

These were the errors that Israel were guilty of in bringing up the ark the first time, for which they suffered, and for which God for a while turned aside from them. Now let us, in the

II. [Second] place, inquire whether we han't been guilty of the same errors in our behavior under that wonderful mercy we received, when God gave such remarkable tokens of his presence amongst us, several years since.

*First*. Let us strictly inquire whether or no we were not too much lifted up with our privilege. Was there too much of an appearance of a public pride, if I may so call it? Were we not lifted up with the honor that God had put upon us as a people, beyond most other people? Were we not foolishly taken with our comparative honor, and pleased to see ourselves lifted above others, too much forgetting what a stiff-necked unworthy people we were? We might well be joyful, but did not we, in the midst of our rejoicing, and playing with harps and psalteries and cymbals, forget our sins and great unworthiness? Was there not too much of an appearance of it in our talk of the great work that was among us, before others of other towns? Was there not too much of an assuming air? Did it not make us something self-sufficient in our way of talking to others, as though we thought we were the *people*, and we were confident that we ourselves were guides to the blind, and a light of them that are in darkness, and instructors of the foolish, and teachers of babes?

Let us be strict in examining ourselves as to this matter, and let us take heed to ourselves, to avoid all appearance of anything of that nature for the future. It surely becomes us, considering how unworthy we are, not to take the least glory to ourselves before God or men, but greatly to humble ourselves. Let us speak humbly of ourselves before others, and walk humbly before them as a people that are fully sensible that no glory belongs to them, and that we in ourselves are no better than the worst of our neighbors. O! let us take great heed that Christ have all the glory, that he alone may be exalted, and that we all may be abased.

And let particular persons strictly examine themselves whether they han't been lifted up with their particular experiences. I think, according

<!-- p. 256 -->

to what observation I have made— as I have had [more] opportunity of very extensive observation than any other person in the town— that is has been a pretty prevailing error in the town, that persons are not sufficiently sensible of the danger of self-righteousness after conversion.
