They seem to be sensible that persons are in danger of it before they are converted, but they think that when a man is converted, he is brought off wholly from his own righteousness, just as if there was no danger of any workings of self-righteousness afterwards.

But this is from a great mistake of what is intended by a man's being brought wholly off from his own righteousness when he is converted. 'Tis not meant that a self-righteousness principle is wholly done away, that there is no remains of such a disposition in the heart. There is as much of the remains of that as there is of any other corruption in the heart.

So a man is brought, when converted, wholly to renounce all his sins as well as to renounce all his own righteousness. But that don't argue that he is wholly freed from all remains of sin. So no more is he wholly freed from remains of self-righteousness. There is a fountain of it left. There is an exceeding disposition in men, as long as they live, to make a righteousness of what is in themselves, and an exceeding disposition in men to make a righteousness of spiritual experiences, as well as other things; and it was well if some more were sensible of it. [A convert is] apt to be exalted with high thoughts of his own eminency in grace.

Let every one examine himself. There is no pride in the world more secret and more difficult for persons to discern in themselves than this pride.

How was it with you in that wonderful time, wherein you received so much? Was not you very apt to look on yourself as an eminent saint, one more eminent than most others? Was it sometimes natural to you to think that God would show you some peculiar favors above others?

Was there not prevailing in you the reverse of that disposition, spoken of, Philippians 2:3, “Each esteem others better than themselves”; and the disposition that the apostle Paul was of, who calls himself “less than the least of all saints” (Ephesians 3:8)?

Let every one examine himself what has commonly been his motive in speaking of his own experience, whether it has not often been your own honor, and that you might be well accounted of by men. And han't this been a temptation to some of you, to set out your own experience as much as you could?

You that think that God has done great things for you: how has it been

<!-- p. 257 -->

with you? Han't you been really lifted up? Don't go away with a notion that you are above danger of it. There is not one of you, no, not the best saint of you all, that is above danger of it. Don't think that you are above danger of it because discoveries have had a tendency to make you lie low and to work by humility. You are in danger of being lifted up with that very humility. None of [you] are better than the apostle Paul, and he was in danger of {being “exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations” given him} (2 Corinthians 12:7).

Therefore, don't think there is no need for you to keep a strict eye upon your own heart with respect to those things. There is need of the strictest scrutiny imaginable, and a continual watch. Therefore let every one deal faithfully with himself in examining what is past, and let us all keep the strictest watch over ourselves for the future. Let us watch over our own hearts and over our behavior. Let us be careful to avoid all appearance of being lifted up with what God has done for us. And if you think that God has given you better experiences than others, yet it will be very imprudent in you to say so, or to say what implies it: for though you seem to ascribe it to God and not yourself, yet it will be as much as to say[^031-note5] that your opinion of yourself is that you are a more eminent saint than most of your neighbors. Therefore 'tis best to avoid such expressions concerning what you have met with: “It seems to me I have met with great things”; “It seems to me God has done great things for me”; “It seems to me I have no cause to be ashamed to speak before kings,” and the like. Whatever you think, you had better avoid such expositions and all expressions that carry in it that you think you are an eminent saint. If you talk of your own experiences, talk of 'em in a very humble manner, and don't be forward to talk of your experience unless it be for good ends. Don't do it for the sake of the good thoughts of others.

And beware you don't set forth your experiences in too strong expressions. You may possibly be in greater danger of this than you are aware of. It is natural in all cases, when men's affections are moved and are flowing— let it be in temporal things or in spiritual things— to speak of things about which they are affected, and set 'em out in very strong expressions.

Natural men that hear those strong expressions are ready to expect that those that speak should live like angels. And when they don't find, then it does 'em a great deal of hurt; it hardens 'em and makes 'em think that all is a mere delusion and fancy, and makes 'em question whether there

<!-- p. 258 -->

be anything in religion. Let us take heed to ourselves to avoid all manner of appearances of pride in our rejoicings. Let us not forget our unworthiness while we rejoice at the bringing up of the ark.

*Second*. Let us examine ourselves, whether we han't been also guilty of the second part of the error that the children of Israel were guilty of in {bringing up the ark the first time}, viz. irreverence, or not treating those great privileges and extraordinary tokens of God's presence among us with due reverence.

And here I would particularly mention one thing [in] which I think some have been guilty of this error to a great degree, and that is in commonly talking of things of religion in a laughing and light kind of manner. 'Tis to be feared that many in the last time of [the] pouring {out of God's Spirit} were in this respect like the children of Israel, that in the midst of their great rejoicings, and playing on harps {and psalteries and cymbals}, they forgot the distinction that was between God and them. They had forgot how great a God that was, whose ark that was that they were then removing, and began to treat it in a light kind of manner.

So it has certainly been in a great measure [with us], and therefore no wonder God has made a breach upon us, and turned aside from us, and left us. This is not the way that the Scripture teaches us to rejoice in God, to rejoice with a light merry sort of an air. But there we are said to “rejoice with trembling” (second psalm, eleventh verse). The meaning {is that we should treat extraordinary tokens of God's presence among us with due reverence}.

Persons talking of things of religion with much laughing and lightness was one thing that greatly obscured the work of God that was here before, and doubtless much offended and displeased the infinite majesty. This did not savor of that reverence that was in Moses on the Mount, when God discovered himself to him [Exodus 3].

Did we savor of that reverence that Jacob showed after God had manifestly discovered himself to him {at Bethel}? He had as much reason to rejoice, {and to play on harps and psalteries and cymbals}, but he says after it, “How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God” [Genesis 28:17]. He sets himself, with the greatest reverence and solemnity of spirit, to give God the glory of what he had done for him there. It don't seem to hold forth a due sense of our littleness, how that God is in heaven and we upon earth.

Such a way of talking of things of religion and of spiritual experiences savors of a great deal [of] freedom that men use with the ark of God. And indeed, 'tis to be feared we have provoked God by being very free and bold in handling the ark.

<!-- p. 259 -->

There is another sort of joy that is a great deal better and sweeter than {a light merry sort of an air}, as many here can testify: a solid, solemn, reverential joy, more apt to bring forth humble tears than a light kind of laughter.

When there is any grace in that kind of joy, that works so there is a great deal of nature mixed with grace. Such experiences are mixed experiences. Those that are purely spiritual are not wont to dispose persons to talk lightly {of religion}.

Such joy is more superficial, is not so deep, nor does it put near so much honor upon God as {a reverential joy}, nor does it so much honor religion in the eyes of others.

When persons that have an hope of conversion talk of things of religion with becoming seriousness, it will have a great deal more tendency to affect and solemnize the hearts of natural men that hear it, than to hear it talked of with an air of lightness. This rather tends to prejudice them against it.

It don't savor of that which we are directed to in Ezekiel 16:63, “That thou mayest remember, and be confounded,” but it savors too much of pride and self-sufficiency and presumption.

*Third*. Let us inquire whether we han't also been guilty of the errors of the children of Israel that was last mentioned, viz. taking more care to testify our respect to God by a show and profession than by obedience to God's commands. It must be confessed that there has been a great deal done at testifying respect to God in outward profession and show. There was in the time of the last outpouring {of God's Spirit} a great deal of religious talk and a great deal of zeal at frequenting religious meetings, as the children of Israel flocked from all parts {to bring the ark to Jerusalem}.

But then, at the same time, did not God see that there were many of his commands with respect to duty to our neighbors neglected? Did not God see that, all this while, men kept their old leaven of malice in their hearts one towards another, kept it alive through the very midst of that wonderful season, ready to break out again when occasion should serve? No wonder, therefore, that God who saw that turned away from us. And han't many of the professors of conversion too much more neglected many of the second-table duties[^031-note6] than they have those things that belong to a fair profession? Han't we been too much like a cake not turned, religious as to the external duties of one table, but not the other? They that place religion chiefly in outward show, such as frequenting religious meetings,

<!-- p. 260 -->

rather than in keeping {God's commands}, will neglect thereto if it proves troublesome.

Let us, therefore, also avoid this error for the time to come. Let us abound in those things that appertain to a good profession, but let us not leave the other undone. Let the principal thing with us be to obey the voice of the Lord. This God did much more require than the other. Jeremiah 7:22-23, “I spake not unto your fathers concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices: but this thing commanded I them, saying, Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and ye shall be my people: and walk ye in all the ways that I have commanded you, that it may be well unto you.” This is the way to have God abiding with us. John 14:23, “If a man love me, he will keep my words: and my Father will love him, and we will come unto him, and make our abode with him.” Let us cast away all the old leaven of malice out of our hearts, and let us henceforward abound in duties of justice and forgiveness, and peaceableness and meekness, and forbearance and long— suffering. This will be the way to have the outpourings of the Spirit of God continued with us.

And of all the external things that we can do to have the Spirit of God continued amongst [us], I believe the most likely thing to be successful to that end, of any one thing whatsoever, is abounding in deeds of love and charity. The abounding in deeds of love is the likeliest way to have the God of love and peace always dwelling with us (Romans 15:33). If we would now manifest our thankfulness for what God does for us by obeying that precept of Christ, Matthew 10:8, “Freely ye have received, freely give,” and should be much in deeds of love and charity,[^031-note7] in helping one another under our difficulties and straits, and promoting any design that tends to encourage that duty, I believe no one external thing whatsoever is so likely to be successful to this end. We see how God has smiled upon the charitable disposition that was manifested when the Reverend Mr. Whitefield was here.

The success of the children of Israel should encourage us to avoid our former errors. They had the joy of the presence of the ark but a little while the first time, because they sought not the Lord in the due order. But when they were sensible of their error, and the second time corrected it, then they were successful; then they actually brought up the ark into the city Zion and placed it {in the tent} with joy and gladness, and had no interruption or allay to their joy.

<!-- p. 261 -->

It was one of the most joyful times in Israel that ever was, and God thenceforth continued amongst them. And if we in like manner correct our former errors, there is no reason to doubt but we shall have like success, and that God, who now is returning to us and calling us a second time to bring up the ark, will henceforward no more depart from us.[^031-note8]

[^031-note1]: MS: “was.”

[^031-note2]: MS: “doubtly.” Alternative reading: “doubtless.”

[^031-note3]: I.e. the suicide of Joseph Hawley, Sr. See *Our Weakness, God's Strength*, in *Works*, *19*, 377–89.

[^031-note4]: The falling of the church's upper gallery on March 13, 1737. See JE to Benjamin Colman, March 19, 1737, in *Works*, *16*, 66–70; and *Undeserved Mercy*, in *Works*, *19*, 628–55.

[^031-note5]: MS: “you.”

[^031-note6]: I.e. the sixth through tenth of the Ten Commandments.

[^031-note7]: In a matter of several weeks, JE would preach a sermon on precisely this theme from Acts 10:4-06 (587). See *Much in Deeds of Charity*, in *The Sermons of Jonathan Edwards: A Reader*, ed. Wilson H. Kimnach, Kenneth P. Minkema, and Douglas A. Sweeney (New Haven, Yale Univ. Press, 1999). 197–211.

[^031-note8]: JE made two notes at the end of the sermon: “Propound Persons,” or announce candidates for full communion; and “Mention Journey,” meaning that JE himself was to go on a speaking tour, apparently downriver. *Sinners in Zion* and *Seeking After Christ*, printed below, both dated Dec. 1740, were preached in Springfield.

## Sinners in Zion

<!-- p. 262 -->

The epitome of the “awakening sermon,” *Sinners in Zion* is distinct in subject matter, in intensity, and in historical self-consciousness. Edwards knows he is preaching this sermon in the midst of a “great and general awakening,” and his listeners know it, too. In many of Edwards' sermons delivered in ordinary times, it is impossible to determine from an internal analysis of the text alone when the sermon was delivered. But not in seasons of revival. In this text, Edwards alludes to the Northampton revival of 1734–35, and to the ensuing years of apathy and quiescence. “Six or seven years ago,” he notes midway through the sermon, “almost all of you would surely have gone to hell in a little time.” But since then another awakening has begun, giving everyone renewed hope and a second chance.

The opportunities Edwards sees in awakening sermons lie on two levels. Individually, they mark a pregnant moment for salvation; no metaphor is too strong, no emotion too powerful to be left out in times such as these. Corporately, the times— and Edwards' sermons— offer speaker and listener the opportunity to be central characters in sacred history. Like later American diarists of the Revolution or the Civil War, Edwards and his listeners know they are living in extraordinary times and witnessing exceptional events. The self-consciousness is high, and so are the prospects.

In reading this sermon, one gets the sense of urgency and importance that encompassed nearly everyone. When the great revivalist George Whitefield preached in Northampton on October 17, 1740, he also mentioned the previous revival as preview to the present. “When I came to remind them of their former experiences,” the Grand Itinerant recalled, “and how zealous and lively they were at that time, both minister and people wept much.”[^032-note1] Whitefield went on to record great success in the Connecticut River Valley wherever he preached.

What Whitefield accomplished in sheer drama, Edwards achieved in verbal imagery. In some of his greatest awakening sermons, most notably *Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God*, delivered just a few months after *Sinners*

<!-- p. 263 -->

*in Zion*, Edwards employed a great panoply of images and metaphors designed to reach all the human emotions. *Sinners in Zion*, however, shows how he could use one central metaphor or parable to address one particular emotion. The parable Edwards chooses is the story of an imaginary church member who does not see death as a reality. This person has not lived his life in such a way as to find any peace when death does approach. As he grows ill, he calls on doctors to heal him, as he has done in the past, but this time to no avail. Terrified, he then calls out to God to allow him to live, but it is too late to save his life or his soul. Eventually his friends ask him what he sees at death's door— perhaps a bright light?— but he can offer them no hope. His soul is then ripped from his body and devoured by hell's demons, and he realizes that there will be no end to his suffering.

Of course, rhetorical exercises like this are never allowed to stay in the hypothetical realm. In the Application, Edwards extends the parable to the congregation, asking which of them would suffer a similar fate. If they fail to turn to God for regeneration, they should expect such an end. And if they do not convert now, it may be too late for them; their hearts may become hard or they may die before another chance arises. And so, with time and eternity in the balance— and history calling— Edwards challenges his listeners to share in the joy of salvation.

If we judge from the number of times Edwards repreached this sermon, he was apparently pleased with both its overall structure and its timeliness. In times of revival, no less than great calamity, sermons could be repeated often to different congregations to maximize the effects of the composition. Edwards repreached this sermon, as well as the one following, *Seeking After Christ*— which sets a very different though complementary tone— in Springfield, Massachusetts, at his brother-in-law Samuel Hopkins' church while on a preaching “journey.”[^032-note2] When we read this sermon, it is clear why Edwards would have liked it so much and why it would have been so effective in promoting revival. For rhetorical effect it is nearly the equal of its more famous counterpart, *Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God*, also repeated in neighboring pulpits, for fanning the fires of revival.

* * *

<!-- p. 264 -->

The manuscript, dated by Edwards “Dec. 1740,” consists of one booklet of twenty-six duodecimo leaves. The two-preaching-unit sermon has a lengthy Doctrine, which is nearly three times as long as the Application. Although this ratio is often an indication of a lecture, the subject matter assures us that it is a regular sermon. The History of Redemption symbol appears beside the date at the upper-right-hand corner of the first page.

This sermon, or parts of it, was repreached at least four times: twice before the Stockbridge period and twice while Edwards was at Stockbridge, once to the English and once to the Indians.[^032-note3] There are marginal vertical lines throughout the manuscript indicating which sections were preached at Stockbridge. Based on the familiarity with the congregation expressed in the Application, and the reference to the revival of seven years earlier, we can deduce that the original preaching was at Northampton. Edwards' shorthand indicates that he delivered the doctrinal part of the sermon at Springfield and preached parts of the sermon again at another unspecified time and place. Another shorthand notation indicates that this sermon preceded *Seeking After Christ* when Edwards repreached it at Springfield, since this sermon defines an abbreviation for Springfield that is then used in the latter sermon.

Sereno Dwight, recognizing the rhetorical power of this sermon, first printed it in his ten-volume *Works of President Edwards* (*6*, 440–57). The text printed here is based on the original manuscript.

<!-- p. 265 -->

[^032-note1]: *George Whitefield's Journals*, p. 476.

[^032-note2]: See above, p. 261, n. 3, for JE's note about a “journey” at the end *of Bringing the Ark to Zion a Second Time*.

[^032-note3]: JE's shorthand notations indicate that he “preached part of the doctrinal part at Springfield” and “preached part of this the second time,” possibly as part of the “Journey” he announces at the end of *Bringing the Ark to Zion a Second Time*. He later “preach'd the Parts mark'd in the margin at Stockbridge,” presumably to the English, and also preached “great Part [to the] St[ockbridge] Ind[ians].”

## Sinners in Zion

> The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?

Isaiah 33:14.There are two kinds of persons among God's professing people. The one are the truly godly, those spoken of in the next verse to the text: “He that walketh righteously, and speaketh uprightly; he that depiseth the gain of oppressions, that shaketh his hands from holding of bribes, that stoppeth his ears from hearing of blood, and shutteth his eyes from seeing evil”; and the other are the sinners in Zion, or hypocrites. 'Tis to be observed that the Prophet in this chapter speaks interchangeably, first to one and then to the other, awfully threatening the one and denouncing God's wrath against them, and comforting the other with gracious promises. Thus you may observe the fifth and sixth verses: there are comfortable promises to the godly. And then, in the eight following verses, awful judgments are threatened against the sinners in Zion. And then, in the two next verses, again are blessed promises to the sincerely godly. And in the former part of the seventeenth verse, and then in the latter of the seventeenth, and in the eighteenth [and] nineteenth verses, again are terrible threatenings to the sinners in Zion. And then, in the verses that follow, again are gracious promises to the godly.

Our text is part of what is said in the chapter to the sinners in Zion.

In the Isaiah 33:10, 'tis said, “Now will I rise, saith the Lord; now will I be exalted; now will I lift up myself.” I.e. “Now will I arise to execute wrath on the ungodly. I won't let 'em alone any longer; they shall see that I am not asleep and that I am not regardless of mine own honor. Now will I be exalted. Though they have cast contempt upon me, yet I will vindicate the honor of my own majesty. I will exalt myself, and show my greatness and my awful majesty in their destruction. Now will I lift up myself. Now I will

<!-- p. 266 -->

no longer have mine honor to be trampled in the dust by them, but my glory shall be manifested in their misery.”

First page of the manuscript of *Sinners in Zion*, 1740. Courtesy of the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University.

And v. Isaiah 33:11, “Ye shall conceive chaff, ye shall bring forth stubble.” I.e. “Ye shall pursue happiness in ways of wickedness, but you shall get no fruit. You are as ground that brings forth no fruit, any more than if only chaff was sowed in it; it brings forth nothing but stubble that is fit for nothing but to be burnt.”

It seems to have been the manner in that land, where the corn grew very rank, when they had reaped the wheat and gathered it off from the

<!-- p. 267 -->

ground, to set fire to the stubble, which is alluded to here. And therefore 'tis added here, “your breath, as fire, shall devour you”; i.e. your own wicked speeches, your wickedness that you accomplish with your breath and with your tongues, shall set fire to the stubble and devour it.

And then it follows in the twelfth verse, “And the people shall be as the burnings of lime.” As they are wont to burn lime in a great and exceeding fierce fire, till stones and bones and all things are burnt to lime, so shall the wicked be burnt in the fire of God's wrath.

“As thorns cut up shall they be burnt in the fire.” As briars and thorns are the encumbrance and curse of the ground where they grow, and were wont to [be] burnt, so shall the wicked that are among God's people and grow in God's field. Hebrews 6:7-08, “For the earth which drinketh in the rain [that cometh oft upon it, and bringeth forth herbs meet for them by whom it is dressed, receiveth blessing from God: but that which beareth thorns and briers is rejected, and is nigh unto cursing; whose end is to be burned].”

And then it follows, in the thirteenth verse, “Hear ye, that are far off, what I have done; and, ye that are near, acknowledge my might”; which implies that God will manifest his glory very publicly, even in the sight of the whole world, call those that are near and those that are far off, by the destruction that he will execute on ungodly men.

“Acknowledge my might”; which implies that God will execute wrath on ungodly men in such a manner as extraordinarily to show forth his great and mighty power. The destruction and misery of the wicked will be so dreadful, that it shall be a great manifestation of the omnipotent power of God, that he can execute misery that is so dreadful; agreeable to Romans 9:22, “What if God, willing to show his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction.”

And then next follow the words of the text: “The sinners in Zion are afraid; fearfulness hath surprised the hypocrites. Who among us shall dwell with the devouring fire? who among us shall dwell with everlasting burnings?”

The sense of the text may be expressed, with a little variation of the words, thus:

#### [Doctrine.]

#### The time will come when fearfulness will surprise the sinners in Zion, because they will know that they are going to be cast into a devouring fire, which they must suffer forever and ever, and which none can endure.

<!-- p. 268 -->

And this I would make the subject of my present discourse. And, more particularly, I would speak to these words,

I. By inquiring who are sinners in Zion.

II. By showing how fearfulness will hereafter surprise them.

III. By insisting on those reasons of this fear and surprise that are mentioned in the text.

IV. By showing why sinners in Zion will be especially surprised with fear.

I. It may be inquired, who are the sinners in Zion.

I answer, that they are those that are in a natural condition amongst God's visible people. Zion, or the city of David, of old was a type of the church, and the church of God in Scripture is more frequently called by the name of Zion than perhaps by any other name.

And more commonly by Zion is meant the true church of Christ, or the invisible church of true saints; but at other times the visible church, consisting of those that are outwardly, and by profession and external privileges, the people of God. And this is intended by Zion in this text.

The far greater part of the world are sinners. Christ's flock is, and ever has been, but a little flock. But the sinners of the world are of two sorts. There are those that are visibly of Satan's kingdom, that are without the pale of the visible church. Such are all that don't profess the true religion nor do attend the external ordinances of it. And there [are] the sinners in Zion.

Both are the objects of God's displeasure and wrath, but his wrath is more especially manifested in Scripture against the latter. The sinners in Zion will have by far the lowest place in hell. They are exalted nearest to heaven in this world, and they will be lowest in hell in another world. The same is meant in the text by “hypocrites” as “sinners in Zion.” Sinners in Zion are all hypocrites, for they make a profession of the true religion, they attend God's ordinances and make a show of being God's worshippers; but all is in hypocrisy. But I hasten to the

II. [Second] thing proposed, which is to show how fearfulness will hereafter surprise the sinners in Zion.

*First*. They will hereafter be afraid. Now many of them seem to have little or no fear. They are quiet and secure. Nothing will awaken 'em. The awfulest threatenings and the loudest warnings don't much move them. They are not so afraid with fear but that they can eat and drink and sleep, [and] go about their worldly concerns, without much disturbance.

But the time will come when the hardest and most stupid wretches will be awakened. Though now preaching won't awaken them, and the death

<!-- p. 269 -->

of others won't awaken [them]; though seeing others awakened and converted won't much affect them; though they can stand all that is to be heard and seen in a time of general outpouring of the Spirit of God without being much moved: yet the time will come when they will be awakened, and fear will take hold of them. They will be afraid of the wrath of God. However senseless they are now, they will hereafter be sensible of the awful greatness of God and that it is a fearful thing to fall into his hands.

*Second*. They will be surprised with fear. This seems to imply two things, viz. the greatness of their fear, and the suddenness of it.

1. The greatness of their fear. Surprise argues an high degree of fear. Their fear will hereafter be to the degree of astonishment.

Some of the sinners in Zion are something afraid now. They have now and then some degrees of fear. They ben't convinced that there is such a place as hell, but they are afraid there is. They ben't thoroughly awakened, but yet neither are they quite easy. They have at times inward molestations from their consciences, but they have no such degrees of fear as to put upon any thorough endeavors for their escape.

But hereafter they will have fear enough— as much, and a great deal more, than they can stand under. Their fear will be to the degree of horror. They shall be horribly afraid, and terrors shall take hold on them as waters. Thus we read of their fear coming as desolation, and distress and anguish coming upon them (Proverbs 1:27). And so 'tis very emphatically said of the wicked, that “trouble and anguish shall prevail against him, as a king ready to the battle” (Job 15:24).

The stoutest heart of 'em all will then melt with fear. Those who were of a sturdy spirit and, it may be, would scorn to own themselves afraid of any man, and were ashamed to own themselves afraid of the wrath of God, their hearts will become weak as water, as weak as the heart of a little child.

And the most reserved of them will not be able to hide his fears. Their faces shall turn pale. They shall appear with fright and amazement in their countenance. Every joint in them shall tremble, and all their bones shall shake; their knees shall smite one against another. And they will not be able to avoid crying out with fear and rending the air with the most dismal shrieks.

2. They shall be suddenly seized with fear. The sinners in Zion often continue secure till they are surprised, as with a cry at midnight. They shall be as it were waked up out of their secure sleep in a dismal fright. They shall see an unexpected calamity coming upon them, more dreadful than they were aware of, and coming at an unexpected season.

<!-- p. 270 -->

With respect to the time when the wicked shall be thus surprised with fear:

(1) 'Tis often so on a death bed. There are many things that pass in their lifetime that one would think might well strike terror into their souls. As when they see others die: persons as young as they, and of like condition and circumstances with themselves, whereby they may see how uncertain their lives are and how unsafe their souls.

It might well surprise many sinners to consider how old they are grown and are yet in a Christless state; how much of their opportunity to get an interest in Christ is irrecoverably gone, and how little remains; and how much greater their disadvantages now are than they have been. But these things don't terrify them; as age increases, so does the hardness and stupidity of their hearts grow upon them.

But when death comes, then they are oftentimes filled with astonishment. It may be, when they are first taken sick, they have great hope that they shall recover, as men are ready to flatter themselves with hopes that things will be as they feign would have them. But when the distemper causes to prevail much upon them, and they see that they are going into eternity— they see that all medicines of physicians are in vain, and that all the care and endeavor of friends [are] in vain; nothing seems to help 'em; their strength is gone; they see that their friends weep over 'em, and look on their case [as] desperate; they see by the countenance and behavior of the physician that he looks upon his case past hope; and perhaps overhears a whispering in the room, wherein they signify one to another that they look upon it, that they are struck with death, and tell one another how that their extreme parts grow cold, their countenance and manner of breathing, and their pulse, shows death, and they begin to be in a cold death sweat; and it may be by and by some one thinks himself bound in duty and faithfulness to let him know the worst, and comes and asks him whether or no he is sensible that he is a-dying— O then how does fearfulness surprise the sinner in Zion! How does his heart melt with fear! This is the thing that he feared ever since he was taken sick, but till now he had hope that he should recover. The physician did not speak as if he despaired; he spake of such and such medicines as being very proper, and he hoped that they would be effectual. And when those failed, the doctor changed his medicines and applied something new, and then he hoped that that would be effectual. And so, though he kept growing worse and worse, yet still he kept hoping.

And then he cried to God to spare him, and made promises how he would live if God would spare his life, and he hoped that God would hear

<!-- p. 271 -->

him. And he observed friends and, it may be, the minister seemed to pray earnestly for him, and he could not but hope prayers would be answered and he should be rescued. But now, how does his heart sink and die within him. How does he look about with a frighted countenance, how quick is the motion of his eye with inward fear, and how quick and sudden are all his motions. What a frightful hurry does he seem to be in.

O how does everything look about him, when he sees pale grim death staring him in the face, and a great and vast eternity within a few hours[^033-note1] of him! It may be still he as [it] were scrabbles for a little hope. He is loath to believe what is told him. He tells those that tell him he is a-dying, that he hopes not: he hopes they are more frighted than there is need of; he hopes that those symptoms arise from some other cause. And like a poor drowning man, he catches at rotten twigs, and clinches his hands about whatever he has within reach.

And as death creeps more and more on him, he sees his twigs break, and all his hopes of life fail. He has nothing but death before him. He sees he must die. O there is nothing else for him but death! He has been hoping, but his hopes are all dashed. He sees this world, and all that belongs to it, is gone. And now come the thoughts of hell into his mind with amazement. O how shall he go out of the world? He knows he has no interest in Christ; his sins stare him in the face. O that dreadful gulf of eternity! He had been crying to God, it may be, since he was taken sick, to convert him; he had some hope, if it was his last sickness, that yet God would pity him and give him converting grace before he died. He begged and pleaded, and he hoped that God would have pity on his poor soul. He asked others to pray for him, and he had been looking day after day for some light to shine into his soul. But, alas, now he is a-dying, and his friends ask him how death looks to him, whether any light appears, whether God has not appeared for him: and he answers, “No,” with a poor, faltering, trembling voice, if he be able to speak at all; or, if his friends ask a signal of hope, he can give none.

And death comes more and more and more upon him, and he is just on the brink of eternity: and who can express the fear, the misgivings, the hangings back and the horrible fright and amazement that soul of a Christless sinner sometimes is in in such a case? Some that have been able to speak have been known in such circumstances to cry out, “O eternity, eternity!” and some, “O a thousand worlds for an inch of time!” O if they might but live a little while longer! But it must not be— go they must.

<!-- p. 272 -->

They feel the frame of nature dissolving, and thus perceive the soul is just a-going, for sometimes the exercise of reason seems to hold to the last.

And what, in such a case, is felt in the soul in those last moments, when the soul as it were just breaking its bonds with the body, and is on the very edge of eternity, going to fetch its leap, and is on the very brink of hell without any Savior or the least testimony of divine mercy: I say, what is felt sometimes by Christless souls in these moments, none can tell; no, it is without the compass of our conception.

(2) The misery of the departed soul of a sinner, besides what it now feels, will consist in great part in amazing fears of what is yet to come.

When the union of the soul and body is actually broken, the body has fetched its last gasp, and the soul forsakes its old habitation and then falls into the hands of devils that fly upon and seize it more violently than ever hungry lions flew upon their prey,[^033-note2] with what horror will it fall into those cruel hands. If we imagine to ourselves the dreadful fear with which a lamb or kid falls into the paws of a wolf, that lays hold of it with open mouth; or of the feeling of a little child that has been pursued by a lion, when it is taken hold of and sees the terrible creature open its devouring jaws to tear in pieces; or the feeling of those forty-two children that cursed Elijah, when they fell onto the paws of the bears that devoured 'em: I say, if we could have a perfect idea of that fright, that terror and astonishment, that a little child has in such a case, yet we should have but a very faint idea of what is felt in the departing soul of a sinner, when it falls into the hands of those evil devils, those roaring lions, that then lay hold of it.

And when the poor soul is carried to hell, and there is tormented and suffers the wrath of the Almighty, and is overwhelmed and crushed with it, it will also be amazed with the apprehensions of what yet remains. To think of an eternity of this torment remaining, O! how will it fill and overbear and sink down the poor soul; how will the thought of a duration of this torment, that shall never never end, cause the heart to melt like wax; how will the thought as it were sink it into a bottomless abyss of darkness and gloominess.

And as those proud sturdy spirits, the devils, do tremble at the thoughts of that greater torment that they are to suffer at the day of judgment, so will the poor damned souls. They will already have vastly more than they can bear. How will they tremble, then, at the thoughts of having their misery so vastly augmented. Persons sometimes in this world are afraid of the

<!-- p. 273 -->

day of judgment. If there be an earthquake, or if there be more than common thunder and lightning, or if there be some unusual sight in the heavens, their hearts are ready to tremble for fear that the day of judgment is at hand. But O! how then do the poor souls in hell fear it, who know so [much] more about it, know by what they feel already, and know certainly that, whenever it comes, they shall stand on the left hand of the Judge to receive the dreadful sentence; and that then they, with both soul and body, must enter into those everlasting burnings that are “prepared for the devils and his angels” [Matthew 25:41]; and probably will know that their misery is to be made an hundredfold greater than it is now.

(3) Fearfulness will surprise them at that last judgment. When Christ appears in the clouds of heaven and the last trumpet sounds, then will the hearts of wicked men be surprised with fearfulness. The poor damned soul trembled in expectation of it every day and every hour ever since it departed from the body. It knew not when it was to be, but it knew that it was to be; and doubtless, long before it came, feared every day that it would come that day. But when the alarm is given in hell that that day is come, it will be a dreadful alarm indeed; it will[^033-note3] fill the caverns of hell with shrieks. And when the souls enter into their bodies, it will be with amazing terror of what is coming. And when they lift up their heads out of their graves and see the Judge, it will [be] a most terrible sight. Gladly would they return into their graves again and hide themselves there, if that might be; and gladly would they return into hell, into their former state of misery, to hide themselves from this awful sight, if that might excuse them. And so those sinners in Zion that shall then be found alive on the earth, when they see this sight, will be surprised with fearfulness. The fear and terror that many poor sinners have when they are dying is great, and beyond all that we can have any idea of; but that is nothing to the horror that will seize 'em when they come to see this sight.

There will not be a wicked man upon earth that will be able to bear it. Let him be who he will: let him be rich or poor, old or young, male or female, servant or master, king or subject, learned or unlearned; let him be never so proud, never so courageous, and never so sturdy: there is not one will be able at all to support himself when he sees this sight. It will immediately sink his spirit; it will loose the joints of his loins; it will make his countenance more ghastly than death.

The rich captains and valiant generals and princes, that would scorn to show any fear at the face of any enemy, that would scorn to tremble at the

<!-- p. 274 -->

roaring of cannon, will tremble and shriek when he hears the last trumpet and sees the majesty of his Judge; it will make his teeth to chatter, and make him cry out and fly to hide himself in the caves and rocks of the mountains, and to cry to the [mountains and rocks to fall on him (Revelation 6:15-16)].

And fearfulness will surprise them when they are dragged before the judgment seat. The wicked hang back when they are going to meet death, but not as they will hang back when they come to meet their great Judge.

And when they come to stand before the Judge and are set at his left hand, fearfulness and amazement will surprise 'em. The majesty of the Judge will be intolerable to 'em; his pure and holy eye, which will behold and search 'em, and pierce 'em through, will be more terrible to their souls a thousand times than flashes of lightning piercing their hearts. There will they stand in a trembling expectation that, by and by, they shall hear the words of that dreadful sentence proceed out of Christ's mouth [Matthew 25:41]. They will have an horrible expectation of that sentence. And what shall they do? Where shall they fly so as to be out of hearing of the awful voice of that sentence? They can't stop their ears so as not to hear it— they must hear it.

And fearfulness will surprise 'em when the sentence comes to be pronounced. At the close of the judgment, that dreadful doom shall be uttered by the Judge. It will be the most terrible voice that ever was heard. The sound of the last trumpet, that calls men to judgment, will be a more terrible sound to wicked men than ever they heard till then; but the sound of the last sentence will be much more terrible than that. There will not be one of all those millions of millions at the left hand, neither high nor low, king nor subject, will be able to support himself at all under the sound of that sentence, and they shall all sink under it.

And lastly, fearfulness shall surprise 'em when they come to see the fire kindle upon the world, in which they are to be tormented forever. When the sentence is pronounced, Christ, with his blessed saints and glorious angels, shall leave this lower world and shall ascend up into heaven. And then shall the flames begin to break out; fire will probably be seen coming down from heaven.

And soon shall the fire lay hold of that accursed multitude, and then their hearts will be surprised with fearfulness. That fire will appear a dreadful fire indeed. O what shrieking, what chatterings of teeth, what chatterings of loins, what distortions of body will there be at that time, when they shall see and begin to feel the fierceness of the flames! What shall they do? Whither shall they go to avoid these flames? Where shall

<!-- p. 275 -->

they hide themselves? If they creep into holes, creep into caves of the earth, yea, if they could creep down to the very center of the earth, it will be in vain: for it shall set on fire the bottoms of the mountains and burn to the lowest hell. They'll see no place to fly, no place to hide themselves. Then their hearts will be filled with fearfulness and shall utterly sink with despair. Thus it shall hereafter be with everyone that is then found a sinner, and especially with sinners in Zion.[^033-note4]

I come now, in the

III. [Third] place, to speak to those reasons, spoken of in the text, why sinners will hereafter be thus surprised with fear.[^033-note5]

*First*. Fearfulness will surprise 'em, because they will know that they are going to be cast into devouring fire. There is nothing that seems to give one a more terrible idea of torment and misery than to think of being cast alive into a fire, especially if we conceive of the soul's remaining quick, without being benumbed by the fire.

The wicked will hereafter have that to make 'em afraid, that they are not only going to be cast into a fire, but into devouring fire; which implies that it will be a fire of extraordinary fierceness of heat, and that nothing can stand before [it].

Oftentimes the fire into which wicked men are to be cast, is called a “furnace of fire” [Matthew 13:42, Matthew 13:50]. Furnaces are contrived for an extreme degree of heat, the purposes for which they are designed requiring it, such as the running and refining of metals, and the melting things into glass. The fire of such earthly furnaces may be called devouring fire, for the heat of some of them is such that even stones will probably be dissolved in them.

Now if a person should be brought to the mouth of such a furnace, and there should see how the fire seemed to glow, so as presently to make everything that was cast into it all over white and bright with fire, and should know that he was now directly going to be cast into this furnace, would not fearfulness surprise him?

In some heathen countries, the manner of disposing [of] dead bodies is to dig a great pit, and to put in it a great quantity of fuel, and to put the dead bodies on the pile and set 'em on fire; which is some image of the burning of dead souls in the pit of hell.

<!-- p. 276 -->

Now if a person was brought to the edge of such a pit, all filled with glowing flames, [and was] going to be cast into it, would it not surprise the heart with fearfulness?

The flames of a very great fire, as when an house is all of a-light [with] fire, do give one something of an idea of the fierceness of God's wrath, such is the rage of the flames. And we see that the greater a fire is, the fiercer is its heat in every part; and the reason is, because one part heats another. The heat in a particular place, besides the heat that proceeds out of the fuel in that place, has the additional heat of the fire all around it. Hence, therefore, we may conceive something of what fierceness that fire will be when this visible world shall be turned into one great furnace. That will be devouring fire indeed. Such will be the heat of it that, as the Apostle says, “the elements will melt with fervent heat” (2 Peter 3:10).

Men can artificially raise such a degree of heat with burning glass as will quickly melt the very stones and sand. And 'tis probable the heat of that great fire, which will burn the world, will be such as to melt the rocks and the very ground, and turn them into a kind of liquid fire; so that the whole world will probably be converted into a great lake and liquid globe of fire, a vast ocean of fire, in which the wicked shall be overwhelmed.

It will be a sea of fire that will always be in a tempest, in which the wicked shall be tossed to and fro, having no rest day nor night, with vast waves and billows of fire continually rolling over their heads.

Which all will be but an image of that dreadful fire of the wrath of God, which the wicked shall at the same time suffer in their souls. We read in Revelation 19:15 of “the fierceness and wrath of almighty God.” 'Tis an extraordinary expression, carrying a terrible idea of the future misery of the wicked. If it had been only said, “the wrath of God,” that would [have] expressed what is dreadful. If the wrath of a king is as the roaring of a lion, what is the wrath of God? But 'tis not only said, “the wrath of God,” but “the fierceness and wrath of God,” or, the rage of his wrath; and not only so, but “the fierceness and wrath of almighty God.”

O what is that! the fierceness and rage and fury of Omnipotence, a Being of infinite strength! What an idea does that give of the state of those worms that do suffer that fierceness and wrath of such an almighty Being! And is it any wonder that fearfulness surprises their hearts when they see this going to be executed upon 'em?

*Second*. Another reason given in the text why fearfulness will hereafter surprise sinners, is that they will be sensible that this devouring fire will be everlasting.

If a man was brought to the mouth of a great furnace, to be cast into

<!-- p. 277 -->

the middle of it, if he knew he should suffer the torment of it but one minute, yet that minute would be so terrible to him that fearfulness would surprise and astonish him.

How much more, if he were to be cast into a fire so much fiercer, as the fire in which wicked men are hereafter to be tormented? How much more terrible would the minute's suffering be?

But if the thoughts of suffering this devouring fire for one minute would be enough to fill 'em with such surprising fearfulness, what fearfulness will seize them when they will know that they are to bear it not one minute, nor one day, nor one year, nor one age, or two ages, or an hundred ages, or ten thousand and millions of ages, one after another, but forever and ever, without any ending at all, and never, never be delivered?

They shall know that the fire itself will be everlasting fire, fire that never shall be quenched. Mark 9:43, Mark 9:46, “To go into hell, into the fire that never shall be quenched. Where their worm dieth not, and the [fire is not quenched].”

And they will know that their torment in that fire never will have an end. Revelation 14:10-11, “The same shall drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is poured out without mixture into the cup of his indignation; and he shall be tormented with fire and brimstone in the presence of the holy angels, and in the presence of the Lamb: and the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night.” They will know that they shall forever be full of quick sense within, and within their heads, their eyes, their tongues, their hands and feet and loins; their vitals shall forever be full of glowing melting fire, fierce enough to melt the very rocks and elements, and also shall eternally be full of the most quick and lively sense to feel the torment.

They shall know that they shall never cease restlessly to plunge and roll in that mighty ocean of fire. They will know that those billows of fire, that are greater than the highest waves, will never cease to roll over them, one following another, forever and ever.

And they will have a more lively sense of eternity than we ever can have. We can have but little sense what an eternal duration is, and indeed, none can comprehend it— it swallows up all thought and imagination; if we go to think, we are presently lost. But they will have another, apter sense of it than we have. O how big will eternity look to them, when they think of spending an eternity in such burnings!

And this is another reason that fearfulness will surprise 'em. The thoughts of eternity will always be amazing to 'em, and will sink and depress 'em to a bottomless depth of despair.

<!-- p. 278 -->

*Third*. The third reason given in the text why fearfulness will surprise 'em at the apprehension of this, is that they will know that they can't bear it. When they see themselves going into that devouring fire, they will know that they can't bear it. They will know that they can't grapple with the fierceness and rage of those flames, for they will see the fierceness of the wrath of God in them. They will see an awful manifestation of Omnipotence in the fury of that glowing furnace.

Their hearts will utterly fail them. Their hands won't be strong, nor their hearts endure. They will see that their strength is weakness. They will know that they shall not be able to grapple with such torments, that they can do nothing in such a conflict. When they come to the edge of the pit and burning lake, and look into the furnace, then they will cry out with exclamations like these: “O how shall I do? How can I bear the torments of that fire? How can I endure them? Who can endure? Where is the man so stout-hearted? Where is there the giant with such strength and with such courage that can bear this? O what shall I do? Must I be cast in there? I cannot bear it! I can never endure it! O that I could return to my first nothing! How can I endure it one moment? How much less can I endure it forever and ever? And must I bear it forever? What, forever and ever, without any end? Never find any refuge, never be suffered to turn into my first nothing? What, be no nearer to the end of it after millions of ages?”

O what dismal contortions and shrieks, and shaking of loins and gnashing of teeth, will there be then! No wonder that fearfulness will surprise them.

I come now to the

IV. [Fourth and] last [thing] proposed in my discourse from these words, to show why it will be especially thus with the sinners in Zion, or sinners that dwell amongst God's visible people, that sit under the preaching of the gospel and have the offers of a Savior, and yet never accept of him, but remain in an unconverted state.

There will be hereafter a very great difference between them and other sinners, a great difference between the most pointed[^033-note6] hypocrite of 'em all and the drunkards, and adulterers, and sodomites, and thieves, and murderers among the heathen, that only sin against the light of nature.

The fearfulness that will surprise them, though it will be very dreadful, yet it will be in no measure so amazing and horrible as that [that] will seize the sinners in Zion.

<!-- p. 279 -->

Because the wrath of God, that fierceness and wrath of almighty God which they will suffer, will [be] mild and moderate in comparison of that which the sinners in Zion will suffer.

God's wrath is manifested in his Word against the wicked heathen, but it is ten times as much manifested against the sinners that have the professions and privileges of a people of God, but yet remain enemies to him. Both Old Testament and New are full of terrible denunciations against such. Read over the books of Moses, and read the Prophets, and you will find 'em full of dreadful threatenings against such. Read over the history of Christ's life and the speeches that he spoke when upon earth, and there you will see what woes and curses be from time to time denounced against such. How often did he say that it should “be more tolerable [for Tyre and Sidon at the day of judgment” than for such (Matthew 11:22)].

Read over the story of the Acts of the Apostles, and their epistles, and there you will find the same. 'Tis the sinners in Zion and hypocrites that are always in Scripture spoken of as the people of God's wrath. Isaiah 10:6, “I will send them against an hypocritical nation, against the people of my wrath will I give them a charge.” The reasons are chiefly these:

*First*. That they sin against so much greater light. Great light is often spoken of in Scripture as an exceeding aggravation to {sin}. He that knows his lord's will, {and prepares not himself, neither does according to his will, shall be beaten with many stripes (Luke 12:47)}.

If men are blind, they have comparatively no sin. But when they see, have light to know their duty and know their obligation, then their sin is great (John 9:41).

When the light that is in men is darkness, how great is that darkness. And when they live in wickedness in the midst of great light, that light is like to be turned into the blackness of darkness indeed.

*Second*. That they sin against such vows. The heathen never professed to be worshippers of the true God. They never pretended to be Christ's disciples, never came under any covenant obligations to it. But God highly resents falseness and treachery. Judas, that betrayed Christ with a kiss, was a greater sinner, and much more the object of God's wrath, than Pilate, that condemned him to be crucified and was his murderer.

*Third*. They sin against so much greater mercy. They have the infinite mercy of God in giving his own Son often set before them. They have the dying love of Christ, have this mercy, this glorious Savior, and his blood and righteousness, often offered to them.

[They] have a blessed opportunity.

[They have] a great price put into their hands.

<!-- p. 280 -->

[They have] that precious treasure, the holy Scriptures, {and} enjoy sabbaths and sacraments.

There is no wrath like that which arises from mercy abused and rejected. When mercy is this way turned into wrath, that is the fiercest wrath. Other wrath is light in comparison of it.

Sinners in Zion, besides their fall by the first Adam, have also a fall by the second. He is a stone of stumbling. And there is no fall like that. The fall by the first Adam is light in comparison of it.

On these accounts, whenever we see the day of judgment— as we shall everyone of us see it— we shall easily distinguish between the sinners in Zion and other sinners by their shriller cries and their louder and more bitter and dolorous shrieks, the greater amazement of their countenances, and the more dismal shakings of their limbs and contortions of their bodies.

### [Application.]

I would conclude with an earnest *Exhortation* to the sinners in Zion, now to fly from the devouring fire and everlasting burnings. You sinners that are here present, you are the very persons spoken of in the text; you are the sinners in Zion. How many are there of those people of God's wrath that sit here and there in the seats of this meeting house at this time. You have often been exhorted to fly from the wrath to come— this is the wrath to come.

You hear today of the devouring fire and of everlasting burnings, and of that fearfulness that will seize and surprise such hereafter. And O! what reason have you of thankfulness that you only hear of it, that you don't feel it, that it has not already got hold of you!

It is as it were following you, and coming nearer and nearer, every day. Those fierce flames are as it were already kindled, in that the wrath of God, yea, the fierceness and wrath of almighty God, burns against you. It is ready for you: the pit is prepared for you with fire and much wood, and the breath of the Lord, as a stream of brimstone, doth kindle it.

Lot was with great urgency hastened out of Sodom, and commanded to make haste and fly for his life and escape to the mountain, lest he should be consumed in those flames that burnt up Sodom and Gomorrah. But that burning was but a flea bite to that devouring fire and those everlasting burnings that you are in danger of.

Therefore, improve the recent opportunity.

<!-- p. 281 -->

Now God is pleased again to be pouring out his Spirit upon us, and he is doing great things amongst [us]. God is indeed come again, the same great God that so wonderfully appeared amongst us some years ago, and that has since for our sins departed from us and left us so long in such a dull dead state, let sinners alone in their sins, so that there has been scarce any signs to be seen of any such work as conversion.

That same God is now come again. He is really come in like manner, and begins, as he did before, gloriously to manifest his mighty power and riches of his grace: he brings sinners out of darkness into marvelous light; he rescues poor captive souls out of the hands of Satan; he saves persons from that devouring fire; he plucks one and another as brands out of the burning; he is opening prison doors, and knocks off their chains, and brings out poor prisoners; he is now working salvation amongst us from this very destruction that you have now heard of.

Now, now is the time! Now is a blessed opportunity to escape those everlasting burnings! Now God has again set open the same door, the same fountain, amongst [us], and gives one more happy opportunity for souls to escape. Now he has set open a wide door, and he stands in the doorway calling and begging with a loud voice to the sinners of Zion. “Come,” says he, “to me! Come fly from the wrath to come! Here is a refuge for you! Fly hither for refuge! Lay hold on the hope set before you!”

A little while ago it was uncertain whether ever we should see such an opportunity again. If it should always have continued as it has been for five or six years past, almost all of you would surely have gone to hell in a little time. Fearfulness would have surprised you, and you would have been cast into that devouring fire and everlasting {burning}. But, in infinite mercy, God gives another opportunity: and blessed are your eyes that they see it, if you did but know your own opportunity. You have had your life preserved through this six years past to this very time, to another time of the pouring out of the Spirit. What would you have done if you had died before it came? How doleful would your case have been. But you have reason to bless God it was not so, but you are yet alive, and now see a blessed day of grace again. And will you not improve it? Have you not so much love to your poor soul as to improve such an opportunity as this? Some, there is reason to think, have lately fled for refuge to Christ: and will you be willing to stay behind, still a poor miserable captive condemned to suffer forever in the lake of fire?

You hereafter will see those of your neighbors and acquaintances that are converted, mounting up as with wings, with songs of joy, to meet their

<!-- p. 282 -->

Lord. And if you remain unconverted, you at the same time will [be] surprised with fear, and horror will take hold of you because of that devouring fire and those everlasting burnings.

It is an awful thing to think of, that there are now some persons in this very congregation, here and there, in one seat and another, that will be the subjects of that very misery that we have now heard of, as dreadful as it [is], though it be so intolerable and though it be eternal.

There are doubtless some now hearing this sermon that the rest of the congregation will, at the day of judgment, see among the devils at the left hand. They will see their frighted ghastly countenances. They will see 'em wring their hands, and gnashing their teeth, and shrieking and crying out.

We now don't know their names. We don't know what seats they sit in, where to look for 'em, or who to pitch upon. But God knows their names, and now sees and knows what they think, and how much regard they pay the warnings that are given on this day.

We han't the least reason to suppose any other but that some of you will hereafter see others entering into glory with Christ and saints and angels, while you with dreadful horror see the fire begin to kindle about you.

It may be he that is the person, is now blessing himself in his heart, and saying with himself, “Well, I don't intend it shall be so.” Everyone here hopes to go to heaven; they would by no means miss of it. If they thought they should, they would be greatly amazed. But all will not go there; it will undoubtedly be the portion of some to toss and tremble forever among the fiery billows of God's wrath.

'Tis not to be supposed that there are some here that won't be in earnest. Let them have never so good an opportunity to obtain heaven, they won't thoroughly improve it. Tell 'em of hell as often as you will, and set it out in as lively colors as you will, they will be slack and slothful. And they never will be like to obtain while they are sleeping and dreaming, and intending and hoping. The wrath of God, that pursues, shall take ['em] by the heels. Hell, that follows after 'em, will overtake, and fearfulness will surprise 'em, and a tempest shall steal them away.

And 'tis not to be supposed that all that are now seeking will hold out. Some will backslide; they will be unsteady. If now they seem to be pretty much engaged, it won't hold.

Times will probably alter by and by, and they won't have obtained; and there will be many temptations to backsliding, and they will yield to them. The hearts of men are very unsteady. They are not to be trusted. Men are very short-winded. They can't tell how to have patience to wait upon God. They are soon discouraged. Doubtless some that are now under convictions

<!-- p. 283 -->

will lose 'em. It may be they won't leave off seeking salvation at once, but they will come to it by degrees. They, after a while, will begin to hearken to excuses not to be quite so constant in duty, and they will begin to think that they need not be quite so strict. They'll say to themselves, they don't see any hurt in such and such things.

There were some that were guilty of backsliding the last time. While the talk was kept alive, they continued to seek. {They continued to seek until} they see some miscarriages of professors.

And they are left behind still. They are to this day in a miserable condemned state, in danger of the devouring fire {and everlasting burnings}, and in twice so dangerous a state as they were in before, and God alone knows what will become of them. And as it was then, so doubtless it will be now.

Some that are here now present in a natural condition are doubtless near death. They han't long to live in the world, and if they seek in a dull way, or if they, after they have sought a while, are guilty of backsliding, death will come upon them long enough before there comes another such opportunity.

When they leave off {seeking salvation}, it won't be without a design of seeking again some time or other. But death will be too quick for them. 'Tis not the manner of death to wait upon folks while they take time to indulge their sloth and gratify their lusts; when his appointed time comes, he'll do his work. Will you put off in hopes of seeing another such time seven years hence? Alas, how many of those that are now in a natural condition may be in hell before another seven years!

Therefore, now let every one look to himself. It is for your own soul's salvation. If you are foolish and won't hearken to counsel, won't improve the opportunity when it is given you, and won't enter into such an open door, you alone must bear it. If you should miss this opportunity and quench your convictions now, and there should come another time of the pouring out of the Spirit, you'll be far less likely to have any benefit by it. As we see now, God chiefly moves on the hearts of those that are very young, that are brought forward more on the stage of action since the last outpouring of the Spirit— those that were not then so much come to years of understanding, and so not so much in the way of the influences of the Spirit. As for those that were grown up and had convictions then, and quenched them, they, most of 'em, are abundantly more hardened, and seem to be more passed over. And so it will probably be with you hereafter if you miss this opportunity and quench the convictions of the Spirit that you have now.

<!-- p. 284 -->

And as to you that had awakenings the last time of the pouring out of the Spirit, and have quenched 'em, and remain to this day in a natural condition, let me call upon you also. Now God is giving you one more such opportunity.

If passing through one such opportunity has so hardened you and been such a great disadvantage to you, how sad would your case be if you should now miss another.

Will you not now thoroughly awake out of sleep and bestir yourself for your salvation, and resolve now to begin again and never leave off more? Many fled for refuge from the devouring fire before, and you was left behind; and others have fled for refuge now, and still you are left behind. And will you always remain behind? Consider, can you dwell with the devouring fire? Can you dwell with everlasting burnings? Shall children, babies and sucklings go into the kingdom of God before you?

How will you hereafter bear to see them coming and sitting down with Abraham, {Isaac, and Jacob} in the kingdom of God, when you yourselves are thrust out and are surprised with fearfulness at the sight of that devouring fire and those everlasting burnings that you are going to be cast into?

Take heed, lest a like threatening be fulfilled upon you with that which we have in Numbers 14:22-23, “Because all those men which have seen my glory, and my miracles, which I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and have tempted me now these ten times, and have hearkened to my voice; surely they shall not see the land which I sware unto their fathers, neither shall any of them that provoked me see it”; together with v. Numbers 14:31, “But your little ones, which ye said should be a prey, them will I bring in, and they shall know the land which you have despised.”

## Seeking After Christ

<!-- p. 285 -->

Edwards begins this sermon by reviewing the events of the Old Testament that culminate in the New with wise men finding the star over the infant Jesus. Utilizing his research into knowledge of “true religion” among ancient and contemporary “heathen” nations,[^034-note1] he shows that Daniel would surely have left astrological instructions for those Persians he ruled, and assumes that the wise men knew of those instructions. Edwards also traces their knowledge to another source, the prophecy of Balaam in Numbers 24:17, and shows that the magi knew that a star would come to guide them. He chooses the wise men's journey as a trope, or type, of a believer's spiritual search for Christ. Like the wise men, one must “be willing to go a long journey to find Christ, i.e. to continue earnestly seeking him a very long time, if called to it.” Yet— and this is the sermon's point— to find Christ is not sufficient. Whereas finding Christ is an event actualized in conversion, seeking Christ is undertaken not once but daily, throughout one's life.

And why should believers, like the wise men, rejoice with exceeding great joy in finding Christ? Edwards gives five compelling reasons: what one finds is exceedingly excellent and lovely; Christ is ready to receive the believer; if one finds Christ, one finds great deliverance, a strong defense, and a fountain full of what one needs.

The joy in finding Christ is heightened by the journey we undertake to find him, as it was for the wise men. The search for Christ is like following the star, referred to by Balaam, that guided the wise men; a star that provides a believer with great light and power. But we should not look to the sky for this star, for it “will not impress on our imagination.” Rather, we ought to look to Scripture. In *A Divine and Supernatural Light*, Edwards warned that “this spiritual and divine light don't consist in any impression made upon the imagination. 'Tis no impression upon the mind, as though

<!-- p. 286 -->

one saw anything with the bodily eyes: 'tis no imagination or an idea of an outward light or glory, or any beauty of form or countenance, or a visible luster or brightness of any object.”[^034-note2] With revivals at fever pitch, these warnings were becoming even more urgent. One senses in this sermon, as with others in this period, a sensitive pastor concerned to ignite a fire without allowing it to rage out of control.

Edwards twice chose this sermon to follow *Sinners in Zion*, first when it was originally preached at Northampton in December 1740 and then when he repreached the two at Springfield, Massachusetts. In the first sermon, on Isaiah 33:14, Edwards admonishes his listeners to flee from their sin and backsliding, vividly showing what a sinner in Zion can expect who does not live a Christian life of faith and charity. In this sermon, now that the sinner has, one hopes, fled from sin, Edwards brilliantly draws this person to an ongoing life with Christ by describing the joy that will be found in the arms of Christ, a joy that is an obvious contrast to the torment found in the deadly embrace of sin.

* * *

This sermon, dated by Edwards “Decem. 1740,” consists of fourteen duodecimo leaves. Shorthand on the first page indicates that it was repreached at Springfield and at Newtown, although the dates are not given. The symbol for the History of Redemption project appears at the top of the first page.

<!-- p. 287 -->

[^034-note1]: See entries in the “Miscellanies” relating to “Traditions of the Heathen” (beginning in earnest during the early 1740s), in which JE attempts to discover corrupted traces of a general ancient revelation of true religion to all the nations. For a study of these and related themes, see also Gerald R. McDermott, *Jonathan Edwards Confronts the Gods: Christian Theology, Enlightenment Religion, and Non-Christian Faiths* (New York, Oxford Univ. Press, 2000).

[^034-note2]: *Works*, *17*, 412.

## Seeking After Christ

> And when they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy.

Matthew 2:10.These words are a part of the story of the wise men that came from the east to see and to worship Jesus Christ after his birth. 'Tis not known who these wise men were. There are various opinions about it. This is certain: that there was at that day a very great expectation in the world of some great person that was to arise in Judea that was to rule over the world, which probably arose from the Jews being dispersed all over the world, as they were after the captivity into Babylon, and so their carrying the prophecies of the Messiah with them.

And 'tis most probable that those wise men that came from the east were some that had received instruction from the holy writing of the Jews that had been carried into the east, first to Babylon, which was many hundred miles to the east of Judea, and afterwards to Shushan in Persia, which was yet a great deal further to the east. There was Daniel, that great prophet exalted to great dignity, and there was Nehemiah, and there was Elisha and Mordecai; and these had the prophecies of the Old Testament concerning Christ with them. And Daniel himself, who was set over the wise men of the east as their master, was himself a great prophet and wrote one of those books of Old Testament prophecy— whose prophecy of Christ is in some respects more particular than [that] of any other prophets— and probably wrote it in Persia when he was in great dignity there, and doubtless left instructions among the great and wise men of that eastern part of the world, whose master he was, concerning Christ, and probably might leave his own prophecy and the other prophecies of Scripture concerning the Messiah in their hands.

The word in the original that is translated wise men is *magai*. And learned men observe that there is to this day in those eastern parts of the world, and particularly in Persia, a sect called by this very name, Magai or Magi— and have been time out of mind— that have many parts of the Old

<!-- p. 288 -->

Testament in their hands and have had 'em delivered down from their forefathers for a great many ages. And it is supposed that they received 'em from the Jews that were carried captive, and particularly from Daniel. 'Tis certain that those wise men or Magi that came from the east to see and to worship Christ, had some further instruction and direction than they had by the light of nature, and that two ways:

1. They were probably instructed [in] one of the prophecies of the Old Testament concerning the star that should arise out of Jacob. This they probably had from Balaam's prophecy. Numbers 24:17, “I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh: there shall come a star out of Jacob, and a scepter shall arise out of Israel, that shall smite the corners of Moab, and destroy all the children of Sheth.”

Balaam himself, who prophesied thus, came out of the east and, it may be, from the same country that those wise men came from, and there might leave his prophecy.

2. They were instructed[^035-note1] by immediate direction from heaven. There was [an] extraordinary hand of God stirring them up to come and seek Christ, and directing them how to find him; as is manifest, because God caused a miraculous star to appear for their direction. This star appeared to 'em in their own country together with an intimation from God that Christ now appeared in Judea, as appears by the second verse. They see this wonderful star and they knew it was a sign that Christ was come, and so came into Judea. It seems this star appeared to them a while and then disappeared; and they came to Jerusalem to inquire after Christ and, while they were diligently seeking him, the star appeared to 'em again, as in the next verse before the text: “When they had heard the king, they departed; and, lo, the star, which they saw in the east, went before them, till it came and stood over where the young child was.”

And then come in the words of the text: “and when they saw the star, they rejoiced with exceeding great joy.”

Four things may be particularly noted:

(1) Whom they had been seeking. They sought Christ. They had come a very long journey to seek him. We read of some that came from the utmost parts of the earth to see the wisdom of Solomon. And probably these came from as great a distance to see and to worship Christ, that was now born into the world to be the Savior of the world. They had doubtless undergone a long fatigue. It was a tedious and wearisome journey, and they had been inquiring of the priests and scribes where they should find Christ.

<!-- p. 289 -->

(2) We may observe how it was discovered to 'em where Christ was. They saw a bright and lovely star that was the emblem of his glory. This arose to them to enlighten and direct them. This star represented Christ, who is called a star rising out of Jacob in Balaam's prophecy, and is said to be the bright and morning star (Revelation 22:16).

(3) We may observe what kind of effect this discovery had upon their minds. The effect was joy in them. As the star arose to their view, joy arose in their hearts.
