## Renewing Our Covenant with God

<!-- p. 509 -->

In February 1742 a disappointed Edwards left for a two-week preaching tour to the area of Leicester, Massachusetts. As his Northampton stand-in he allowed a young protégé of his, Samuel Buell, to fill the Northampton pulpit. To Edwards' joy and dismay, Buell set the congregation on fire. People cried out in meeting and, as Edwards described it, “the whole town seemed to be in a great and continual commotion, day and night.” Indeed, the town was “such in some respects as I never saw it in before.” Buell stayed on for several weeks after Edwards' return, and their combined efforts were rewarded with “a very great revival of religion.” During this time, individuals saw visions and went into trances, lying motionless for twenty-four hours at a time. Among these was Sarah Pierpont Edwards, whose narrative of her ecstatic religious experience during this period so impressed her husband that he later used it in *Some Thoughts Concerning the Revival*.[^061-note1]

In mid-March Edwards sought to build on the momentum by drawing up a draft of a covenant renewal for the church. Covenant renewal had been used in New England churches since the late seventeenth century as a means of renewing loyalties to the religious and social ideals of the Puritan experiment. Basically, members of the church would recovenant, or rededicate, themselves to following the ways of God as a body of believers. After the draft had been vetted by the church's “principal men,” the deacons, and the town's religious societies, Edwards “led the people into a solemn public renewal of their covenant with God.”

To have a covenant renewal at this time was a logical step for Edwards. First, it provided another means of reasserting the power of the church over members' lives, as seen earlier in *The Means and End of Excommunication*. But more pressingly, this act could renew and channel revival fervor. With its emphasis on Christian behavior and discourse, too, the covenant

<!-- p. 510 -->

crystallized prominent concerns of Edwards' over the previous two years. He laid the groundwork on March 9 by preaching a sermon on Isaiah 44:3-05, in which he sought to bind recent converts to the church as well as encourage the preservation of the revival spirit. He told his people that by this act of covenanting they were “subscribing to the head” and joining the commonwealth of God.[^061-note2] At the close of the sermon, Edwards announced that the following week the congregation would adopt the covenant.

On March 16 Edwards preached *Renewing Our Covenant with God*. In this sermon, preparatory to the ceremony, Edwards called on Northampton to renew its covenant with the Lord as one body. Throughout the revival time, many *individuals* had turned to Christ and *personally* renewed their covenant with Christ. Now Edwards called for a *collective* rededication. There were many reasons for such a call. One of his primary goals throughout this revival was to avoid the downturn in enthusiasm of seven years earlier. If individuals would hold themselves and others accountable to the group, this would tie them together in the bonds of Christian love and watchfulness.

Though ostensibly solemn and celebratory, this sermon is a jeremiad. Rather than a warning of punishment which assumes a collective accountability, it is a call for collective accountability so that the church of Northampton can stand closer to God. Yet Edwards is aware that recovenanting is not specifically mandated in Scripture— a problem that had plagued the practice since New England clergymen began it in earnest earlier in the century as a means of eliciting reform. Thus he pulls together a great deal of evidence to legitimate the act. He first uses examples from Scripture and then appeals to the “light of nature.” Lastly, he considers the nature of church membership, which assumes participation in a collective body of believers. Church members may have joined as individuals, but in doing so they became part of a community. To Edwards' way of thinking, he is not creating a community anew but merely holding its members to the spiritual bylaws to which they have already agreed.

The defensive tone of *Renewing Our Covenant* suggests that not everyone in the congregation was convinced that a covenant renewal was necessary or even legitimate. The sermon is structured around a series of propositions that contain a number of objections and answers, perhaps actual objections presented to Edwards. His defense of covenant renewal

<!-- p. 511 -->

as not “superfluous” also suggests that a segment of the church still resisted. While Edwards viewed the covenant as a sign of the people's consent to obey God, many in the congregation could have viewed it as a sign that they were to obey the minister and rein in their material ambitions.

To read the covenant is to see why there might have been objections to it.[^061-note3] It is unusually long for a covenant renewal and its demands were clearly unrealistic, even for the most harmonious of communities— which Northampton was not.[^061-note4] The covenant resounds with Edwards' insistence on the social evidences of Christianity. Roughly the first half of the piece deals with individual moral behavior— particularly economic behavior— that affected other individuals or the community as a whole. The people of Northampton were to deal fairly and openly with one another, render everyone his due in business, make restitution for any wrongs, and avoid unjust reflections upon the characters of others. Those in positions of power were not to use their influence either for personal gain or to further the interests of parties. The youth of the parish were to avoid irreligious pastimes as well as “freedoms and familiarities in company” that led to sexual promiscuity. Ironically, at this very time some young men of the parish were making salacious use of a book on midwifery to mock young women. In two years this scandal would come to light, and Edwards and his people would be embroiled in the “Bad Book” case as he brought the young men up for public rebuke.

The sermon *Renewing Our Covenant* and the covenant renewal of 1742 therefore reflect the changing relationship of Edwards and his church. In the coming years, Edwards would use the covenant as a measuring stick to point out— in increasingly vigorous terms— his people's spiritual and moral failures.[^061-note5] The 1740s would see increased instances of conflict between minister and people, as Edwards struggled against what he perceived as increasing worldliness and disrespect in the congregation, and the people against what they perceived as their pastor's efforts to accrue power and to dictate over their lives. Consequently, Edwards increasingly isolated himself from his congregation, devoting less effort to his sermons and instead writing on the nature of conversion and working in the interest of revival abroad. If he could not hope for awakenings at home, he

<!-- p. 512 -->

would look for them elsewhere. In the process, pastor and congregation left each other behind.

* * *

This sermon is eight duodecimo leaves in length. Edwards inscribed it “March 1742.” It has no Exposition or Application; instead, it is characterized by a series of propositions, some containing lists of objections and answers. To judge by the lack of repreaching marks and later emendations, the sermon was not delivered again.

The outlined nature of the written text allowed Edwards to extemporize as much as he may have needed. Each page is divided into two columns, and each column in turn is divided into “boxes” of various sizes by horizontal lines. Within each “box” Edwards wrote topical statements, fragmentary key phrases, or even single words that would help him maintain the sermon's general flow. This manuscript's columnar form is one of Edwards' first in this format. By the middle of the 1740s, nearly all of his sermons are written in this fashion.

## Renewing Our Covenant with God

> [And if it seem evil unto you to serve the Lord, choose you this day whom ye will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were on the other side of the flood, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land ye dwell: but as for me and my house, we will serve the Lord. And the people answered and said, God forbid that we should forsake the Lord, to serve other gods; For the Lord our God, he it is that brought us up and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, from the house of bondage, and which did those great signs in our sight, and preserved us in all the way wherein we went, and among all the people through whom we passed: And the Lord drave out from before us all the people, even the Amorites which dwelt in the land: therefore will we also serve the Lord; for he is our God. And Joshua said unto the people, Ye cannot serve the Lord: for he is an holy God; he is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions nor your sins. If ye forsake the Lord, and serve strange gods, then he will turn and do you hurt, and consume you, after that he hath done you good. And the people said unto Joshua, Nay; but we will serve the Lord. And Joshua said unto the people, Ye are witnesses against yourselves that ye have chosen you the Lord, to serve him. And they said, We are witnesses. Now therefore put away, said he, the strange gods which are among you, and incline your heart unto the Lord God of Israel. And the people said unto Joshua, The Lord our God will we serve, and his voice will we obey. So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and set them a statute and an ordinance in Shechem. And Joshua wrote these words in the book of the law of God, and took a great stone, and set it up there under an oak, that was by the sanctuary of the Lord, And Joshua said unto all the people, Behold, this stone shall be a witness unto us; for it hath heard all the words of the Lord which he spake unto us: it shall be therefore a witness unto you, lest ye deny your God.]

Joshua 24:15–27

<!-- p. 514 -->

#### [Propositions.]

Prop. I. A visible people of God on some occasions are called solemnly and publicly to renew their covenant with God.

Here we have an account of such a transaction. We have many instances of it in Scripture. [In] Moses' time. Deuteronomy 29:1-12,

These are the words of the covenant, which the Lord commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, beside the covenant which he made with them in Horeb. And Moses called unto all Israel, and said unto them, Ye have seen all that the Lord did before your eyes in the land of Egypt unto Pharaoh, and unto all his servants, and unto all his land; the great temptations which thine eyes have seen, the signs, and those great miracles: yet the Lord hath not given you an heart to perceive, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, unto this day. And I have led you forty years in the wilderness: your clothes are not waxen old upon you, and thy shoe is not waxen old upon thy foot. Ye have not eaten bread, neither have ye drunk wine or strong drink: that you might know that I am the Lord your God. And when ye came unto this place, Sihon the king of Heshbon, and Og the king of Bashan, came out against us unto battle, and we smote them: and we took their land, and gave it for an inheritance unto the Reubenites, and to the Gadites, and to the half tribe of Manasseh. Keep therefore the word of this covenant, and do them, that ye may prosper in all that ye do. Ye stand this day all of you before the Lord your God; your captains of your tribes, your elders, and your officers, with all the men of Israel, your little ones, your wives, and thy stranger that is in thy camp, from the hewer of thy wood unto the drawer of thy water: that thou shouldest enter into covenant with the Lord thy God, and into his oath, which the Lord thy God maketh with thee this day.

Joshua's time [Jos 24:15-27].

Asa's time. 2 Chronicles 15:12-15, “And they entered into a covenant to seek the Lord God of their fathers with all their heart and with all their soul; that whosoever would not seek the Lord God of Israel should be put to death, whether small or great, whether man or woman. And they sware unto the Lord with a loud voice, and with shouting, and with trumpets, and with cornets. And all Judah rejoiced at the oath: for they had sworn with all their heart, and sought him with their whole desire; and he was found of them: and the Lord gave them rest round about.”

Jehoiada's time. 2 Kings 11:17, [“And Jehoiada made a covenant between

<!-- p. 515 -->

the Lord and the king and the people, that they should be the Lord's people; between the king also and the people”].

Josiah's time. 2 Kings 23:3, [“And the king stood by a pillar, and made a covenant before the Lord, to walk after the Lord, and to keep his commandments and his testimonies and his statutes with all their heart and all their soul, to perform the words of this covenant that were written in this book. And all the people stood to the covenant”]. 2 Chronicles 34:31-32, [“And the king stood in his place, and made a covenant before the Lord, to walk after the Lord, and to keep his commandments, and his testimonies, and his statutes, with all his heart, and with all his soul, to perform the words of the covenant which are written in this book. And he caused all that were present in Jerusalem and Benjamin to stand to it. And the inhabitants of Jerusalem did according to the covenant of God, the God of their fathers”].

Nehemiah's time. [Nehemiah 9-10].

Old Testament examples. New [Testament examples].

Reason.

No instance of public fasts and thanksgivings. Light of nature teaches.

*Inq*. What are the occasions on which this is to be done? {I} answer in two things:

*First*. There are some duties required in Scripture that the Scriptures don't appoint particular seasons or occasions [for]: so fasts and thanksgivings. [And there are] some that are for stated seasons or sabbaths.

*Second*. When 'tis so, 'tis to be governed by applying general rules to particular cases by human discretion, especially the discretion of those that are set on purpose to lead and instruct the church of God in religious matters.

*Inf*. 1. Hence objections against such a thing as a proper means to promote religion and our good are a reflection on the wisdom of God.

*Obj*. That it is not a proper means because it makes our guilt the greater.[^062-note1] Here it may be laid down as a maxim, that that objection is of no force at all if it don't hold everywhere. Where [does] the good of the objection hold? [It] don't hold against all covenanting. [It was] of no force of old. [It is] of no force now in other covenanting. The same objection may be made against all means of grace.

It is true in appointing their sins it makes their bonds the faster.

*Answ*. That is one reason why it is appointed, one way that the wisdom of God saw it proper. Joshua made it as strong as possible. Nehemiah made the People confirm it with an oath and a curse. So Asa (2 Chronicles 14:4).

<!-- p. 516 -->

*Inf*. 2. Hence a people may be guilty of greatly offending God by refusing to hearken to his call, by refusing when properly called to it, though there be no particular command, when proved, when called by those that are set to be leaders.

*Inq*. Whether we are called of this day. In order to this, we must look into two things:

(1) The occasions on which we have Scripture examples. Here we find several occasions on which such things were done, [which] were great and remarkable dispensations of providence towards his church, calling extraordinarily [to] duty to God, when God [was] introducing a new state of his church. Times of reformation, reformation from idolatry. But not only so; also reformation of other evils.

Not only after great declensions, but on other occasions: in Moses' time; [in] Joshua's time.

(2) How far these occasions agree to this present time. Why did not those that make these objections object against binding themselves so strong when they came into the church? Was it because it was only in formality that you made that covenant?

[It is] no objection, that [you] are bound already.

*Inq*. What is the benefit of such a public covenant?

[*Answ*.] (1) 'Tis a public honor to God, part of the worship he requires, very often mentioned in Scripture.

[*Answ*.] (2) 'Tis for the good of a people, as it is a great restraint. [It] puts 'em in mind of their duty and obligation. [It is] a means of hearty self-dedication to God, makes their bonds the stronger and so restrains the conscience.

*Prop*. II. In solemn, public renewals of the covenant with God, 'tis proper to insist [in] particular on those sins that people are especially in danger of.

*Prop*. III. The strictness of the duty required in the covenant and the great difficulty of observing, it is no argument against making such a covenant.

If persons do but truly resolve and make it their true and faithful wish and endeavor […].

*Prop*. IV. That a people should report their manifestations of consent to such a covenant. [They may] do it several ways. [It] may be done without superstition or superfluity.

*First*. A people must manifest their consent (2 Kings 23:3).

*Inq*. What ways are proper for them to manifest their consent?

<!-- p. 517 -->

*Answ*. 1. In general, by some kind of speaking. There are several ways of speaking.

[Answ.] 2. The particular way of speaking is not prescribed and therefore left to human discretion, especially the discretion of those that are set to lead. Making obeisance [is] nowhere prescribed.

[*Answ*.] 3. 'Tis evident by Scripture that signing with the hand is not an improper way. There is no one way of manifesting consent for which there is so express Scripture warrant as this— more than making obeisance. 'Tis evident by that in Isaiah 44:5, [a] prophecy of what shall be at the beginning of the glorious times— “one shall subscribe with his hand”— that 'tis a proper way.

[*Obj*.] It may be objected that that is a figurative expression.

*Answ*. If it be, God would not represent it by that which is improper to be done.

This was done in Nehemiah's time. The reason why the common people did not sign was not that it was not proper but because it was impracticable. There is nothing in the act that can render it more improper for common people in an affair wherein they act for themselves as much.

'Tis common in the Christian church to do both in a new and extraordinary covenanting, as in the settlement of churches.

And so when God brings his church into a new and extraordinary state.

*Second*. To have special manifestations of consent, or to show consent in several ways as confirming one another, is not superstition and may be expedient. So here. In human contracts [it is] not thought superfluous. [There are] human covenants. So by divine appointment [it is not superfluous] in the servant that would serve his master forever. So in public renewals of the covenant with God from time to time.

Here particularly 'tis proper that in cases where a people [would show their consent], each one for themselves, they should do something to make the act an act of public worship before the Lord. So in Nehemiah's time.

*Third*.[^062-note2] That there should be some sign of their consent remaining, to be a memorial of their consent that was given. So in Joshua's time.

Signing with the hand is convenient on that account.

I will now conclude by saying a few words with respect to that affair of covenanting that is now under consideration.

As I have said before, it appears to me that [a visible people of God on some occasions are called publicly to renew their covenant with God].

<!-- p. 518 -->

However, I would have all act freely. Only I will give one caution: take heed of spiritual [pride][^062-note3] in the affair. I'll tell you wherein will be your temptation to spiritual [pride][^062-note4] in this affair: it may arise from a loathness to appear singular or to be distinguished. And so be engaged to have many with you or to overthrow[^062-note5] the whole design.

Whatever your minds be as to yourself, take heed you don't do the devil's service by hindering others.

[^062-note1]: MS: “object against any.” The phrase has been treated as an intended deletion.

[^062-note2]: In the MS, JE accidentally listed this heading as the second subpoint under Proposition IV.

[^062-note3]: MS: “sp.”

[^062-note4]: MS: “sp.”

[^062-note5]: Read “or you will overthrow.”

## Keeping the Presence of God

<!-- p. 519 -->

In his recollections, Samuel Hopkins tells of an encounter that Edwards had in 1742, following the Buell awakening, with a parishioner in his congregation, a person of a “warm temperament” who was “carried away by feelings.” The man confessed to Edwards that he was distressed by his pastor's “moderation and quiet. I fear that some of your people will continue to sleep till they fall into hell, and I can scarcely refrain, at times, from rising in the midst of your service, and calling on them to awake.” Edwards' response was indicative of his increasingly negative attitude towards lay enthusiasm: “If you should, sir, I shall request the tithing-man to take you by the hand and lead you out of the house.”[^063-note1]

In *Seasons of Ingathering*, Edwards had energetically defended the recent awakenings against critics. Now, in *Keeping the Presence of God*, preached for the colony-wide fast of April 1742, he assumes the role he would play more and more: though no less energetic a supporter and encourager of the movement, he himself becomes critical of its excesses— supposed visions and revelations, boasting of religious experiences, and censoriousness. Edwards has been witnessing the unraveling of the revival, precisely what he had warned against the previous month in *Renewing Our Covenant* but to no avail. Just as he had seen seven years ago, the subjects of revivals were exhibiting signs of self-confidence, security, rashness, disrespect of authority, and dissension. It was time for him to speak out, even if it meant putting a damper on religious zeal. At times in this sermon, as when he dismisses some persons' “great discoveries” as “little else but strong impulses, beats of animal spirits, great imaginations,” Edwards outdoes even Charles Chauncy in his analysis and condemnation of revival excesses. One is less likely to imagine Edwards speaking this way in Boston, where he would have felt compelled to defend the revivals more strenuously; but he could do so in his own pulpit, where he was freer to assume different “voices” as occasion required. The colony-wide fast was one such occasion.

Edwards must deal directly with several urgent problems. His tone imparts

<!-- p. 520 -->

a sense that the events he is describing are happening as he speaks— even that the very thing he is trying so desperately to keep, the presence of the Holy Spirit, is slipping through his church's fingers. First and foremost, he must strike the right note: encouraging converts to seek more of God's presence— “high transports” and “flights”— while coming down hard on errors that have cropped up. He begins by asserting that many of those who had much of God's presence in the past eventually forsook God. He then launches into a catalogue of texts spanning virtually the entirety of Scripture (doubtless he could have provided more) to prove his point. Why has this backsliding occurred? Because of a lack of obedience to God and lack of dependence on him. The solution is to continue to seek God, and to do so in the proper manner, which is in earnest prayer and in other traditional religious “duties.” Once having obtained God's presence, converts too often felt satisfied with themselves and confident of their eternal state; Edwards counters by pointing out that true believers exhibit proper humility and know that they “are vastly short of the perfection that is to be sought after.” Then comes an interesting objection: How can we go on seeking God's presence when our bodily frames can no longer bear it? Here is the first explicit reference to revival behavior, namely, physical manifestations such as fits and trances, as seen in Sarah Pierpont Edwards' own experience earlier that year. In reply, Edwards asserts that believers must go on nonetheless and leave the care of the body to God, “the Author of it.”

In the second head of the Doctrine, Edwards describes how converts can retain God's presence. He expresses his advice in the negative, giving reasons why the Spirit's influence has dissipated. He names spiritual pride, the need for circumspection among converts, and the habit of those who have experienced God to “come to a stop in striving.” We cannot expect to have God's continued presence with us, Edwards states, if we go “in our by-paths”; we must walk in the way God has directed. Both converts and unregenerate men can use their natural powers as well as “improve special assistance” from God.

The Application explicitly attributes the errors Edwards has identified to the people of Northampton. Converts must “be sensible you are not out of danger of the devil and a corrupt and deceitful heart.” Strict watch and care must be exercised. Spiritual pride— the “chief root of all the extravagances”— dominates his concerns. Some who have reputations as “eminent saints” and are the admiration of others are puffed up with their own importance. Others are censorious, presumptuous, think they are above instruction, or are overly bold in expressing their religious experiences or

<!-- p. 521 -->

overly confident in estimating their own spiritual states. For Edwards, this demonstrates an unfortunate reality of awakenings and of religious experience in general: there is a mixture of the spiritual and the carnal that leads to a “degenerating of experiences.” In this regard the devil is especially active, playing upon the pride and imaginations of converts to make them think they are something more than they actually are, or can do something they actually cannot. One example is that people think they can “utterly root out and abolish all natural affections,” for Edwards a foolhardy brand of perfectionism. In response, he instructs his listeners not to “go beyond the rule” of God's word and our “present state.” Do not intrude upon the minister's prerogative to correct “religious offenders,” he insists. Instead, engage in religious conversation with neighbors and in secret fasting. To “Christian societies” like Northampton, Edwards warns: Beware of human imagination and claims of “immediate testimony” of saving faith. He even brings in Thomas Shepard to refute the notion of an “absolute promise” conveyed by God to the mind of the believer.

This sermon provided Edwards with an outline, and even some specific passages, for *Some Thoughts Concerning the Revival*, which he would write late in 1742. For example, Edwards could draw at some length from the sermon in writing Part IV, “Showing What Things Are to Be Corrected or Avoided in Promoting This Work, or in Our Behavior in It.” In the sermon as in the treatise, Edwards locates the causes of errors in three principal things: spiritual pride, wrong principles, and Satan's delusions. Parallels between sermon and treatise are provided in the footnotes.

Of particular interest here is Edwards' use of Thomas Shepard's writings at several points toward the end of the sermon. Conjuring the name of one of the most revered Puritan theologians of conversion was no doubt an effective way for Edwards to bolster his arguments. For Edwards to do so in the pulpit was even more remarkable. If we are to judge by Edwards' printed works, he seems to have gained an increasing respect for Shepard's writings, especially as he began to speak out more against Antinomian behavior— the very thing against which Shepard had inveighed during his own time. In addition, Shepard was accorded great respect by the pious of New England, as evidenced by the reprinting of several of his works in the 1740s.[^063-note2] In *Religious Affections* Edwards was to cite Shepard seventy-five times, second only to the Bible.[^063-note3]

<!-- p. 522 -->

*Keeping the Presence of God* illustrates two trends in Edwards' sermonic writing. First, he tended to deliver the substance, if not the exact content, of treatises in sermon form first. This was a habit of his going back to *Justification by Faith Alone*. The second trend, however, was something new Beginning with the waning of the Great Awakening, he devoted more and more time to the production of treatises. He increasingly perceived his audience as larger than his local setting. This sermon charts that shift. It also reflects the growing distance between Edwards and his congregation as each became disenchanted with the other. With a critical edge softened by a lingering pastoral and personal concern that was natural after fifteen years, this sermon sets the tone for his final years at Northampton.

* * *

The manuscript consists of twenty duodecimo leaves. Edwards inscribed it at the top of page 1, “Fast April 1742.” The text is an example of Edwards' later outlined sermonic form: its pages are divided into two columns, with each column further divided into smaller boxes. Within these, Edwards wrote, in or more less complete fashion, the major points and ideas for the sermons followed by telegraphic subpoints on which he could expand extemporaneously.

<!-- p. 523 -->

[^063-note1]: William Patten, *Reminiscences of the Late Rev. Samuel Hopkins* (Boston, 1843), 26–27.

[^063-note2]: E.g. *The Saints Jewel* (Boston, 1743), *Sound Believer* (Boston, 1736 and 1742), *Three Valuable Pieces* (Boston, 1747), and *Certain Select Cases Resolved* (Boston, 1747).

[^063-note3]: *Works of Jonathan Edwards*, *2*, *Religious Affections*, ed. John E. Smith (New Haven, Yale Univ. Press, 1959), 54.

## Keeping the Presence of God

> And he went out to meet Asa, and said unto him, Hear ye me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin; The Lord is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you.

II Chronicles 15:1–2.[Azariah was sent by God to the leaders of Judah] after they and the people had enjoyed rest and quietness, just after exceeding great prosperity and an extraordinary manifestation of God's favor in answer to prayer.

1. Who they are that Prophet is sent with a message to.

2. The importance.

3. [The] message itself.

(1) A promise.

(2) A threatening.

#### Doctrine.

#### The way for those that have the presence of God not to lose it, is to take heed to themselves as to these two things, viz. that they don't forsake him, and they still seek him.

In handling this subject I would, first, particularly consider and explain these two things recommended in the doctrine; and secondly, I would show that this is the way for those that have the presence of God not to lose it.

I. I would particularly consider and explain these two things, that those that have the presence of God ought to do.

*First*. They must take heed to themselves that they don't forsake God.

[Those that have the presence of God are] apt to forsake God.

Hence 'tis so exceedingly and abundantly insisted on in God's Word that we should take great heed to ourselves, with earnest resolution and

<!-- p. 524 -->

diligence and a strict watch, that we don't depart from God. I shall mention a considerable number:

Deuteronomy 4:9, “Take heed to thyself, and keep thy soul diligently, lest thou forget the things which thine eyes have seen, and lest they depart from thy heart all the days of thy life: but teach them thy sons, and thy sons' sons.”

Deuteronomy 5:28-29, “And the Lord heard the voice of your words, when ye spake unto me; and the Lord said unto me, I have heard the voice of the words of this people, which they have spoken unto thee: they have well said all that they have spoken. O that there were such an heart in them that they would fear me, and keep all my commandments always, that it might be well with them, and with their children for ever!”

Chapter Deuteronomy 10:12-13, “And now, Israel, what doth the Lord thy God require of thee, but to fear the Lord thy God, to walk in all his ways, and to love him, and to serve the Lord thy God with all thy heart and with all thy soul, to keep the commandments of the Lord, and his statutes, which I command thee this day for thy good?”

Job 23:11, “My foot hath held his steps, his way have I kept, and not declined.”

Job 27:6, “My righteousness I hold fast, and will not let it go: my heart shall not reproach me so long as I live.”

Proverbs 4:23, “Keep thy heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life.”

John 15:4, “And abide in me.”

Acts 11:22-23, “Barnabas exhorted them all, that with purpose of heart they would cleave unto the Lord.”

1 Corinthians 15:58, “be ye steadfast, unmoveable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, forasmuch as ye know that your labor is not in vain in the Lord.”

1 Corinthians 16:13, “stand fast, quit ye like men, be strong.”

2 Corinthians 11:2-03, “I am jealous over you with a godly jealousy.”

Ephesians 6:11-12, “put ye on the whole armor of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.”

Philippians 4:1, “stand fast in the Lord, my dearly beloved.”

1 Thessalonians 3:8, “now we live, if ye stand fast in the Lord.”

2 Thessalonians 2:15-17, “Therefore, brethren, stand fast, and hold the traditions which ye have been taught, whether by word, or our epistle. Now our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God, even our Father, which hath loved

<!-- p. 525 -->

us, and hath given us everlasting consolation and good hope through grace comfort your hearts, and stablish you in every good word and work.”

Hebrews 2:1-03, “Therefore we ought to give the more earnest heed to the things which we have heard, lest at any time we should let them slip. For if the word spoken by angels was steadfast, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward; how shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation; which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord, and was confirmed unto us by them that heard him.”

Hebrews 3:6, “But Christ as a son over his own house; whose house are we, if we hold fast the confidence and the rejoicing of the hope firm unto the end.”

And Hebrews 4:14, “Seeing then that we have a great high priest, that is passed into the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our profession.”

Hebrews 10:23, “Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering.”[^064-note1]

Hebrews 12, at [the] beginning, “Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us.”

Persons may depart from God in either of these two respects: first, as to obedience to him; second, as to dependence on him.

1. As to obedience to him.

They that have the presence of God should take heed to themselves that they walk closely with God.

Keep their eye on him, on all his commandments.

Keep their eye on their hearts.

Keep their eye on their ways, to observe all by-paths. Look straight forward.

Keep their eye on the snares [they are] encompassed with.

Keep their eye on God's providence.

Keep their eye on Christ's example, on the precepts of Christianity, [on the] things [of] the Christian spirit. Always be mindful of the holy eye of God, of the strict account [they must give].

Keep hold on the hand of Christ.

2. Those that have the presence of God should take heed to themselves that they don't depart from God as to dependence on him.

<!-- p. 526 -->

*Second*. They that have the presence of God ought to continue to seek him.

Not only take heed not to go from him that they have found, but still seek him as though they had not found him. Those that have most of the presence of God should continue earnestly to seek God still as much as if they had not found him. So the Apostle, who had found God probably in as high a degree as ever: “Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:12).

They have found him but in part. [So they should] seek him as much as when they had not found him at all, as before conversion, or when under desertion.

[They should seek him] earnestly and laboriously and constantly, every day. In the following things:

(1) In earnest desires, not resting in past attainments, though never so high.

(2) Humble and earnest prayers.

(3) By renewedly relinquishing all other things for the blessings that are sought, and doing it more and more.

(4) All manner of duties should be performed in such a manner as that therein they should seek God.

Thus God should still be sought by those that have most of the presence of God, and the greatest degree of the manifestations of his favor and smiles.

So David commanded that it should be in Israel. 1 Chronicles 22:19, “Now therefore set your heart and soul [to seek the Lord your God].” The following reasons may be given why:

(1) Because those that have obtained most are vastly short of the perfection that is to be sought after.

(2) Those that have obtained most of that which is of the right kind, they see most how they fall short.

(3) They have more than others to excite their desires and appetites after perfection.

(4) They are under greater obligations than others to aim at perfection.

(5) They have more light to see their obligation.

(6) God has given 'em more strength and more talents. The more talents [they have] to improve, the more business and the greater work they have, the more to take care of, [and the] more strength [to do so].

(7) We are commanded to “seek the Lord while he may be found,” and

<!-- p. 527 -->

“to call [upon him while he is near” (Isaiah 55:6)]. He is near in the highest sense.

*Obj*. Why should persons that have most of the presence of God seek more when some of them have more already than the frame of their bodies can well bare?

*Ans*. 1. God's people must seek that they may come up to the rule God has given, and leave the care of the frame of the body to the Author of it. When Christ came to the disciples after they had been toiling all night, {at his word they let down the net and enclosed a great multitude of fish (Luke 5:5)}.

[*Ans*.] 2.[^064-note2] The great effect on the body is not only owing to the degree of the presence of God, but to many other things that are accidental: the particular manner [of it], the newness [of it], or other circumstances causing surprise. These things are found in the experience of some that have been very much overcome in their bodily strength.

'Tis probable the days are coming when God's people will have vastly more of heaven in their souls, without so great an effect on their bodily frame. That matter may safely be left with God. He does take care; none have yet died.

Thus those that have the presence of God should take great heed to themselves that they don't forsake God, and earnestly to seek him. So did Asa and the children of Judah and Benjamin, according to the word of Azariah in the text. See the ninth verse of the context and onward.

I come now to the

[II.] Second thing proposed, viz. to show that this is the way for those that have the presence of God not to lose [it].

Two things: first, God would not depart from them; second, if not, [they] may expect to lose [it].

1. If these things were observed by those that have much of the presence of God, they would not lose [it]. There is a promise in the text: “[The Lord is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you].”

I don't intend that it would always be alike with [everyone]. [There is] much more encouragement of the continuance of God's presence to those that have it in the use of these means, than of the bestowment of it on those that have never obtained it— though the latter seldom fail. There is a vast difference. As 'tis in temporal things: [it is] much easier,

<!-- p. 528 -->

with a care, to preserve a state of health than to recover a broken constitution.

There are innumerable absolute promises, or promises that imply it How many promises [are there] in Scripture of God's hearing prayer, [of his] being found of them that seek him? The promises of giving to him that hath, of preserving his saints, not forsaking them, promises of feeding them that they shall not lack bread, [that] waters shall be found, [and their] wanting no good thing?

God is not a wilderness or a land of darkness. God is a good father, not wanting to his children. Christ is a good shepherd. The prodigal son would not have wanted bread.

There are many promises of increase. “[The righteous shall] flourish like [the] palm tree” [Psalms 92:12], “[Now there was a long war between the house of Saul and the house of David: but David] waxed stronger and stronger, [and the house of Saul waxed weaker and weaker” (2 Samuel 3:1)].

Those that have much of the presence of God han't only far greater advantages to have it still, and have it more abundantly than natural persons have to seek {the presence of God}, but than saints under desertion. [They have] greater strength, greater assistance. God is nigher to 'em. It is a time of favor with them. 'Tis an easy thing for them to keep the presence of God comparatively.

If they don't forsake him, 'tis not his manner to forsake them. Where are the men that have[^064-note3] had much of the presence of [God], that have lost it and fallen into a cold dark state, unless it was by means of their forsaking God in some of those ways that have been mentioned— giving way to some lust, spiritual pride, worldliness, sloth, or some other hateful [lust]. You that have lost [it], you can't one of you say that you lost it in this way of thus taking earnest heed to keep close to God and still earnestly seeking him.

The three chief reasons why persons' great light and comfort have lasted but a little while, but they have {quickly lost it}, have been these:

(1) Rising of spiritual pride.

(2) Not being sensible of need of vigilance and circumspection at such seasons.

(3) Their coming to a stop in striving, as though now they had apprehended. If persons stop, they won't stop long before they go back. As a

<!-- p. 529 -->

person's running up a stream: though the stream ben't so strong, yet there is a stream to stop [him], and a strong one, till we get to heaven. 'Tis up hill till we actually get there.

2. If persons that have the presence of God don't attend these things, they may expect to lose God's presence. If you forsake him, he will forsake you. [You] can't expect to have the presence of God any other way than in a way of walking with him. [You can't expect to] have[^064-note4] the presence of God unless it be in his ways, not in our by— paths. God has given us faculties to be exercised, talents to be improved, ordinances to be used, commands to be attended [to].

Abundant experience shows that, for want of these things, God's people lose the tokens of his presence.

*Obj*. We can't keep close to God, and seek him when we have his presence, without his help.

Thus persons are ready to lay the blame of their losing {the presence of God} to God.

*Answ*. 1. There are many things we can do with no more than common assistance.

[*Answ*.] 2. Those that have the special presence of God, have special assistance present with them. If they will exert themselves as they may do, they can do a great deal more.

[*Answ*.] 3. If they therefore do these two things— be faithful in using their natural power, and in improving that special assistance they have— God won't leave 'em. When souls lose God's presence, their calamities begin through want of daily using these.

### Application.

[*Use*] I. Hence we may learn the reason why formerly persons' first experiences and comforts used commonly to be the greatest. It is a shameful thing that [it] is so. It is not agreeable to the method laid out in Scripture.

God's people seemed to have been strangely in the dark. God seems heretofore to have hid from the eyes of his people the way of their duty.

[*Use*] II. Hence those that heretofore had the presence of God and have lost it, may see what they have to repent of and condemn themselves for.

*Use* III. Of *Exhortation* to those that have lately been favored with much of the sensible and sweet tokens of the presence of God, to take earnest heed to themselves in those things spoken of in the doctrine.

<!-- p. 530 -->

*First*. Take heed you don't forsake God. Here I would particularly request of those that have lately been favored with much of the sweet tokens of God's presence, to hearken to me in the following things that may be for their direction and help to prevent their departing from God:

1. Be sensible you are not out of danger of the devil and a corrupt and deceitful heart, even in your highest flights and best frames. It is a great mistake [to think] that there no danger of going astray because God is near you. Indeed, there is great encouragement in it that you shall be succeeded in a way of vigilance and circumspection. But to think that even then you han't need of the greatest watch and care, and are not in great danger without it, is presumption. 'Tis a presumption by which many herein have been woefully answered. Many persons, through want of a sense of danger in such circumstances, and so neglecting, {depart from God}. 'Tis one principal means of persons' losing the presence [of God]: they have grown secure.

As long as [we are] in this world, we are in a world where Satan reigns, in the enemy's country. [We are] not out of his reach. And though God be willing to defend and protect, yet he expects great care and labor. This whole life is appointed as a state of labor, as a race and battle. 'Tis a great mistake [to think] that the devil can't come in. I have known it in abundance of instances: the devil has come in, even in the midst of the most excellent frames. It may seem a great mystery, but no greater than that the ark should be delivered over,[^064-note5] [that the Philistines should] come into the temple at Jerusalem and carry 'em into house of their god.

Christ [was] taken and carried into the wilderness immediately after the [descent of the] Holy Ghost. Christ in the heart of saints is liable to [be] carried captive even quickly after the descent of Holy Ghost and [a] voice from heaven saying, “This is my beloved Son.”

Therefore be vigilant, you that live in high degrees of light, you who have lately had the Holy Ghost like a dove [descend upon you]. That[^064-note6] direction of Christ to his disciples is never out of date in this world, Luke 21:36, “Watch and pray always, that you may be accounted worthy to escape all these things, and to stand”; and that, 1 Peter 5:8, “Be sober, be vigilant.” Ephesians 5:15-17, “walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is.”

<!-- p. 531 -->

2.[^064-note7] Let me particularly urge you to watch exceedingly against spiritual pride.

(1) There is great danger. I know great degrees of the spiritual presence of God tend greatly to restrain and keep down pride. But yet 'tis not all grace. And though in such cases there be much to restrain one way, so there is much to tempt and provoke it another. Temptations in such cases are often exceeding great. To be highly loved and exalted of God tends to feed pride exceedingly, if there be any left. The apostle Paul himself was not out of danger (2 Corinthians 12:7).

Seeing others admire, [and] especially being much resorted to and respected as an eminent saint, better than others, [tends to feed pride].

(2) Consider that no corruption is so apt to work as pride. It was the first sin. [It] lies deepest, [is] most active.

(3) [There is] no corruption that has so many and so secret ways of working. The image of the devil chiefly consists in it. And [there is] no sin so like him for secrecy, subtilty, appearing in so many shapes, coming unsuspected and undiscovered, appearing as an angel of light.

If it is mortified and suppressed in one shape, yet it rises in another. It appears often under the disguise of great humility. It takes occasion to rise from everything, even real grace, yea, real humility.

It is a sin that has many lives. If you kill it, yet it will live still. If you think it is all gone, yet 'tis there still. If you seem to destroy it, yet there it is still.

There are a great many kinds of it, that lie in different forms and shapes, that corrupt the heart and lie one under another, like the coats of an onion; if you pull off one, there is another underneath.

You had need to have the greatest watch imaginable with respect to this matter, and to cry most earnestly to the great searcher of hearts: for he that trusts his own heart is a fool.

(4) Nothing is more hateful and abominable, nothing so contrary to the spirit of the gospel. [Pride is] the sin of the devils.

(5) Nothing is so pernicious in its consequences. The Spirit is very often quenched by it. 'Tis frequently the means of persons' losing the comfortable presence of God. In some that have been exalted high, the consequences have been most woeful. The devil commonly comes in at the door in all the delusions that zealous persons are led away with. [Pride is] me chief root of all the extravagances {we have lately seen}.

Therefore strive that you may be kept humble. Persons are never so safe

<!-- p. 532 -->

as when kept truly humble and dependent, [as] little children. [And they are] never so much in danger as when spiritual pride rules.

But for your better direction in this matter, I would mention some of the ways of spiritual pride's working:

*1*.[^064-note8] When it makes 'em censorious. [It makes 'em] talk in a censorious way, condemning others about [them], forgetting themselves. [It makes 'em] think much about others' deadness more than their own.

Humility makes it natural to esteem others better. Evangelical hypocrites pretend greatly to advance Christ, but are bitter and censorious (Shepard).[^064-note9]

*2*. [Spiritual pride] makes it seem natural to take a great deal upon 'em, as if they were the persons.

*3*. It adds fierceness and bitterness to zeal.

*4*. When persons begin to think they don't need instruction.

*5*. An unsuitable boldness and confidence. [They] describe what is the way, what is the truly Christian spirit.

The most excellent experience works that way, as experience as well as Scripture shows. [Spiritual pride works in] some that have been carried the highest of any whatsoever.

3.[^064-note10] Take heed of a gradual degenerating of experiences from spiritual to carnal. There is such a thing. The Apostle speaks of it (Galatians 3:3). I have seen it in abundance of instances: after experiences are come to a great height, they begin to degenerate. [The persons' experiences are] less and less pure and spiritual.

It comes to pass thus in all experiences that Christians have in this world. There is a mixture. There is something natural and something spiritual. It is just like the blasting of fruit through the excess of moisture.[^064-note11] Through want of distinguishing and want of watchfulness, the natural part increases and the spiritual decreases. The devil ventures the natural part to increase.

There is often a mixture of three things with great discoveries: natural passion, a degree of secret spiritual pride, and imagination. The devil

<!-- p. 533 -->

works with these. And the person, being insensible of his danger and through ignorance not distinguishing, by and by their great discoveries come to little else but strong impulses, beats of animal spirits, great imaginations. And the person, because he is violently moved, still imagines he has great discoveries, and spiritual pride then is risen to a great height. Long observation confirms me in this.

The[^064-note12] Apostle probably has respect to something of this nature, 2 Corinthians 11:2-03, “I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ. But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.” The devil is too subtil for us. Eve thought she was getting higher in knowledge when she was eating the forbidden fruit. [She thought she was] going to be like a god.

Take heed to yourselves, that your experiences don't gradually degenerate, that they may be, on the contrary, more and more pure and unmixed.

4. Consider whereby any of you have formerly departed from God, and so lost his comfortable presence.

5. Remember that a departure from God commonly comes upon persons like a chronical distemper.

6.[^064-note13] If you would not expose yourself to be led aside by the devil, don't affect to go beyond the rule. [Don't affect to go] beyond the present state. [Don't affect] utterly to root out and abolish all natural affections.[^064-note14] [Don't affect] to pray no more for near relations than others.[^064-note15] [They go beyond the rule who] neglect to take care of their families to spend all their time in religion.

7.[^064-note16] Don't spend much time in disputing about religious offenders. 'Tis none of your business to go about to regulate disorders. Take heed that while you blame others for invading the office of a minister, you don't invade it yourself. I desire you would come to me and talk with me. I claim it as what belongs to me to regulate.

8.[^064-note17] Let nothing that is said against high transports discourage the highest degree of a spiritual sense. Be filled as full as you will. Let the effect on

<!-- p. 534 -->

your bodies be what they [will]. Ephesians 5:18, “be not drunk with wine.” Canticles 5:1, “eat, O friends, drink, yea, drink [abundantly].”

9. Help one another in religious conversation. How beautiful [it is] to see a company talking together of [the] things of the glory of Christ. When you meet together accidentally, if your spirits are solemnized by religious conversation, [then] sing praises.

10.[^064-note18] Don't altogether neglect the duty of secret fasting. There are many special occasions they will find that are greatly engaged in religion. Matthew 6:16-18, “Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They shall have their reward. But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; that thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly.”

I have now told you the way in which you may have the presence of Christ continued, and may have it more and more. I come now to the

*Second* branch of this exhortation, to exhort those that have the presence of God to the second thing mentioned {in the doctrine}, viz. earnestly seek God. Thus you that have found Christ should hold Christ fast and not let him go. As the spouse says, Canticles 3 at the beginning, “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth: I sought him, but I found him not. I will rise now, and go about the city in the streets, and in the broad ways I will seek him whom my soul loveth.”

*Use* III of *Direction* to both natural men and Christians.

[*First*. To] natural men, to keep the common influences of the Spirit of God. [They should not] rest in what they have obtained [or in the] degree of earnestness they have.

*Second*. To Christians at a sorrowful distance from Christ.

*Third*. To Christian societies. Beware of false experiences.

1. Imagination. (Shepard.)[^064-note19]

2. Immediate testimony. [It is] without evidence.

Mr. Shepard does abundantly insist on the delusion of such as suppose that they have an absolute promise made to them in particular as the first ground of their faith, and thus get their assurance by way of immediate testimony from heaven, without any reflex act or having any work of the

<!-- p. 535 -->

Spirit in themselves.[^064-note20] Men don't know that they are godly by believing that they are godly. We know many things by faith. Hebrews 11:3, “By faith we understand that the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.” “Faith is the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1). Thus men know the trinity of persons in the Godhead, that Jesus is the Son of God, that he that believes in him will have eternal life, the resurrection of the dead. And if God should tell a saint that he hath grace, he might know it by believing the word of God. But it is not in this way that godly men know that they have grace. It is not revealed in the Word, and the Spirit of God doth not testify it to particular persons. Some think that the Spirit doth testify it to some, and they ground it on Romans 8:16, “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God.” They think the Spirit reveals it by giving an inward testimony to it, and some godly men think they have had experience of it, but they may easily mistake. When the Spirit of God doth eminently stir up a spirit of faith and sheds abroad the love of God in the heart, it is easy to mistake it for a testimony. And that is not the meaning of Paul's words. The Spirit discovers the grace of God in Christ, and thereby draws forth special actings of faith and love; which are evidential, but it doth not work in way of testimony. If God do but help us to receive the revelations in the Word, we shall have comfort enough without new revelations.

3. A seeing Christ in his love as independent of a seeing him in his glory.[^064-note21] Shepard denies this.[^064-note22]

## Appendix: Dated Sermons, January 1739–December 1742

<!-- p. 537 -->

The following list records the extant sermons that Edwards preached from January 1739 through December 1742. Sermons are listed according to the original Schafer number (named for Thomas A. Schafer, who first arranged the sermons and put in chronological order the early, undated ones), followed by the title, if printed, or by the Scripture text, a statement of the doctrine, date of composition, and any other relevant information, if unpublished. Sermons delivered in the same month are listed in canonical order. In some cases, more precise dating of a sermon consequent to its original numbering may be noted in its description. Sermon texts followed by an asterisk are printed in previous editions. Unless stated otherwise, the manuscript is in the Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University.

499. Psalms 24:7-10. “Jesus Christ entering into his glory after his suffering was a sight worthy to be beheld with great admiration.” Jan. 1739.

500. Matthew 23:15. “Wicked men are the children of hell.” Jan. 1739.

501. Luke 4:38-39. “When persons are restored from dangerous sickness, their business should be to serve and minister to him that has restored them.” Jan. 1739.An unidentified epidemic hit Northampton in late 1738. In October, Ebenezer Hunt recorded in his diary that “Pelatiah Holbrook died after a sickness of 5 weeks, Oliver Warner was sick about 3 weeks ([Hunt's] Apprentices) & I was unable to work about a fortnight.” Judd MSS, v. 1, Mass. Series, “Abstracts & Extracts from Deac. Ebenezer Hunts Journal,” p. 24.

502. Luke 6:48. “They that would build an hope of heaven, well should dig deep and lay their foundation on a rock.” Jan. 1739.

503. Ephesians 1:10. “Jesus Christ is the great medium and head of union in whom all elect creatures in heaven and earth are united to God and to one another.” Originally two lectures.The MS is a fragment. Only two leaves remain of the first lecture; the second commences on the third leaf with the date, “Feb. 1738, 9, ” at the top.

<!-- p. 538 -->

504. Genesis 3:11. “The act of our first father in eating the forbidden fruit was a very heinous act.” Feb. 1739. Four sermons.

505. Acts 9:13-15. “'Tis so with respect to God's bestowment of saving mercy on some persons, that there is no other account to be given of it but that he will show mercy.” Feb. 1739.

506. 1 John 3:15. “When a man is converted, eternal life is begun in him.” Feb. 1739. Repreached May 1755.

507. Psalms 66:18(a). “'Tis in vain for any to expect to have their prayers heard as long as they continue in the allowance of sin.” Mar. 29, 1739. Fast.

508. Isaiah 51:8. “The work of redemption is a work that God carries on from the fall of man to the end of the world.” A series of thirty sermons in twelve booklets. Mar.–Aug. 1739.First published in Edinburgh in 1774 under the title, *A History of the Work of Redemption*. See *Works*, *9*.

509. Matthew 25:46. “The misery of the wicked in hell will be absolutely eternal.” Apr. 1739.

510. *Christ the Spiritual Sun* (Malachi 4:2). May 1739.

511. Proverbs 4:7. “An interest in Christ should be sought above all things in the world.” June 1739.

512. Acts 6:1-03. “The main business of a deacon, by Christ's appointment, is to take care of the distribution of the church's charity for the outward supply of those that need.” June 14, 1739.

513. Luke 1:77-79 (a). “How a sinner that has offended God should be reconciled to him again and restored to his favor, could be known no other way but by divine revelation.” July 1739, repreached Nov. 1756. Lecture delivered at New Haven.

514. *The Means and Ends of Excommunication* (1 Corinthians 5:11). * July 22, 1739, on the excommunication of Mrs. Bridgman. Dwight ed., *6*, 569–80.

515. 2 Corinthians 8:5. “We ought to give our own selves to Jesus Christ, to yield and devote ourselves to God.” July 1739.

516. Romans 12:4-08. “The offices that Christ has appointed in his church, do respect either the souls or bodies of men.” Aug. 19, 1739, “On occasion of the ordination of the deacons.”The members installed that day as deacons were Stephen Wright, Noah Cook, and Ebenezer Pomeroy, Jr.

517. Psalms 19:12. “'Tis an exceeding hard thing for men to be sensible of those things in themselves that are sinful and offensive to God.” Sept. 1739.

518. Luke 9:61-62. “Looking back after persons have once engaged is

especially disagreeable and mischievous in religion.” Sept. 1739.

### Undated Sermons

693a. Genesis 19:17. “'Tis needful for those that seek an escape from God's wrath to avoid these things: lingering, looking back and trusting in anything short of the true refuge.” C. 1741. According to Ebenezer Parkman's diary, Edwards preached this sermon at Westborough, Feb. 2, 1742 (Tracy, *Great Awakening*, 204).

693b. Genesis 25:29-34. Theme: Esau selling his birthright. C. 1741–42. MS at Andover Newton Theological School.

693c. Psalms 1:3 (a). “Christ is to the heart of a saint like a river to the root of a tree that is planted by it.” C. 1742. MS at Andover Newton Theological School.

693d. Psalms 18:25. No MS. Ebenezer Parkman records in his diary that JE preached on this text at Grafton or Sutton, Feb. 1, 1742 (Tracy, *Great Awakening*, 204).

693e. Proverbs 27:1. “We ought to behave ourselves every day as though we had no dependence on any other day.” C. 1739–41.

693f. John 12:23. No MS. According to Parkman's diary, JE preached on this text at Leicester, Jan. 28, 1742 (Tracy, *Great Awakening*, 204).

693g. John 12:32. Three MS fragments [c. 1739–41], apparently parts of an Application for one sermon, rewritten for repreaching, or parts of Applications for more than one sermon. The first contains Uses I–III, beginning, “I. Call upon and exhort all that are in a natural condition now at this time to turn from their sins to God.” The second fragment contains another Use III: “I would apply myself to such as have an interest in the Lord Jesus Christ.” Fragment three, dating from the fall or winter of 1739–40, contains the last part of a first Use; p. 8 begins “2dly. Consider how excellent a state you are invited to.” Parkman states that JE preached on this text at Westborough, Feb. 2, 1742 (Tracy, *Great Awakening*, 204).

693h. Hebrews 2:3. “They that neglect so great salvation as is offered in the gospel, do bring themselves into exceeding danger of damnation.” No MS; copy at Andover Newton Theological School.
